title: Everything Detroit Lions QB Jared Goff Said After Panthers Loss
full_text:
Here is everything Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff said, following a Sunday Night Football loss to the Carolina Panthers.
If he felt like the team was going to pull out a win towards the end of the game?
"Yeah, I did. I thought we just needed that first score to cut it to one score. I had the drive before we scored on that I thought we would get it done on; we didn't. But just getting the ball with two minutes and a chance to win it is all we want, and we had the chance. Feels like we, I, let us down a little bit not scoring there at the end to win the game."
On if self-inflicted wounds have been a theme this season and how to work through those?
"Yeah, too many penalties, right? Too many pre-snap stuff. Starts with me, communication and the whole thing, just making sure guys are on the same page and being a little cleaner there. We had a couple holding calls or something, a couple post-snap penalties, those are going to happen, but the pre-snap stuff can't happen.
Iff the self-inflicted wounds are surprising?
"Yeah, maybe something I need to spend a little more time on."
On having a 2-2 record after the first four games
"Yeah, the whole season's ahead of us with 13 games left now, and I've done some good things. This one's going to sting certainly because we had our chances to win it. But yeah, whole season ahead of us and a lot of ball ahead of us and a lot of things to get right. I know one thing, we're going to stick together and stay insulated in our bubble and lean on each other and make it right."
On getting wide receivers Isaac TeSlaa and Jameson Williams involved in the deep ball and if that’s a positive takeaway from the game?
"Yeah, a couple of them. It was good to hit. There's probably a couple more we would like to have, but it's good to hit.
On if the run game inefficiency tonight and against Buffalo have any kind of commonality?
"No, other than it wasn't as efficient as we would like. I don't know. I would have to watch it to give you a better answer, but no, it wasn't great ."

title: Former Detroit Lions Trash Defense, Secondary
full_text:
Two former Detroit Lions are not fans of the current defense.
During another letdown performance by defensive coordinator Kelvin's Sheppard's unit against the Carolina Panthers, former cornerbacks Darius Slay and Jerry Jacobs took to social media to share their assessment of the secondary.
Slay shared, "Lions I got a lot of love for ya'll but man this defense is bad bad."
Jacobs pointed out, "Over the years I was there our secondary wasn't solid either. But boy ole boy I'll be lying if I say this secondary they have rn is hard to watch."
Many supporters recall Kindle Vildor being a veteran defensive back that played with Jacobs. After a supporter called out the coaching staff, Jacobs shared, "Kindle better than all the corners on the depth chart rn let’s be honest!!!"
Lions I got a lot of love for y’all but man this defense is bad bad😮‍💨
Over the years I was there our secondary wasn’t solid either🤣💯 but boy ole boy I’ll be lying if I say this secondary they have rn is hard to watch🤷🏾‍♂️
The vibe in the locker room, after a disappointing 32-26 road loss, was reportedly one of frustration.
"I just feel like, we’re just not winning. Like we’re not doing things that I know we can do, and I don’t know. So it’s, we got to figure it out now, and again, it’s the NFL. The person you’re going against, it’s his job, too. It’s his career," said linebacker Jack Campbell. "It’s how can I win, and how can I win my one-on-one? How can I make my play even if it’s not my gap? How can I get to the ball ? Get the guy down? Honestly, at the end of the day, go get the ball. We’re not doing that.”
Sheppard is currently squarely on the hot seat, but still has support, for the time-being, of head coach Dan Campbell and the roser.
“I have the utmost faith in him. I think we have the utmost faith in him. But we have to evolve as a defense, and we have to grow," said Aidan Hutchinson. "We can’t keep putting our offense in these shootout-like games, because it just puts stress on them, man.
"We just got to do better as a unit. I think we all support Shep fully. Yeah, man, we got to get a win next week.”

title: Dan Campbell Must Send Clear Message By Firing Kelvin Sheppard
full_text:
The Detroit Lions couldn't have stopped a nosebleed if they tried Sunday night against Bryce Young and the Carolina Panthers.
Just as the Lions have done to opposing quarterbacks all year, they made Young look like an MVP-caliber passer , resulting in a 329-yard passing day for the fourth-year pro.
Meanwhile, Detroit had no answer for Carolina pass-catcher Tetairoa McMillan. McMillan ran past D.J. Reed and Lions defenders all night, finishing with a game-high 14 receptions for 192 yards and two touchdowns.
The Lions proceeded to surrender a staggering 32 points and 445 yards of offense in the primetime affair, marking yet another underwhelming performance this season from defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard's unit .
And to add insult to injury, the Panthers played the Week 4 contest without three of their starting offensive linemen (guard Damien Lewis and offensive tackles Ikem Ekwonu and Taylor Moton) and two of their top three receivers (Jalen Coker and Xavier Legette).
Unquestionably, it was a pathetic and inexcusable performance from the defensive side of the ball. And through four games now, the Lions have allowed an unfathomable 31.8 points per game. If the season ended today, that total would rank as the third-most points per game in the NFL in the last 40 years.
On top of that, Detroit has given up the most yards in the league through four weeks (1,695). Plus, that total is just 21 yards shy of the number of yards allowed by the 0-16 2008 Lions over the season's first four weeks (1,716).
And that's hardly the end of the damning stats for the Lions’ defense. There's also this: the team has surrendered 1,308 yards through the air through four games. Unsurprisingly, that's also a league-worst mark, and no other team in the NFL in 2026 has even permitted 1,200 passing yards.
No ifs, ands, or buts about it, Detroit's defense has failed Dan Campbell's squad time and time again this season. And it's the primary reason why the Lions came up short in a winnable game against an injury-ravaged Panthers team Sunday night.
With just an adequate showing from Sheppard's unit, Detroit would have captured the Week 4 victory and improved to 3-1 on the season. But instead, Campbell & Co. are now 2-2, with no answers in sight for the defense.
And why aren't there any answers in sight? It's not simply due to the injury-decimated nature of the Lions’ secondary. Sure, being without starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph and fellow defensive backs Thomas Harper and Avonte Maddox is far from optimal. And there's no doubt the back-end of the defense would be much stronger with each of them healthy and able to play.
Yet, the team's defensive woes are deeper rooted than that. On a consistent basis this season, the Lions’ defensive gameplans have paled in comparison to those of the opposing offenses, and that falls directly on the shoulders of Sheppard.
On a weekly basis, it is his responsibility – and no one else's – to get the defense ready for whatever the opposition is going to throw at it. And in large part, the former linebackers coach has failed to do just that.
Most points per game allowed in a season in the last 40 years: 2020 Lions – 32.4 2008 Lions – 32.3 2026 Lions – 31.8 (through 4 games)
Consequently, the second-year coordinator should absolutely bear the brunt of the blame for the defense being ill-prepared and ill-equipped to make adjustments through the first quarter of the 2026 campaign.
And please don't try to defend Sheppard by saying he hasn't had enough time to prove his worth as an NFL coordinator. That's hardly a valid excuse any longer for his shortcomings.
With 21 games now under his belt in the role, he's had enough time to get acclimated to being a defensive play-caller. And if anything, he's done the polar opposite, appearing increasingly in over his head with each passing week.
Campbell was asked about the coordinator's future in Detroit following the Week 4 loss.
“I’m not talking about all that,” Campbell told reporters Sunday. “I’m talking about getting better right now with what we got, and that’s what we’re going to do. We’re going to find a way to get better with what we got.”
Sorry, Dan, but the ship has sailed on that being a viable solution for the defense.
Nearly a season and a half into his stint as Lions defensive coordinator, it's become clear as day that Sheppard's not cut out to be a coordinator at the NFL level.
Yes, he has a refreshing level of passion for the game, and from all accounts, connects well with the players.
Yet, his future in the league is not as a play-caller. That realization should have also already set in for Campbell and the Lions’ front-office brass .
Undoubtedly, the time is now to pull the plug on Sheppard and make a change at coordinator.

title: Lions Grades: Offensive Rally Can't Mask Defensive Disaster
full_text:
The Detroit Lions were exposed defensively in front of a national audience.
The Lions were picked apart by Bryce Young over the course of the game, and couldn't do enough on offense to keep pace with the Carolina Panthers. The result was a 32-26 defeat, which drops the Lions to 2-2 on the season.
Here are grades for each position group in Sunday's game.
Jared Goff had a big game through the air with the run game struggling for most of the evening. Goff finished with 412 passing yards and a touchdown, but it ultimately wasn't enough as the team came up short on the final drive.
Goff remains without a turnover through the first four games of the season, but missed in key situations and had his final pass to Isaac TeSlaa come up one yard short resulting in a turnover on downs.
Jahmyr Gibbs added a rushing touchdown to his tally, but with the team playing from behind was relegated to mostly a receiving option in the second half. He was held to a season-low 46 rushing yards on 15 carries as the Panthers made a concerted effort to keep him in check.
Gibbs did have an impressive pass-protection rep, as he stepped up into the hole to pick up a blitzing linebacker to give Goff time to throw on one second-quarter snap. Sione Vaki contributed with a 17-yard reception but did not have any carries.
Jameson Williams had his struggles with drops, but came up big to lead the team with a season-best 102 receiving yards on six catches. Williams had multiple big catches, but narrowly missed what could've been a touchdown in the first half when a pass from Goff appeared to go through his hands.
Amon-Ra St. Brown had eight catches for 75 yards, while Isaac TeSlaa had his second-straight big game with 95 receiving yards on four catches. It was TeSlaa who had the biggest grab of the night, as he hauled in a 57-yard catch in the third quarter to set up a field goal.
After news broke earlier in the day that the Lions and Sam LaPorta had broken off contract extension talks, LaPorta made his case for a hefty pay day. The Iowa product hauled in eight passes for 84 yards and a touchdown.
Brock Wright had an early penalty, but had a big block to help spring Gibbs for a chunk play in the first half and also had an eight-yard reception.
The Lions were up-and-down in the trenches offensively. Despite the Panthers having one of the league's worst run defenses, they couldn't get Gibbs going on the ground. There were also some concerning snaps where Goff had passes batted down at the line.
Tate Ratledge had a critical false start that pushed the offense back five yards on a critical fourth-down in the fourth quarter.
In the second half, the Lions didn't face a ton of pressure as the Panthers elected to devote more players to pass coverage. Goff was only sacked once, which came on the final drive of the game.
Alim McNeill had a strong start, notching a sack on the Panthers' first drive to get his third on the season already. He would add a tackle for loss and two quarterback hits to his tally throughout the game.
Aidan Hutchinson was held without a sack, and faced two and sometimes three players on his way to rush the quarterback on a snap-to-snap basis. D.J. Wonnum was also quiet, though he did have a big stop on a Bryce Young scramble to give the Lions one more chance at the end of the game.
Detroit's linebackers struggled with spotty tackling and were poor in pass coverage throughout the night. Jack Campbell continued a troubling start to the season by failing to make an impact, as he was beaten in coverage by failing to get to his drop zone in time on multiple occasions.
Carolina routinely took advantage of some struggles with discipline, as Young was able to hold the linebackers with play-action fakes and roll out to connect with tight end Darren Waller on multiple occasions.
On a brighter note, rookie Jimmy Rolder recorded his first career tackle for loss on the first defensive series of the game.
The Lions were gashed through the air by Young, who entered the game with one of his top receivers being placed on injured reserve earlier in the week. However, Young quickly got going with Tetairoa McMillan who dominated the Lions.
At one point, McMillan had recorded a catch with seven different defenders covering him over the course of the game. He had 147 receiving yards by halftime, and finished with two scores and 192 yards. Young threw for 329 and garnered MVP chants by the game's conclusion.
D.J. Reed was beat on McMillan's first touchdown, while Christian Izien was beat on the second. Rock Ya-Sin exited the game with a hamstring injury and was ruled out, which could lead to the team being in need of further reinforcements depending on the severity of the injury.
Izien recorded a sack, while Ennis Rakestraw had a nice pass breakup to force the Panthers to settle for a field goal in the fourth quarter.
Jake Bates connected on both of his field goal attempts, including a 54-yard boot on the team's first possession. However, that attempt was nearly made longer as they had Juice Scruggs run on late and were forced to take a timeout.
Special teams woes continued in the second half, when a big stop was nearly derailed by a running into the kicker penalty by linebacker Trevor Nowaske. The penalty was ultimately declined because it was five yards and not 15, which saved the group from further issues.
The Lions will have some tough evaluations to endure after another primetime disappointing performance. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard had few answers for the Panthers' passing attack, as Young's connection with McMillan dominated the game.
Elsewhere, the staff had some uncharacteristic miscues from an operation standpoint. A player ran on late prior to Bates' first field goal which forced the team into a timeout. Then, they were forced to take a delay of game penalty in the fourth quarter that turned a fourth-and-15 into a fourth-and-20.
Offensively, the Lions were efficient through the air but couldn't convert in some big situations. They opted for a hook-and-ladder on their fourth-and-20 in Carolina territory, but the trick play came up unsuccessful.
Ultimately, the team has to find more answers as they prepare for a gauntlet following the bye week in Week 6. Next week's game against the Cardinals will be Detroit's last before the bye, and offers them a chance to reclaim some momentum before two straight divisional games after the bye.

title: Everything Dan Campbell Said After Disappointing Panthers Loss
full_text:
Here is everything Detroit Lions Dan Campbell said, following a 32-26 loss to the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium.
"All right. Got to give those guys a lot of credit. They did a heck of a job. We knew coming in here that those guys were going to lay it on the line. They still got plenty of weapons and the fight was going to be there and they showed up. That team showed up. We got ourselves in a hole there, which is frustrating, you know? The penalties that showed up in critical moments hurt us. And then at the end of the day, we had our opportunities. Our defense came up with a stop and we had the ball with about two minutes left to go win the game and we just couldn't get it done. So that's frustrating, but if you told me we're going to get the ball to go win it at the end, I believe we're going to win a lot more of those than we're not. So that's probably the silver lining, that we had our opportunity. What's not good is we were down two scores and had to fight our way back."
Do you feel like the team took a step back defensively?
"Well look, really to start the game, we didn't do well enough in the coverage aspect. They had a couple of things in there, the RPOs (run-pass-options) that got us. They put your run-pass-hook defender in conflict there a little bit and he's got such a quick release. That got us a little bit early. I thought we handled some of that in the second half, but the issue was, then the run got us and we started bleeding yards there in the second half. That's the one thing we couldn't let happen. We couldn't start giving up those run yards because now you're opening up everything for them. But I think even bigger is we got no takeaways. We have to get takeaways. We just have to. We got nothing. So not good enough."
If he needs to dive deeper into this defense, especially in the secondary?
"Well it's, there, again, I need to see. I think one of the things coming into this game was for me it was about discipline and effort. You know, effort's always going to be a big deal, but, man, those two combined going into this game, I wanted to see discipline, I wanted to see effort. I'm going to be anxious to just look at the tape and see what that looked like really in all areas. Look, it's not good enough right now. That's the bottom line. It's just not good enough. We got to score more points. We got to be more efficient than we've been. We got off to a slow start. We had two opportunities there at the end and we didn't get it done. So, we got to be better there and got to get takeaways on defense. That's going to have to be our recipe."
Do the Lions have the right personnel on defense?
"Man, I'm not even going to worry about all that. My job is to get these guys going, man. We've got guys on the back end that can cover. We've got guys that can hit. We got to pull this thing together and find the right combination of coverage versus pressure and job responsibility, putting guys in the right spot to do what they do and so this is a work in progress. We're four games in. There again, we just have to find a way to get better. I thought we would play better than we did last week and as a whole we didn't. We did some things that were good. The fact that we fought our way back into that game, that always gives you hope. But, man, we had our opportunity. We got to finish it out. So you always want to be able to clean up the errors after a win. When you don't, it gets tough. Certainly not good enough."
On wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan and thoughts on guarding him coming into the game
"Yeah, we knew he was going to be an issue, especially since [wide receiver Jalen] Coker got hurt. That would be a guy that they would probably try to get the ball to and really a lot of those were those RPOs [run-pass-options] early in the game. Those were just those quick strikes right up the hash, right up the seam. That's something we didn't -- I mean, we worked but that was a little something that they kind of mixed in, some of that more of it than the norm. I think we finally settled in a little bit there in the second half, but there again we gave up the run. Look, he's a really good receiver and he made some plays, none of them bigger than that one at the end to extend the game there. We ended up getting the stop. That was a huge catch over there on the sideline. The guy's got range and he's got outstanding hands. And there again, look Bryce (Young) is -- nothing that Bryce did shocked me today. Bryce is a hell of a quarterback, man. He just is. He's dangerous, he's got a quick release. He can process it, he can see it, he's mobile, he can move around in the pocket. He was tough, tough today."
Is there a timeline for considering a change at defensive coordinator?
"Yeah, I'm not talking about all that, man. I'm talking about getting better right now with what we got and that's what we're going do. We're going to find a way to get better with what we got."
On what gives you the most confidence that you can get better on defense?
"There's other things that we can do. We've tweaked a little bit every week here. There's still some things that we can try that we haven't yet, try to settle some things down and see if we can help. Look, it's all a work in progress. You just keep working through it and find a way to improve. We didn't today. It wasn't good enough."
If maybe playing a little bit more man coverage and other things that can be done differently on defense?
"Yeah, there's some things we can mix in here that we haven't done a ton of this year and that's next step. Let's see what we can do. I want to exhaust everything here. Let's exhaust everything we have. It's the same thing on offense. We got to find a way to be a little bit more efficient here. We can't stall out. When we do, we got to get a faster start, which we haven't done. Let's look at it and let's get it fixed. But I know this, we go into panic mode when we've got 13 games left and we're 2-2, that's not the right thing to do. I just don't believe that. I never have. So, you know, I know there's frustration. Look, I'm frustrated. I know the players are frustrated . But it's also, and you're a few plays away, a few penalties away. Whatever it is from now you're not in a two-score game and now you're back in control instead of having to fight your way back from the deficit we were under there."
Could you potentially make a move at the coordinator position later in the season?
"Yeah dude, I'm going to always do what's right by this team. What I truly believe is the best thing and the right thing to do, always. I'm always going to do that. That's the most important thing is what's right for the players and what gives us the best opportunity to win."
On his impressions of the discipline on both sides of the ball?
"Absolutely. I can tell you it's one thing to say it. Like honestly, it's 100% on me, because it's one thing to say it, it's a different thing when it's not coming across. You can talk about being in a stressful environment, what goes on in those type of situations, but the bottom line is I'm not getting that across. I'm not getting it done right now, because it's still happening So, I put that squarely on my shoulders, that I'm not getting it coached properly. I'm the one who's going to get this fixed. I'm the one who is going to fix this whole discipline thing, whatever it takes."
On deep balls on the last drive:
"Yeah, we had a double move with J-Mo (Jameson Williams) and they rolled over the top there. It just took a minute with a safety that far back over it so it ended up being a ball holder and it got sacked. It was unfortunate, but he was trying to give it a go. We hit a couple things down field today on double move, but also just kind of spreading the field and letting him run. I thought [quarterback Jared] Goff did a heck of a job stepping up, making some of those throws. Those are big plays. That one just got us, ended up getting strung out a little bit and ended…

title: 6 Winners, 8 Losers From Lions Loss to Panthers
full_text:
The Detroit Lions had to wait around on Sunday, watching the NFC North all pick up wins over their opponents before their number was called. The Lions traveled to Carolina for Sunday Night Football.
The Lions secondary did not have a memorable night, and it cost the Lions in the end. Bryce Young threw for 329 yards and the Panthers won 32-26.
Here are six winners and eight losers from the Lions' loss to the Panthers, which dropped them to 2-2 on the season.
The first drive alone pushed McNeill into the winner category. The Raleigh, NC, native had a happy homecoming. He had two run stuffs and a drive-ending sack on third down to thwart any hopes of Carolina pulling even to begin the game.
In the second quarter, McNeill nearly took a Bryce Young handoff after he was left unblocked.
Bates was consistent on the night. The kicker hit all four field goal attempts and both extra points as the Lions needed every one of his 14 points to stay in contention with the Panthers. He hit a season-long 54-yard kick to end Detroit's first possession.
The former Lions first-round pick had a rough start, losing a ball that should have been caught early in the game. However, he came alive later in the opening half, with a massive 49-yard catch to set up a game-tying field goal at halftime.
Williams finished as the leading receiver for Motown on the night, with 102 yards as four separate pass catches finished over 75 yards.
TeSlaa continues to impress with his limited touches. One week after he recorded the longest catch of his career, the Arkansas product set a new high with a 57-yard deep shot that he was able to grab after burning two defensive backs.
TeSlaa caught a few more passes in the fourth quarter, finishing with 95 yards. Unfortunately, his last catch was two yards short of the first down, ending the Lions chances of a comeback.
Despite the Panthers having one of the worst run defenses in the NFL, the Lion defense put their offense in a bad spot that forced the pass game. Goff needed to step up and deliver, and the former top overall pick delivered.
Goff slung the ball for 412 yards on the night, but struggled as the offensive interior allowed pressure and compromised the pocket. That resulted in batted balls, but Goff was able to keep Motown in contention until the last play.
LaPorta was a part of the lethal Lions passing offense, finishing with eight catches for 84 yards and a late touchdown to keep Detroit in contention. The Iowa product breathed fresh life when things looked bleak in the second half.
LaPorta became the go-to player for conversions, and was open on multiple targets that got deflected.
The center had his first rough patch of the young season on Sunday. In the first quarter, Scruggs had a mental lapse, forgetting to stay on field for the field goal unit and costing Dan Campbell a timeout.
The very next play he was on field, first down on the ensuing drive, Scruggs committed a holding penalty. In the Penn State product’s defense, it was a play where Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs turned opposite directions for a handoff, turning it to an awkward pitch.
Scruggs was also part of the offensive interior that was pushed into Jared Goff’s lap, allowing a sack, multiple pressures, and batted balls by the defensive interior that changed the entire trajectory of the game.
For the second straight week, DJ Reed was the primary man in coverage on a touchdown. Reed was burnt by reigning NFL Rookie of the Year Tetairoa McMillan, with the receiver getting a step and easily hauling the ball in.
Reed entered the night ranking 92nd among corners in yards per reception allowed, at 20.3. Sunday night did not help his case.
In the second half, Reed was the primary man in coverage for a 16-yard catch by Darren Waller after a penalty set the Panthers back with a long field ahead. They would score on that drive.
McCreary remained in the lineup for Week 4, and it was not a week to remember. Although he had a pass breakup in the second quarter, he was part of a secondary that allowed McMillan to go over 190 yards for a career game. McCreary was assigned with the first rounder a few times, and it did not go well.
Additionally, the former Titan was flagged for a pass interference in the third quarter. He was burned on the next drive by John Metchie as the Panthers jumped into field goal position to take a two-possession lead.
Campbell continued his slow start to the season. The Pro Bowler was out of position at points, continuing to be a step behind where he was expected. Campbell missed two tackles on separate scoring drives for the Panthers, which loomed large in the loss.
It was a tough Sunday night for Wright. The backup tight end added a catch for eight yards on the night, but also accounted for 20 yards in penalties. On the opening drive, Wright had a false start.
On the opening drive of the second half, Wright was again whistled, this time for a 15-yard unnecessary roughness.
Miller was in for a rough matchup, squaring off against Panthers premier EDGE Jaelan Phillips. The rookie was able to hold his own against the former Dolphin, but also left early twice for false start penalties, including once in the red zone.
Bryce Young threw at will against the Lions, and Rakestraw saw his fair share of targets when in coverage. Unfortunately for the former Lions’ second round pick, Rakestraw was beat in coverage during one of the most critical plays of the night. McMillan was open after a Hutchinson pressure forced Young out of the pocket.
Rakestraw’s leap was mistimed, and McMillan corralled the ball and the defensive back falling slammed the receiver’s toe into the turf to complete the second foot down for a catch.
Gibbs was not his typical self against the Panthers, taking a hard shot early that resulted in an incomplete catch and being held in check in the rushing game. The Panthers, who were among the bottom of the league in rush yards allowed, contained Gibbs to 46 yards on 15 carries.
Between his drop and overall quiet night, Gibbs did not meet his own standards.

title: Takeaways From Detroit Lions 32-26 Loss Against Carolina Panthers
full_text:
The last time the Detroit Lions stepped foot at Bank of America Stadium, they left on the losing end of the scoreboard, having lost to the Carolina Panthers, 32-26.
"That was a different head coach, different team in some regards," Dan Campbell explained to reporters this week. "That's been a while. I mean, we don't ever want to give up what we gave up when we were out there to any opponent. But no, I'm not talking about that. That hadn't come up about what went down in '22 out there. It's so much different. But we know that they're capable of running the football. They don't do a ton of it, but when they do, it's effective and they've got good schemes, good tight ends with, this back hits it, so they have versatility in their scheme.
"They’ve got gun, they’ve got pistol, they've got under center, and then they've got all the keepers off of it, which makes the run game dangerous because of all the keepers and boots and what Bryce (Young) can do with it and then the shots off of it. So, it's a dangerous team. It's a dangerous offense with Bryce at the helm.”
Despite another week of practice, Detroit's defense had another atrocious performance, looking completely outmatched again in Carolina. True to form, the worst pass defense in the league could not stop the passing attack of the Panthers.
After 60 minutes of action, the Lions record fell to 2-2 on the season.
Here are the key takeaways from the Lions' 32-26 loss.
The Panthers won the opening coin toss and elected to defer. Detroit's offense got their weapons involved early, targeting Jahmyr Gibbs, Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown in the first three plays.
Unfortunately, a Brock Wright penalty put the offense behind the sticks and slowed down the growing momentum. The Panthers' defense bringing pressure disrupted Drew Petzing's offense.
Detroit took an early 3-0 lead on a made 54-yard field goal from kicker Jake Bates.
The Lions were a little undisciplined in the first 15 minutes of the road contest. Juice Scruggs was slow to get on the field on Bates' field goal attempt, forcing the team to take an early timeout.
Multiple penalties put the offense behind the sticks, including a Scruggs penalty on the Lions second offensive possession.
Carolina was able to score their first touchdown on their second offensive possession. An eight-play, 72-yard drive was capped off by a Chuba Hubba 15-yard scamper.  Quarterback Bryce Young started the first two drives going 7-for-7 and 68 passing yards.
Bully ball @AlimMcneill pic.twitter.com/Gx172krR6P
After the Panthers took a 13-6 lead, Goff was able to lead the offense on an 11-play, 68-yard scoring drive to tie the game at 13-13.
Detroit was effective on third down, converting three times to keep the chains moving.
A defensive pass interference call on second-round wideout Isaac TeSlaa setup the offense at the one-yard line.
Gibbs capped off the drive with a one-yard scamper. The former first-round pick, with his first touchdown of the game, has totaled seven scrimmage touchdowns through the first four games of the season.
The only Lions player with more scores through the first four games of any season was Calvin Johnson, who had eight scores back in 2011.
Go get it, Waymo pic.twitter.com/Sq11q0qoS0
The Lions dealt with a number of issues in coverage during the first half of Sunday's game. Young dominated to the tune of 15 completions on 20 attempts for 178 yards. Detroit's defensive backs struggled to contain Tetairoa McMillan, which led to multiple explosive plays for the Panthers.
D.J. Reed was beat in coverage on a long pass from Young to McMillan, which resulted in a 32-yard score to give the Panthers a 13-6 lead in the second quarter. Though Detroit would rally to tie the score at 16 by the half, it was ultimately another half to forget for a secondary that has faced plenty of criticism.
McMillan was a force in the first two quarters, catching nine passes for 147 yards and a score by halftime.
To begin the third quarter, the Lions still did not have any answers for McMillan. After another touchdown to begin the second half, he was up to 11 receptions for 162 yards and two touchdowns with 9:33 left in the quarter. The Panthers took a 22-16 lead, as the Panthers kicker missed his second extra point of the game.
Detroit was able to find themselves in the red zone frequently, but came away with field goals instead of touchdowns far too often.
The Panthers defense was able to clamp down when Detroit was able to move the football into their side of the field.
Late in the game, Detroit cut a 13-point deficit down to six, after Goff found tight end Sam LaPorta in the end zone on an eight-yard score.
1.) Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill, a native of Raleigh, halted the Panthers first drive with a 10-yard sack, his third of the 2026 NF  season.
2.) Jameson Williams had an opportunity for an explosive grab in the first quarter, but was unable to haul a solid toss from Jared Goff.
3.) Isaac TeSlaa had a career-long reception of 57 yards on the Lions first possession of the third quarter.
4.) Former Lions cornerback Darius Slay even commented on the poor defense, sharing on social media, "Lions I got a lot of love for y’all but man this defense is bad bad."
5.) Detroit had nine penalties called for a total of 67 yards.

title: Lions Week 4 Inactives Against Panthers: Is DE Ahmed Hassanein Playing?
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have revealed their official list of players who are inactive against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium.
Offensive lineman Ben Bartch was previously ruled out. Defensive back D.J. Reed, who was limited at practice all week due to a rib injury, has been ruled active for the Sunday Night Football contest against an NFC South opponent.
Others not suiting up this week include defensive back Bishop Fitzgerald, defensive end Ahmed Hassanein, tight end Tyler Conklin, linebacker Devin White and defensive lineman Mekhi Wingo.
A player that has an opportunity for more playing time this week is cornerback Ennis Rakestraw. After being inactive the first two weeks of the regular season, the former second-round pick had an opportunity to suit up against the New York Jets.
Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard explained this week what factored into Rakestraw playing more in Week 3.
"Well, the active inactive deal is a 46-man roster on game day and it's hard. It's hard numbers-wise," Sheppard explained. "What's best for the team? Again, we were carrying four tight ends then. So, now we went three tight ends, an extra corner. Well, who's that? Alright. Is that a corner? Is that a safety? Does (Bishop) Fitzgerald go? These are all the conversations that's happened that starts with Dan (Campbell) and Brad (Holmes). And then we get in the room, 'What's the plan this week, Shepp? What are you looking to do? How do you want to do it? Do we need this guy?' So, that's kind of how that kind of transpires."
The third-year defensive back had a productive training camp, but also battled injuries near the end of the summer.
"If you guys remember at the tail end of training camp, Ennis had an injury. He was playing kind of at a high level, honestly, coming out of scrimmage, one of his better outputs of camp since he's been here in three years," Sheppard said. "And then he got injured. Luckily for us, it wasn't long-term. So, he was just kind of coming back from that injury, getting back in the groove. So, to just throw him out there without a lot of time on task, I think he had about two weeks off , we felt wasn't the right thing to do."

title: Setting Lions Fans Expectations For Isaac TeSlaa Against Panthers
full_text:
Detroit Lions second-year wide receiver Isaac TeSlaa had a big showing last week against the New York Jets.
After a quiet start to the season through two games, TeSlaa came up big with four catches for 66 yards in the team's win over the New York Jets. Included in that effort was a 49-yard catch and run to set up the Lions' game-winning touchdown in the fourth quarter.
Detroit has high expectations for TeSlaa, whom they traded up to get in the third-round of last year's draft. While it's been a quieter start than expected, he has a chance to boost his totals in Detroit's Week 4 game against the Carolina Panthers.
This week alone, the Panthers have placed both of their starting cornerbacks on injured reserve as both Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson will be sidelined. As a result, Detroit's receiving corps could thrive.
Detroit has two established stars in their receiver room with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams. With such a banged up secondary, the Panthers will likely do whatever they can to limit the stars which could open up TeSlaa.
Sports Betting Dime's Drew Ellis believes TeSlaa could have a good shot to contribute, as he's picking TeSlaa to go over his projected over/under receiving total. Currently, the over/under is set at 17.5 (-113) on DraftKings Sportsbook.
"The second-year receiver has seen an increased role in the offense the last two weeks, upping his receptions and yards every week this season," Ellis told Lions OnSI. "He’s coming off a 66-yard performance against the Jets last week and now faces a Carolina defense that is just as banged up in the secondary as Detroit is. That should lead to a lot of strong matchups for TeSlaa and for the Lions to design some play calls to get him the ball. With the total so low, we just need 1 or 2 receptions to make this over hit."
Through three games, TeSlaa has totaled five catches for 92 yards and is still looking for his first touchdown of the season. He had six scoring grabs on 16 total catches as a rookie last season.

title: Victory Monday Fact or Fiction: Packers’ Season Is Lost Despite Beating Bucs
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The old ABC Wide World of Sports slogan was, “The thrill of victory and the agony of defeat.”
There was no thrill of victory for the Green Bay Packers after edging the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Only the muted feeling of another lackluster performance, the agony felt by linebacker Edgerrin Cooper following his torn Achilles and the anguish felt by teammates knowing what that injury meant to the rest of the team.
How will the Packers pick up the pieces without their star linebacker?
“Yeah, I don’t know, Pete,” coach Matt LaFleur said to Pete Dougherty of The Green Bay Press-Gazette after the game. It was an atypically short answer, a combination of equal parts frustration over the way his team played and honesty in knowing there’s no way to replace Cooper.
At least he didn’t utter the next-man-up nonsense. No offense to Isaiah McDuffie, who probably is one of the better backup linebackers in the NFL. There’s just no way any player can replace Cooper, a chess-piece defender for coordinator Jonathan Gannon.
The reality, of course, is there’s no next man up for Cooper. It’s going to take the other 52 players on the roster, all playing harder and better, to pick up the slack.
Cooper was Gannon’s best option in replacing Micah Parsons to start the season. He leads the team with three sacks and six tackles for losses. He’s second with 30 tackles. In just more than one half of work against the Buccaneers, he had one sack on the opening possession and an interception to end the half. He had a team-high nine tackles while playing barely more than 50 percent of the snaps.
That dynamic skill-set was a reason why the defense was able to adapt as well as it did without Parsons.
On Saturday, NFL insider Tom Pelissero reported that Parsons probably won’t play in a game until November . A peek at the schedule shows there are four games between now and November. Those games are against:
The Chicago Bears, who have won back-to-back games with backup quarterbacks. They are first in the NFL in total offense and ninth in scoring.
The Dallas Cowboys, who are tied for second in the NFL in scoring and are fifth on third down behind the high-flying combination of Dak Prescott throwing to George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb.
The Detroit Lions, who are fifth in the NFL in scoring and sixth in total offense behind the elite combination of quarterback Jared Goff, running back Jahmyr Gibbs and receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams.
The Carolina Panthers, who are fourth in the NFL in scoring and total offense with rising quarterback Bryce Young and big-time receiver Tetairoa McMillan.
Can Green Bay’s defense, which has played well enough for the team to be 3-1, somehow stop those offenses without one of the best pass rushers in football and one of the game’s top linebackers?
That seems like almost an impossible mission. Cooper is ninth in the NFL in sacks. Of the eight players ahead of him, he’s No. 1 with 30 tackles and one of only two players with an interception. He is a field-tilting player, whether it’s stopping the run, dropping into coverage or rushing off the edge.
If the defense is going to suffer without Cooper, which would be the predictable result, then it will be up to the offense to pick up the slack.
Matt LaFleur is the offensive mastermind given a new contract. Jordan Love is one of the highest-paid quarterbacks in the NFL.
And yet, the offense, in a word, stinks.
The Packers are 27th with 18.3 points per game. They entered the week ranked last in the NFL in third-down conversions at about 27 percent. They actually performed worse on Sunday at 20.0 percent.
After their best day of the season, the Packers are still last in the NFL with 58.0 rushing yards per game and 31st with 3.2 rushing yards per attempt.
The Packers are last in the NFL with 2.5 fumbles per game. Jordan Love has been victimized by the most drops and the highest drop percentage. They have been guilty of the second-most holding penalties and the fifth-most pre-snap penalties on offense.
“There was some positive things, but we’re never going to be satisfied with scoring 17 points in the game,” LaFleur said. “That’s just not to our standard and we’ve got to find ways when we have opportunities in the red area to convert. We can’t be turning the ball over, can’t have penalties.
“That is a stingy defense … but I also think that we also have to clean up a lot of stuff. Like, too many penalties (and) turnovers. Ball-carriers have got to hold onto the ball. We put the ball on the ground way too much. And this stuff’s got to get fixed, and it’s got to get fixed now.
Now, with the rival Bears next on the schedule, would be good timing.
If the blockers learn how to block without holding, if the linemen can learn the snap count, if the backs can hold onto the ball, if the receivers can catch the ball then, yes, the Packers have a chance. A real chance.
The addition of Laken Tomlinson at left guard paid dividends against the Bucs, and the addition of Kevin Zeitler at right guard should do the same. This could quickly become a decent offensive line, which might not sound like a tremendous compliment until you remember Love getting knocked into the middle of next week by unblocked defenders the first few games.
Love has shown he can be a high-level quarterback. Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft are legit weapons. Maybe the line will rescue the running game.
There’s just too many “maybes” and “ifs” to believe the Packers can save their season. Sure, they could wind up being playoff contenders heading into January, but nobody should be satisfied with another nine-win season and one-and-done playoffs.
This is Titletown, after all. It’s not Seventh Seed City or Playoff Bubble Boulevard.
“We won, but it’s the same thing I said after the Jets game,” said tight end Tucker Kraft, who dropped what should have been an easy touchdown catch. “We’re still out there making [mistakes]. We’re excited, we’re happy, winning on the road is hard. But we’re still beating ourselves up.”
Between Cooper’s torn Achilles and the self-inflicted black eyes, the Packers look like a team that’s on the ropes.
For the coaches and high-priced players who remain healthy, it’s time to put up or shut up. Learn the snap count. Hang onto the ball. If they can’t do the simple things, how on earth are they going to do the hard things necessary to beat the really good teams coming up on the schedule?
Verdict: Fact, unless the Packers really can get things “fixed now.”

title: Three Overreactions From Packers’ Win Over Buccaneers Include Pain, Slop
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – A win is a win. The Green Bay Packers took care of business, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 17-14 on Sunday.
It was a huge win, let’s make that clear. The distance between 2-2 and 1-3 is one game in the standings but miles apart in reality. However, speaking of reality, a reality check is coming.
The Packers’ two wins have come against teams with one win. Their four games have come against teams with six wins. The FCS portion of the schedule is over. The big boys are coming.
Let’s dive in with this week’s Overreactions.
Leave it to center Sean Rhyan to provide the real talk.
Asked about Edgerrin Cooper’s Achilles injury, Rhyan said: “We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse, it seems like.”
There’s no such thing as curses. Right? Well, here’s the season-ending carnage from the last 11 months.
From 2025: Tight end Tucker Kraft’s torn ACL, center Elgton Jenkins’ broken leg with ligament damage, defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt’s broken leg with ligament damage, right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele’s partially torn patellar tendon, edge rusher Micah Parsons’ torn ACL.
From 2026: Receiver Jayden Reed’s neck injury, Bako-Bewele’s complete tear of the same patellar tendon and, now linebacker Edgerrin Cooper’s torn Achilles.
Those are just the big-name players. It seems like every injury is a major injury, whether it’s Warren Brinson slipping on the practice field or Cooper looking to see who tripped him following a noncontact injury on Sunday.
Statistically, the Packers weren’t especially injured last season. It’s just that they suffered some season-ending injuries to big-time players at about the worst possible time. This year, according to Rotowire’s weighted severity score , the Packers entered Week 4 ranked 10th in injuries.
Some injuries are easy to explain. Last year, Rhyan’s foot hit Kraft’s knee against Carolina. Brinson fell on Wyatt at Detroit. Other injuries are harder to explain because of their noncontact nature. Why did Parsons’ knee give out on him at Denver? Why did Cooper’s Achilles tear at Tampa Bay? Should Bako-Bewele have had a more extensive surgery last season in hopes of preventing this year’s injury? Who knows – that decision was made by the team and Bako-Bewele’s team using the best information available.
Everyone wants to know who to blame, and the answer is I don’t know. It would be impossible to figure out how much the Packers spend on their strength and conditioning program, let alone get those numbers from the other 31 teams to add some context. Money wouldn’t be the only measuring stick, anyway.
The Packers hired a new strength and conditioning staff in 2024, led by Aaron Hill, and he implemented some obvious changes in creating a more extensive and dynamic warm-up routine. The reality, though, is if there was one tried-and-true way for players to stay healthy, every team would be doing it. In last year’s NFLPA report card, the training room and staff got a C (the training room has since been updated, to Parsons’ approval ) and the strength coaches got a B.
Coach Matt LaFleur played his starters in the preseason based on a study that found that players who play in the preseason tend to be healthier in the regular season. Well, so much for that.
It would be easy to chalk it up to bad luck. Or a curse. Maybe the Packers really have just been unlucky and the Injury Gods will grace them for the rest of the decade.
What’s undeniable is injuries ruined last season – they were 9-3-1 entering the Denver game in which Parsons and Bako-Bewele went down – and probably have ruined this season, too. In our preseason roster rankings, which are based on skill and salary (rather than just skill), Parsons was second, Bako-Bewele was eighth, Cooper was 11th and Reed was 16th. They are critical players, and they’re all out for the season.
How does a team that had a limited margin for error, anyway, overcome the losses of some of their best players? That seems impossible, especially with how the healthy players have performed.
The Packers really should have blown out the Buccaneers. Jordan Love vs. an undrafted rookie at quarterback? Especially Love with time in the pocket against a rookie quarterback? That’s an all-time mismatch.
Instead, the Packers held on for dear life because of their own inability to do elementary-level things.
The Packers were guilty of 10 penalties for 66 yards. The Buccaneers were guilty of only four penalties for 17 yards. This wasn’t one-sided refereeing, as you might argue was the case at Minnesota in Week 1. This was a one-sided lack of discipline.
“We’ve got to clean up the penalties,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “We’re stagnant right now, we’re moving backwards a lot of the time and not having positive plays and it’s putting us in some tough third-down situations.”
If you think that was a postgame comment, no, it wasn’t. That’s what Love said on Wednesday.
Good thing everyone was listening to the captain’s message.
The Packers have been guilty of 48 total penalties and 42 accepted penalties. Only the Browns with 51 and 43, respectively, have been guilty of more. By penalty yards, the Packers are first (or worst) with 344. There have been 17 pre-snap penalties and 10 holding penalties.
The NFL records for most penalties and yards in a season belong to the 2011 Raiders, who were guilty of 163 accepted infractions for 1,358 yards. This year’s Packers are on pace for 179 penalties for 1,462 yards. The franchise records are 135 penalties for 1,103 yards.
Plus, there were two red-zone fumbles – MarShawn Lloyd foolishly trying to run over Antoine Winfield and Kaleb Johnson at the goal line.
On offense, the Packers lead the NFL in fumbles and drops. On defense, they are second in first downs allowed by penalties.
“We also have to clean up a lot of stuff,” LaFleur said, rightly agitated after the game. “Like, too many penalties, turnovers. Ball-carriers have got to hold onto the ball. We put the ball on the ground way too much. And this stuff’s got to get fixed and it’s got to get fixed now.”
That sounds good, but will it actually happen? The reality is the Packers are an undisciplined team with no signs of progress. Penalties and fumbles are part of the game, but LaFleur’s team has an ongoing problem. At this point, the only Super Bowl that the Packers will be competing for is the Super Bowl of Slop.
The Packers are 2-2, which is probably what most of us were thinking at the start of the season by projecting a loss to the Vikings, a win at the Jets, a win over the Falcons and a loss to the Buccaneers. The path to 2-2 veered a bit, but they are .500.
But now what? The Bears are coming to town on Sunday; they are 3-1 and just won back-to-back games with backup quarterbacks. After that, they will host the Cowboys, who are 2-2 with a walk-off loss to the powerhouse Ravens. Then, it’s off to Detroit, which is 2-2 with a superb top of the roster. Then, it’s a short-week home game against the Panthers, who looked phenomenal on offense in beating the Lions to improve to 2-2.
It doesn’t get easier after that with a game at the Patriots (2-2 but reigning AFC champs), a home game against the undefeated Vikings (4-0), road games at the Rams (2-2 and Super Bowl favorites ) and Saints (1-2; host Atlanta on Monday), and home against Buffalo (3-1).
The Packers went 2-1 against the Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers, who have a combined record of 2-9. Those eight teams coming up have a combined record of 21-14.
The Packers had to hang on for dear life against the winless Bucs. An offense led by Jordan Love and Matt LaFleur ranks 27th with 18.3 points per game.
On the bright side, the offensive line was solid against the Bucs and should get better once Kevin Zeitler enters at right guard and the new front builds chemistry week after week. With time, Love can carve up defenses. If Love has time, Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft can make things happen.

title: Snaps, Studs and Dud From Packers’ Win Over Buccaneers
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers’ victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wasn’t artistic but it was important. Over the last 10 years, teams that start 2-2 have a 41.0 percent chance of reaching the playoffs while teams that open 1-3 tumble to 14.5 percent.
So, it wasn’t pretty, but the 17-14 victory, which was powered in part by a new offensive line, was pretty important.
Here’s a look at the snaps along with a couple studs and one dud following a 17-14 victory.
The Packers played 60 snaps on offense against the Buccaneers.
Quarterback: Jordan Love played every snap. After taking a beating in the first three games – he had been on the receiving end of more quarterback hits than any player in the league – he was not sacked and hit only twice, according to the official stats.
Running backs: Last week against Atlanta, Kaleb Johnson outsnapped MarShawn Lloyd. Against Tampa Bay, Lloyd played 33 snaps, Johnson played 17 and Chris Brooks played 10. Brooks started and had an explosive run but missed most of the game with an injured ankle.
Johnson broke two tackles on his 31-yard run but fumbled for the second time in his three games. Lloyd caught a career-high five passes, including a 16-yarder that he punctuated with a hurdle, but also fumbled.
“I think a great teacher’s the bench,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “If guys don’t start holding onto the ball, they’re going to be sitting on the bench.”
That’s a great statement and we all know his point. But, from a practical perspective, it would have left the Packers with you or me playing running back.
Receivers: On a sweltering day, Matthew Golden played 53 snaps – by far the most of the group. Christian Watson played 41, followed by 23 for Skyy Moore, 11 for Bo Melton and two for J. Michael Sturdivant. Including the Jets game in which Jayden Reed was injured, it’s clear the Packers are opting for more of a player-for-player replacement in the slot with Moore than a committee approach.
Watson and Golden through three games were on a pace to blow by 3,000 combined receiving yards. The Bucs limited Watson to three catches for 47 yards and Golden to three catches for 21 yards. Golden caught a touchdown pass but had a drop that was oh-so-close to being a fumble. He has a drop in every game, which is stunning considering how well he caught the ball in camp.
Tight ends: All is normal at tight end with Tucker Kraft playing all but five snaps. It was a typical workload from before last year’s ACL tear. Mark Redman’s value as a blocker is evident. That’s why he played a season-high 28 snaps. Josh Whyle, who was banished to special-teams work the past couple games, played 14 snaps, one more than Jonnu Smith.
Kraft had one touchdown catch but should have had two. His first two receptions were vintage run-after-catch plays. He finished with six catches for 42 yards; by our count, 41 yards came after the catch.
“My drop rate right now is terrible,” he said. “I’m on the JUGS. I’m trying to fix it. But I got to continue to press on my ball-catching ability because I can’t do anything with the rock if I don’t get it.”
Redman had a 25-yard catch and Smith had a 19-yard catch. Getting two explosive gains from the backups would be huge going forward.
Offensive line: The No. 1 line for this week went the distance. Travis Glover, who hadn’t played in a game since the 2024 playoffs, was the surprise starter at right guard and rewarded the team for its decision. Glover was never in the mix to be the starting right guard – the coaches went from Anthony Belton to Jacob Monk early in training camp and never changed direction – but clearly should have been.
Laken Tomlinson, who was signed last Saturday, deserves credit for being able to play every snap after not being in a training camp.
The line was guilty of four penalties (two by Tomlinson) and five pressures (three by Morgan). The run blocking was hit or miss. Take away the big runs by Johnson and Brooks, the other 17 carries by the backs gained 27 yards.
The Packers played 63 snaps on defense against the Buccaneers.
Defensive tackles: The Packers were shorthanded with Warren Brinson placed on injured reserve and Anthony Campbell out again with an ankle injury. Things only got worse after Devonte Wyatt left the game with an ankle injury.
Fortunately for the Packers, Wyatt returned, so the rest of the unit didn’t melt into a puddle at crunch time. As usual, Karl Brooks led the way with 35 snaps. Javon Hargrave was next with 29, followed by Wyatt with 25, Chris McClellan with 24 and Jonathan Ford with a season-low 13 as the Packers spent most of the game in nickel.
They combined for two solo tackles (one each by Wyatt and McClellan) and seven assisted tackles. Hargrave had the only quarterback hit in by far his best game of the season.
Edges: Lukas Van Ness, as usual, led from a snaps perspective with 46. A week after playing less than backup Dani Dennis-Sutton, Barryn Sorrell was second with 33 snaps. Dennis-Sutton and Brenton Cox played 24 apiece.
Van Ness had three pressures but couldn’t make the play on two potential sacks. Cox went from 0 to 100 in 0.5 seconds when he saw a bad shotgun snap and almost took down Jalon Daniels for a safety.
Linebackers: Zaire Franklin played every snap. He’s going to have to step up big time following Edgerrin Cooper’s Achilles injury. Is he capable? The eight tackles were solid from a box-score perspective.
Cooper dominated in what probably were the final 34 snaps of his season. He led the team with nine tackles and added one sack and one interception. Isaiah McDuffie played 25 snaps and Ty’Ron Hopper played five snaps when McDuffie was being checked with an injury.
Cooper’s injury doesn’t only impact the defense. McDuffie is a core player on special teams, where he is the unit captain. How much can he play on special teams if he’s an every-down player on defense?
Hopper and Nick Niemann played a team-high 16 snaps on special teams apiece, followed by McDuffie with 14.
Cornerbacks: Keisean Nixon played all 63 snaps and Brandon Cisse played 54 before dropping out late to be evaluated for a concussion. Carrington Valentine, not Benjamin St-Juste, was the next man up.
Nixon made one of the big plays of the game when he blew up a receiver screen for a loss of 3 on Tampa Bay’s second-to-last series. It was a relatively easy day, given the quarterback, but Nixon was excellent.
Safeties: Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams went the distance – they’ve played every snap this season – and Javon Bullard played a season-high 60. Including special teams, Williams has played a team-high 305 snaps this season.
There’s no getting around the enormity of Cooper’s injury. He’s been arguably the team’s best player this season and was on his way to establishing himself as one of the best linebackers in the NFL. In three-and-a-half games, he had three sacks and six tackles for losses – more than he had all of last season.
Cooper had a third-down sack on the first possession and an interception just before halftime. The Packers wouldn’t have beaten the lowly Buccaneers without him; now they’ll have to somehow win the rest of the season without him.
“ We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse , it seems like,” center Sean Rhyan said.
Williams had a huge day, too. Tampa Bay’s second possession of the game crossed midfield when Williams made a spectacular interception on a pass intended for top receiver Emeka Egbuka. And then he played the role of closer with a second-down sack and fourth-down pressure.
“Hell of a game,” fellow safety Xavier McKinney said. “He can be really f***king good.”
A player who’s not “f***king good” is MarShawn Lloyd. There are glimmers. On Green Bay’s opening possession of the second half, which resulted in a touchdown, he turned a tackle for loss into a 5-yard gain on third-and-1. It was a low-key huge play. The hurdle on the 16-yard catch was impressive, as well.
However, he fumbled at the end of the play when he foolishly tried to run…

title: Packers Report Card: Grades From Win Over Buccaneers Include Gold Star
full_text:
The report card is in for the Green Bay Packers after they escaped with a 17-14 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday.
The Packers were desperate for a victory, so they needed to find any way to get to 2-2. Falling to 1-3 would have been a crushing blow considering the Buccaneers were starting an undrafted rookie quarterback making his first NFL start.
Green Bay’s offense was good enough, even if it could not get out of its own way at times. Its defense stole the show, but has some major injury questions to answer moving forward.
Let’s dive into it with this week’s grades.
Any conversation about Green Bay’s passing offense starts with the guys up front. The Packers retooled their offensive line after last week’s disaster against Atlanta. Laken Tomlinson and Travis Glover were the new starters at guard with Anthony Belton, Jordan Morgan and Sean Rhyan manning their usual positions.
The results? They were positive. No, they were not perfect. Tomlinson was penalized twice, Glover was flagged for holding and Belton was tagged with a false start, but they were able to run a functional offense.
After Jordan Love had taken 31 hits, according to PFF, in the first three games, he took just two vs. Tampa Bay, with Morgan and Rhyan charged with one apiece. That means the two new starters did not give up any. Belton played what might have been his best game as a pro.
There are still plenty of things to work on in this phase of the game. Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Bo Melton each had one drop that was a killer in the situation it came in. Christian Watson was tagged for a pass interference penalty, though it seemed like a soft call.
Love threw a terrible interception when the Packers were looking for a score to ice the game.
Ultimately, the Packers scored just 17 points. They’ve scored more than 20 points just once, and they’ve never scored more than 22 points in a game this season.
This is an offense that was supposed to take a massive step forward this season. To date, that has not happened.
Could it? Sure. They need to clean up their mistakes,
Next week against the Chicago Bears would be a good time to start.
The run game was better than it had been through the first three weeks. That’s also a low bar to clear. Green Bay’s ground game was historically bad through the first three weeks, where a simple 6-yard gain felt like winning the Super Bowl.
They were able to create some explosive runs with Kaleb Johnson and Chris Brooks rumbling for 31 and 27 yards, respectively. They finished the day with 86 rushing yards on 25 carries. That’s not great, but it’s much better than it has been.
The bad news? Johnson and MarShawn Lloyd put the ball on the ground on Sunday. Johnson has two fumbles in three games in his three games. Lloyd’s fumble fell harmlessly out of bounds, but that has been an issue for him, as well.
After the game, Matt LaFleur said the bench was a really good teacher as to how he was going to curb Green Bay’s fumbling issues in the backfield.
The problem with that is that the only running back to not cough up the ball on Sunday was Brooks. He left the game with an ankle injury and did not have his pads on in the second half. Johnson and Lloyd were the only other backs that were active.
Could it be time for Pierre Strong next week? It does not seem like any decision is imminent for insight as to when Josh Jacobs could return to the field. This is who Green Bay has in the backfield.
They’ll need to focus on the good things they did while also fixing their ball-security issues.
This week’s degree of difficulty changed significantly when Baker Mayfield was ruled out with a thumb injury. Credit to Jalon Daniels, who did some nice things in his starting debut. He even had his team in a position to win the game largely due to a litany of mistakes the Packers continued to make on offense.
Daniels had the Bucs offense threatening field-goal range to force overtime when Jonathan Gannon decided he was going to take matters into his own hands.
With Micah Parsons and Edgerrin Cooper on the sideline, he called the number of the guy who has been one of his top players this season. That was safety Evan Williams.
“He always preaches players not plays,” Williams said after the game. “For him to call my number in that situation, it means a lot to me.”
To Williams’ credit, he made the plays. He had one interception early in the game and two pressures on the final series, including a sack on second down and another that forced a game-saving incompletion.
Gannon is going to be calling Williams’ number a lot more with Cooper out for the season and Parsons not set to return for another month .
Overall, the Packers picked off Daniels twice, sacked him three times and only allowed one pass play of more than 20 yards. They kept everything hemmed in.
Next week’s challenge remains to be seen. If Caleb Williams returns to Chicago’s starting lineup, that’s an offense that scored 59 points in the one game Williams started and finished.
Even if it isn’t, Chicago’s offense has been able to create plays with Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent under center.
For this week, however, the Packers pass with flying colors.
The Bucs wanted to run the ball to take pressure off their young quarterback. That stands to reason for any team in that situation.
To Tampa’s credit, it found enough ways to move the ball on the ground, even with Daniels himself. Daniels carried eight times for 55 yards. Bucky Irving rushed 16 times for 61 yards.
In total, Tampa Bay carried 31 times for 141 yards. That’s a 4.54-yard average. The challenge the rest of the season got much stiffer following Edgerrin Cooper’s injury, which is feared to be a season-ending torn Achilles .
On Sunday against the Bears, they will face one of the best rushing attacks in the NFL.
The Packers were fine on Sunday, but they’ll need to be much better next week.
What a weapon the Packers drafted with Trey Smack. A rookie kicker always comes into his first season as a major question mark. Yes, it’s only been five games, and his coach, Cam Achord, will be quick to point out that Smack is only as good as his last kick.
Well, his last field goal was a 58-yard bomb that gave the Packers a 10-7 lead at halftime.
Daniel Whelan was uncharacteristically inconsistent on Sunday, but the Packers did not give up any explosives in the return game and he added three more inside-the-20 punts to his tally. They did not create any either, though Skyy Moore’s 11-yard punt return gave the Packers great field position. It was a pretty ho-hum day on special teams, with a big exclamation point from a budding star at kicker.
The move to start Travis Glover at right guard was one that easily could have been met with skepticism. A sixth-round pick in 2024, Glover had not started a game in his first three seasons. In fact, he had been a healthy scratch for more games than he had played snaps on offense in his career. In fact, he hadn’t played in a game this season.
The move paid off. In the absence of Kevin Zeitler, who could be good to go next week, Glover allowed zero pressures and held his own against a defense that was likely licking its chops after the first three weeks of the season.
The only real misstep that LaFleur had was punting on fourth-and-2 from Tampa Bay’s side of the field on Green Bay’s first possession.
Yes, they were facing an undrafted rookie and trusting the defense in a spot like that is defensible. It’s also just incredibly passive. Green Bay could have taken hold of the game early. Perhaps it was a sign that LaFleur did not trust his team in that spot. He was more aggressive as the game went on.
There are things that need to be cleaned up. LaFleur’s team is penalized too much and his best players make too many sloppy mistakes.
The star of the show, however, was defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon. Gannon has proven to be an excellent hire. Save for a disaster against the Falcons where the whole team played poorly, Green Bay’s…

title: Sean Rhyan Nailed It Following Crushing Injury to Packers Star Edgerrin Cooper
full_text:
The hits just keep on coming for the Green Bay Packers.
All-Pro defensive end Micah Parsons, who the Packers mortgaged their future to acquire at the end of training camp last year, suffered a torn ACL late last season that ruined their Super Bowl hopes. He might miss another month’s worth of games.
Veteran running back Josh Jacobs remains out indefinitely following an offseason arrest.
High-priced left guard Aaron Banks has played 22 snaps in four games.
Explosive slot receiver Jayden Reed suffered a season-ending neck injury during the second snap at the Jets.
Standout right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele suffered a season-ending knee injury on the next play.
The Packers beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 17-14 on Sunday, but it was the case of one small step forward and a few giant steps back. Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, arguably the team’s best defensive player without Parsons, suffered a torn Achilles during the second half. He took one step on a third-down blitz and fell to the turf. He turned around to see who tripped him; nobody tripped him. It was his Achilles, and he quickly grabbed his ankle.
“I would suspect” that Cooper will miss the rest of the season, coach Matt LaFleur said.
How can the Packers make life miserable for quarterbacks without Parsons’ game-wrecking ability? How will the Packers find offensive balance without Jacobs? How can the Packers maximize their passing game without Reed? How can the Packers block without Banks and Bako-Bewele?
How can the defense survive without all the havoc Cooper creates?
Football is a cruel sport. Injuries are no excuse, they say. Next man up, they say.
“We’ve been kind of hit with some type of curse, it seems like,” center Sean Rhyan said.
The Packers aren’t the only team that’s injured, obviously. It’s a way of life in the NFL. But the football Gods seem to have something against green and gold.
“It’s terrible,” linebacker Isaiah McDuffie, the presumptive new starter, said. “That’s the sh****est part about this game. Guys going down, your brothers going down, I hate to see that and I just feel for him.”
Cooper is an ascending third-year star. He single-handed destroyed the Buccaneers with nine tackles, one sack and a critical interception during the first half alone.
The Packers need him. Obviously. And especially without Parsons. He’s an all-around, dominating force with three sacks and seven tackles for losses in three-and-a-half games. It’s exactly what everyone forecasted following his powerhouse finish to his rookie season. Cooper, for his part, should be parlaying his elite-level play into a contract extension.
The Packers will turn to their next man up because, well, what would they do otherwise? Play 11-on-10? Forfeit the season? McDuffie is a solid, experienced linebacker. But he’s not Cooper, in the same way that Lukas Van Ness isn’t Parsons, Skyy Moore isn’t Reed and the veteran guards aren’t Bako-Bewele.
“There’s no words you can tell someone in that moment,” said tight end Tucker Kraft, who was having a monster breakout season last year when he suffered a torn ACL.”
“Coop wasn’t alone in his draft class. We got Ty’Ron Hopper in there, too,” Kraft continued. “It’s just the next-man up mentality, as cliche as it sounds, as sad as it sounds, to lose one of our weapons like that. Very unfortunate, but it is what it is.”
It will be all hands on deck in the Packers’ quest to stay afloat until Parsons returns. And not just the linebackers. Everyone needs to play better, whether it’s another of young standouts like Evan Williams, or veterans like Zaire Franklin and Keisean Nixon.
“It definitely numbs it down a little bit, the thrill of a win, just because I feel like guys all know what he means to this team, what he means to this defense,” said Williams, who had an early interception and two critical blitzes to help clinch the game.
“He’s somebody that just sets the tone into every game. He’s somebody that’s going to get us all jumpstarted. That’s going to be definitely a tough hole to fill but again, at the same time, it’s a next-man-up league. We’re definitely praying for him to come back and get his rehab done and come back as fast as he can, but other people got to step up and show what they’re capable of. That’s the name of the game.”
It is because, again, what’s the alternative?
It will be incumbent on players like Franklin, the defensive captain who was relishing his time with Cooper, to lead by word and by deed.
“That’s one of those things that it’s a win, but it don’t feel like a win,” he said. “Obviously, me and Coop, we’re locked in. So, just my boy going down, that hurt. But, obviously, Duffie stepped up in a major way. That’s who he is. That’s who he’s been his whole career, that’s why he’s got a ‘C’ on his chest. He’s a special player. He’s going to make plays when we need them, too.
“So, it’s just the next-man-up mentality. I understand when a superstar like Coop goes down, guys have got to step up and make plays and that’s what we did.”
Can they do it against the juggernaut Bears offense on Sunday? The explosive Cowboys the following week? The dynamic Lions after that?
Really, it all seems like too much to overcome. The Packers were a flawed team, anyway, with a limited margin for error. Now, they’ve lost their best player. The team crumbled after Parsons’ knee injury last year. Can the Packers survive without Cooper long enough for Parsons’ return to be meaningful?
The situation seems bleak, but the show will go on.
“You can’t let that affect the way you play,” Williams said. “You’ve just got to do your job. As soon as you start to do too much and feel like you’ve got to make plays or fill in for somebody that’s gone, that’s when there’s holes in the defense and explosives start to show.
“So it’s just about doing your job and trusting the man next to you, even though that’s not going to be Coop. I’ve got trust in all the guys in this locker room. We put in a lot of time in training camp to get to this point right here. Regardless who it is, we’re going to ride with him all the way.”
