title: Evan Williams Leads Winners, Losers From Packers’ Win at Buccaneers
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers went into Tampa Bay on Sunday desperate for a win. They were 1-2, and had just gotten the brakes beaten off of them by the Atlanta Falcons last Thursday.
They caught a break when they did not have to face Baker Mayfield, who killed them the last time he started against them in December 2023. Instead, they faced undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels, who was making his first career start. Furthermore, he was the first undrafted rookie to start in the first four weeks of the season since the 1970s, according to the Fox broadcast.
The Packers entered the fourth quarter with a 17-7 lead and a chance to finish the job, as they talked about all offseason. Try as it might, the offense could not give the game away. Two fourth-quarter turnovers were erased by two huge plays from safety Evan Williams.
He leads off are our weekly winners and losers from Green Bay’s 17-14 victory over Tampa Bay.
The Packers were looking for a spark in the first half as Tampa Bay started to drive the field with Jalon Daniels and their run game making some headway against their defense.
Daniels loaded up to throw the ball near the left sideline as Williams dove in front of the receiver for an interception that was initially ruled incomplete before a quick conference rightfully ruled that Williams had made the play.
Later in the game, Williams broke up a pass to force a fourth down. He was all over the field.
The best players, however, save their biggest plays for the biggest spots of the game. Williams did just that as Jonathan Gannon sent him on a blitz late in the fourth quarter with the Bucs threatening to tie or take the lead.
Williams hemmed Daniels into the pocket and got him on the ground for a critical sack. The Bucs had two downs to pick up 16 yards.
Gannon went back to the well sending Williams on a pressure to try and ice the game.
Williams did not finish off the sack, but he held onto Daniels’ foot long enough to make sure that he could not get much mustard on a desperation heave to Ted Hurst. The ball fell harmlessly incomplete, and the Packers escaped Tampa Bay with a win.
For a defense desperate for playmakers, Williams is certainly emerging as one of them in the secondary.
The Packers looked like they were going to trail at halftime when Edgerrin Cooper made his presence known to finish the first half.
Jalon Daniels dropped back to pass and attempted to hit his checkdown in the middle of the field when Cooper took flight.
He dove in front of the running back for a diving interception. His catch, and return, gave the Packers the ball in scoring range and led to Trey Smack’s 58-yard-bomb as time expired.
Unfortunately for both the Packers and Cooper, he left the game on a cart after an injury that did not look good. He was ruled out almost immediately with an Achilles injury.
Cooper has been one of Green Bay’s best players this season. If he is down for a significant period of time, that would be an enormous blow to the defense.
Not for performance issues. Jonathan Gannon’s defense remains the most consistent group on this team. However, he's starting to lose some of his studs.
Micah Parsons is not coming back this week, and who knows when he will be. To add to the list of questions that Gannon must answer on a given week, now he's lost star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper for the season with an Achilles injury.
“I would suspect that, yes,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Cooper missing the rest of the season.
Losing top players makes the job harder for any coach. Without Cooper and Parsons, Gannon is likely down his top two players. He'll be working overtime to earn his paycheck this week and for the rest of the season.
What a weapon that Trey Smack has turned out to be for the Packers’ special teams. He’s able to score from almost any spot on the field. That’s a slight exaggeration, but he’s been a clear upgrade in the kicking game through four weeks this season.
A new competitive advantage in the NFL is the ability to make kicks from more 55-plus and longer. The Packers did not have that option a season ago with Brandon McManus kicking injured, and kicking poorly.
Smack has now made two kicks from that distance, as he added another one on Sunday to give the Packers a 10-7 lead at halftime.
Yes, the bar to clear was low coming into Sunday's game but the Packers looked much better up front. They had two new guards in the lineup with Laken Tomlinson and Travis Glover getting the starts on the left and right side. They were not clean. Tomlinson was penalized twice and Glover once. Right tackle Anthony Belton was tagged with a false start. Left tackle Jordan Morgan missed a block on a run play in the first half.
For the most part, though, they were able to run a functional offense. Jordan Love was not under duress on every single snap. They found minor glimpses of being able to put a ground game together.
“It was it was great,” Love said. “I think the O line did a great job today (with) pass protection, run game. Obviously, just keep me clean, give me some time. They did a great job, and you could feel the difference back there for sure.”
Was it perfect? No. There's still a lot of issues that need to be worked out.
What it was, was functional. Which is progress at this point in the season and should only grow with the potential addition of Kevin Zeitler to the starting lineup next week.
“I think it just calms down the O-line,” coach Matt LaFleur said last week of the veteran additions. “When you have veterans in there who have been through the war, certainly we’ve got young guys playing beside them, that can definitely settle things down. We’re just trying to get these guys integrated, get them up to speed, ramp them up and see what they can do.”
If wasn’t great, but it was calm – much calmer – to the benefit of Love’s health and welfare.
At the risk of sounding like fictional dad from That 70s Show , Red Foreman, it’s not hunting season, but if it was, you’d think the Packers were hunting a foot.
They continue to shoot themselves in the foot regularly on offense. If it’s not their quarterback getting hit, it’s drops. If it’s not drops, it’s penalties. If it’s not penalties, they’re losing yards in goal-to-go situations.
It’s not like role players are the ones making these mistakes either. Often, it Green Bay’s stars.
Tucker Kraft dropped a would-be touchdown on Green Bay’s first scoring drive of the game. Jordan Morgan was beaten on a down block that resulted in a TFL on first-and-goal from Matthew Golden bailed them out, though, with a nifty catch on fourth-and-goal at the goal line.
Golden would join the drop party later with a catch that was initially ruled a fumble, but instead just ended a drive on third down in the second quarter.
Christian Watson was tagged for a questionable pass interference play in the first half, but that essentially killed a drive.
Jordan Love threw what might have been a killer interception as the Packers were looking to ice the game in the fourth quarter. That came on the heels of a Kaleb Johnson fumble at the goal line.
Save for Johnson, those are all of Green Bay’s stars in their offense. They cannot continue to make these mistakes with the gauntlet that is on their schedule through the next four weeks.
How many chances is Bo Melton going to get to make a big play down the field? There probably aren’t many with a passing game that is structured around Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft.
Melton had a chance on Green Bay’s opening possession to put the Packers in the red zone, or even score a touchdown if he could have kept his footing.
Instead, as Melton laid out on a perfectly thrown ball from Jordan Love, who was operating from a clean pocket, and dropped the ball as he fell to the turf.
It’s just one play, but just Green Bay’s offense has not proven capable of overcoming much, if any adversity throughout the course of the season. They have to make the plays that are in front of them.
The Packers have had some…

title: ‘I’m Sick’: Packers Beat Buccaneers But Hit With Another Devastating Loss
full_text:
Even when the Green Bay Packers win, they lose.
The Green Bay Packers beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 17-14 on Sunday. However, they lost star linebacker Edgerrin Cooper to an Achilles injury in the third quarter.
With their first drive of the second half, the Packers drove to a touchdown that extended their lead to 17-7.
On a third-and-8 on the ensuing possession, safety Xavier McKinney blitzed from the left side of the defense for a sack. On the right side of the defense, Cooper took one step forward and fell to the turf. He acted as if he had just been tripped – he was not – then grabbed his ankle. A couple minutes later, he was driven off the field on a cart.
The Packers ruled out Cooper with an Achilles injury.
“Man, I’m sick,” quarterback Jordan Love said.
“Not good,” coach Matt LaFleur said of Cooper’s outlook. “I would suspect that” he will miss the rest of the season.
The Packers, already playing without Micah Parsons following last year’s knee injury and with right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele and receiver Jayden Reed out with season-ending injuries sustained during the Week 2 win at the Jets, it was another devastating blow to a team that opened the season with Super Bowl aspirations.
Love was 22-of-30 passing for 197 yards with touchdowns to Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft. Critically, he was not sacked. The Packers were 2-of-10 on third down but 3-of-3 on fourth down.
Green Bay improved to 2-2 and will host the rival Chicago Bears on Sunday.
“We’ll take the win, for sure. We needed that,” Love said.
Jordan Love’s interception gave the Buccaneers and their undrafted rookie quarterback, Jalon Daniels, a chance late in the game. On third-and-3, Daniels hit tight end Cade Otten for 4 to give them a first down at the 40 at the 2-minute warning.
On the next play, Daniels hit Otten in the flat for a catch-and-run gain of 14. After Cooper’s replacement, Isaiah McDuffie, missed a point-blank sack of Daniels, Evan Williams made amends on the next play by dropping Daniels for a loss of 6.
A short pass on third-and-16 made it fourth-and-11 with the teams exchanging timeouts with 1:34 to go. Williams struck again with another well-timed blitz. He grabbed Daniels around the leg and hung on for dear life; Daniels’ pass was short of the mark to end the game.
With the Packers clinging to a 17-14 lead, they drove to the brink of a touchdown on a methodical drive early in the fourth quarter. On third-and-3, Love hit Christian Watson for 18. On third-and-4, linebacker Alex Anzalone was called for defensive holding – a ticky-tack call against Skyy Moore.
This had been a flirt-with-disaster drive, though. Travis Glover, the surprise starter at right guard, was flagged for holding. Tucker Kraft, who dropped one touchdown pass but caught another, was flagged for a false start. The Packers overcame those miscues, and then got a huge break when MarShawn Lloyd’s fumble bounced out of bounds at Tampa’s 16.
Finally, on first-and-goal at the 3, Kaleb Johnson got the ball knocked loose by, officially, defensive tackle A’Shawn Robinson. The Bucs recovered at the 4 with 9:06 to go.
The Packers’ defense rose to the occasion. After the Bucs gained a first down on a receiver screen, Keisean Nixon blew up another receiver screen. On third-and-14, center Graham Barton’s shotgun snap appeared to hit him in the butt. Daniels recovered but was sacked by Brenton Cox at the 1.
The Packers took over at the Bucs’ 33 after Skyy Moore’s 11-yard punt return. On first down, Love’s checkdown to Lloyd gained 13 after he hurdled cornerback Zyon McCollum. However, moments later, Love fired one up the seam to Matthew Golden. Cornerback Jacob Parrish came off his man, tight end Jonnu Smith, and made a big-time interception, which gave the Bucs the ball at their 15 with 4:18 remaining in regulation.
The new offensive line, with veteran addition Laken Tomlinson at left guard and with Travis Glover making his first start at right guard with Kevin Zeitler not ready, Love was not sacked.
“It was great,” Love said. “I think the O-line did a great job today, just keeping me clean, giving me some time. You could feel the difference back there, for sure.”
The Packers led 10-7 at halftime thanks to interceptions by Evan Williams and Cooper turning into a touchdown catch by Matthew Golden and a 58-yard field goal by Trey Smack.
Daniels, Tampa Bay’s undrafted rookie quarterback, played with solid poise in the first half. However, he made two big mistakes that allowed Green Bay to take the lead.
First, he thought he had Emeka Egbuka at the sideline. Instead, Williams made a brilliant interception before tumbling out of bounds. One play later, Chris Brooks took advantage by excellent blocking from the new left-side tandem of Jordan Morgan and lake Tomlinson along with tight end Mark Redman for a gain of 27. That was, as you might have guessed, the team’s longest run of the year.
Late in the half, the Buccaneers were on the move toward the go-ahead score. Instead, Cooper jumped in front of a pass to Kameron Johnson. His return to the Bucs’ 44 set up Smack for his bomb to give Green Bay the lead at intermission.
With the ball to start the second half, the Packers got a chance to double up. And they did, with an 80-yard touchdown drive to extend their lead to 17-7.
On the first play, Love threw a wobbly pass over the middle to Redman for a gain of 25. Then, on third-and-1, MarShawn Lloyd sidestepped a tackle for loss for a 5-yard run and a big first down. One play later, Kaleb Johnson rumbled up the middle for 31 yards to the 5. Center Sean Rhyan, starting right guard Travis Glover and Redman had key blocks on the team’s new long run of the year.
Finally, on third-and-2, Love looped one to Tucker Kraft at the pylon. The play was initially ruled as incomplete but coach Matt LaFleur won the challenge. With a 10-point lead, the Packers were in good shape against a rookie quarterback.
Or so it seemed. With Cooper and his backup, Isaiah McDuffie, on the sideline, Daniels drove the Buccaneers to a touchdown. On third-and-3, Daniels broke contain and flipped the ball into the flat to running back Kenneth Gainwell, who was open against Zaire Franklin and scored. Just like that, it was 17-14 with 14:49 to go.

title: Studs and Duds as Packers Lead Buccaneers at Halftime
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers lead the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 10-7 on Sunday.
The Packers took a 7-0 lead on Matthew Golden’s leaping touchdown catch on fourth-and-goal at the 2. It was the third fourth-down conversion on the drive, which was set up by Evan Williams’ interception.
The Buccaneers, after going three-and-out on two of their first three possessions, took advantage of a short punt by Daniel Whelan for a 54-yard touchdown drive. Sean Tucker gained 8 on fourth-and-1 before scoring from the 2.
The Packers took their halftime following Edgerrin Cooper’s interception and Trey Smack’s 58-yard field goal on the final play. Green Bay will get the ball to start the second half.
Here’s our first-half winners and losers.
Evan Williams isn’t just one of the NFL’s best young safeties. He’s one of the best safeties, period.
Williams, who entered the game with a team-high 25 tackles, baited Jalon Daniels into an interception on the second possession. Daniels fired a pass at the sideline to top receiver Emeka Egbuka. Williams, though, made a sensational interception at the sideline. The Packers turned the turnover into a touchdown.
Then, late in the first half, Williams made a superb pass breakup on third-and-1.
Edgerrin Cooper progressed through the concussion protocol on Saturday and dominated on Sunday with nine tackles, including one sack, and an interception late in the first half that at (at least) a six-point swing as the Packers took a 10-7 lead into intermission.
COOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOP 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/kApADhGYbt
It wasn’t a bad start for Jordan Morgan. He, obviously, had a key role in Jordan Love having time in the pocket throughout the half.
However, on first-and-goal at the 1, he missed linebacker Josiah Trotter as Chris Brooks lost 2 yards. On second down, he was pushed into the backfield by big, powerful A’Shawn Robinson, which doomed MarShawn Lloyd to a loss of 3.
The Packers scored a touchdown, anyway.
Here’s the Tucker Kraft that the Packers signed to a big contract extension before Week 1. That he got off to a slow start to the season was no surprise – he was coming back from a torn ACL, after all.
On the opening series, Kraft took a screen for 17 yards. It was vintage Kraft with 18 yards after the catch and two broken tackles. On the second possession, he converted a fourth-and-1 with an easy 10-yard catch run. Later on the drive, on fourth-and-1, he took a quarterback sneak for 3, with Jordan Morgan and even Jordan Love providing the blocking.
And then, on the first play of the second quarter and on a continuation of the fourth-and-1 drive, Kraft was wide open in the corner of the end zone and dropped a perfectly placed ball by Love.
First, on fourth-and-goal at the 2, Matthew Golden drew his third pass-interference penalty of the season. It was a bit of a weak call, to be sure, with Jordan Love and Golden not on the same page, but Jacob Parrish had his arm wrapped around Golden for a moment.
That was electric! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/VLkxJO2SFL
On the next play, Golden caught a fade over Keionte Scott for the touchdown. It was teach-tape stuff, with Golden winning at the line of scrimmage, making the catch and spinning away from Scott to keep the ball out of harm’s way.
However, after the Buccaneers tied the game 7-7, Golden beat Parrish cleanly for what should have been a catch and first down. Instead, Parrish knocked the ball loose. The fumble was overturned by replay but the fourth-down drop meant a punt.
This week, coach Matt LaFleur mentioned Bo Melton as one of the “committee” members who would help replace Jayden Reed.
Well, on third-and-2 on the opening possession, Melton broke free up the seam for what should have been a catch of 30-plus yards into the red zone. Instead, he dropped the ball when he hit the turf.
“We got the guys for it,” Melton said of replacing Reed. “As you can see, we make plays at receiver. We have a bunch of guys who have made plays, who continue to make plays. We trust and believe in ourselves regardless. We’ve done it before. It’s nothing new. Even when J-Reed was here, guys were playing. Guys were still getting their opportunities. Your role might increase but we’re always ready for that. That’s part of the game. That’s what you want.”
For the first time this season, Jordan Love didn’t spend his time getting hit from the left, hit from the right or hit up the middle. Love wasn’t sacked and was hit only once – by Vita Vea, who eventually bullied Sean Rhyan into the lap of Love.
Against a blitz-happy defense, it was a strong performance with Laken Tomlinson starting at left guard and Travis Glover getting the start at right guard.
The running game was, generally, terrible. Chris Brooks had a 27-yard run, with left guard Laken Tomlinson, left tackle Jordan Morgan and tight end Mark Redman getting Brooks into the clear. The Buccaneers, who entered the game ranked second in the NFL against the run, hadn’t allowed a run of longer than 14 yards to start the season.
Otherwise, though, it was a whole lot of nothing. Brooks’ other three carries gained 3 yards, MarShawn Lloyd had five carries for 5 yards and Kaleb Johnson had three carries for 3 yards. So, other than the one big run, the Packers’ backs carried 11 times for 11 yards.
The Packers haven't handled the blitz well this year and now will face "blitz monster" coach Todd Bowles. That's among 3⃣ reasons why they'll lose. https://t.co/QxzVB3QXAs Then again, the new linemen will be one of 3⃣ reasons why they'll win.⬇️ https://t.co/3KwFYpCPMF

title: Packers’ Offensive Line at Buccaneers Features One Newcomer, One Curveball
full_text:
On Wednesday, the Green Bay Packers signed Wisconsin native and former Wisconsin All-American Kevin Zeitler to be the team’s starting right guard.
Without a training camp to get into prime condition physically and with just three practices to get ready mentally, Zeitler is inactive for Sunday’s game at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Based on warmups, the starting offensive line will consist of Morgan at left tackle, Laken Tomlinson at left guard, Sean Rhyan at center, Travis Glover at right guard and Anthony Belton at right tackle.
We half-joked about this this week. https://t.co/LU7f9gh3lN
Glover, obviously, is a major curveball, though he did take a few first-team reps while reporters were present this week.
Tomlinson and Glover are the team’s fifth and sixth starters at guard this season.
Travis Glover was a sixth-round pick by the Packers in 2024. He played in seven games as a rookie and logged 13 snaps on offense. His big chance came in the playoff loss to the Eagles to cap his rookie season. Due to injuries, Glover was thrown into the fire with 23 snaps at left guard and five snaps at right guard. He was benched at one point after being found guilty of three penalties.
Glover spent last year on injured reserve – coach Matt LaFleur had called him one of the team’s most improved players at the time of the injury.
This training camp, his time was split between right guard and right tackle. This preseason, he played 39 snaps at right tackle and 28 snaps at right guard. He allowed two pressures in the passing game.
Another homecoming was put on hold. Donovan Jennings, who was born in Tampa and played his college ball in Tampa-based South Florida, will be one of the backups this week.
“It’s a pretty cool feeling to be able to play all my college home games in the stadium that I'm about to play in the next level,” Jennings told Packers On SI on Friday. “But just want to go in there and get a win at the end of the day.”
Jennings started in place of Aaron Banks at left guard in Week 1 against Minnesota but struggled along with the rest of the line. Banks returned for Week 2 but dropped out at halftime; Jennings got another chance but suffered a hand injury and couldn’t finish the game. In Week 3, the Packers turned to Jager Burton at left guard, and that was a disaster.
Jennings was hoping for a chance to make amends for his performance at the Vikings. And maybe he will with a potential guard rotation on a hot day.
“Yeah, that’s pretty much what I want to do,” he said. “I want to go out there for the team, go out there and get the ‘W’ like we know and just get the ball rolling. Me personally, I want to go out there and play my brand of football. I'm just excited – really excited – to go out and play good.”
The Packers signed Laken Tomlinson off the Cowboys’ practice squad on Saturday, Mekhi Becton to the practice squad on Monday and Kevin Zeitler to the roster on Wednesday. Of those three former first-round picks, Tomlinson will start, Becton was not elevated from the practice squad and Zeitler is inactive.
“I feel like I can come in and provide some stability, some toughness, some leadership, as well,” Tomlinson said this week. “Obviously going into Year 12, I’ve played a lot of ball. I feel like I still got a lot left in the tank. I feel like I can bring a lot to the team.”
That’s what the Packers are counting on. Their budget-busting starter at left guard, Aaron Banks, has played only 22 snaps this season and is inactive again. Tomlinson, who has started 162 games in his career, will get the call.
“I’m here working with the coaches,” he said. “I’m here learning the playbook, everything. Familiarity with the scheme, it helps a ton and now it’s just going out there and working with the guys.”
On a miserably hot and humid day, it will be interesting to see how many snaps Tomlinson is capable of playing. Jager Burton struggled at left guard last week against Atlanta and was questionable on the final injury report with a groin injury.
“Feel great, honestly,” he said. “The work I’ve put in this offseason, it’s been phenomenal. I have a great team back home. Definitely a humbling experience throughout this whole process, but the hunger is still there.”
Of playing on Sunday, he said: “Whatever Coach wants. Anything they want from me, I’m ready to go.”
Zeitler took the same approach. He just didn’t have the three weeks on Dallas’ practice squad to get ramped up.
“It’s been great, honestly,” Zeitler said on Friday . “An absolute whirlwind in every possible way but it’s been great to get back on there. It’s great getting back into football, learning all sorts of new stuff and, like, thought theories. It’s just great. So, keep it rolling.”
Green Bay’s offensive line has been by far the biggest reason for the team’s slow start in terms of wins and losses, points scored and overall efficiency.
According to Pro Football Focus, 34 quarterbacks have faced at least 15 under-pressure dropbacks. Love has faced the third-highest pressure rate, as he’s felt the heat on 44.4 percent of his dropbacks.
Love is not a good quarterback when under pressure – he was the least-accurate passer in the league last season and is struggling again. His 36.0 completion percentage ranks 29th. Being under constant duress and taking more hits than any quarterback in the league has only heightened the issues. It’s hard to play quarterback when you don’t know if you’re going to be hit, when you’re going to be hit and who you’re going to be hit by.
Pass block grades in true pass sets only You'll never guess who comes in last here pic.twitter.com/6ChM4tRjpl
The run game has been equally atrocious. Are Green Bay’s running backs good, mediocre or bad? Who could possibly answer that question when they’ve been hit at or behind the line of scrimmage almost 44 percent of the time?
Which RBs are getting met in the backfield the most Data: @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/A4HUrzShFX
Or they’re averaging barely 1.3 yards per carry before contact?
Rushing Yards Before Contact / Attempt 1. LAR  3.13 2. BUF  2.92 3. DET  2.65 4. BAL  2.20 5. SF  2.11 ... 32. LV  1.01 Data: @FantasyPtsData pic.twitter.com/FWnduXXD4f
It’s, obviously, a different game for a running back when you can guild up a head of steam instead of having to dodge defenders almost instantly.
The Packers have who they have at tackle. Their left tackle is Jordan Morgan, a former first-round pick. Their right tackle is Anthony Belton, who is starting in place of premier blocker Zach Bako-Bewele. Their center is Sean Rhyan, who was given a contract averaging $11 million per season based on a half-season of performance.
Where the Packers could act boldly was at guard, with left guard Aaron Banks inactive for the third time in four games this season due to knee and toe injuries and right guard Jacob Monk inactive with a quad injury after three poor starting performances.
So, belatedly, general manager Brian Gutekunst signed Laken Tomlinson off Dallas’ practice squad, Kevin Zeitler from his home in Nashville and Mekhi Becton to the practice squad. ( Becton was not elevated for the same reason as why Zeitler is inactive.)
Zeitler and Tomlinson are proven blockers, not just in the run game but the pass game. They will be immediate upgrades, especially when they are fully acclimated. The hope, presumably, is that will be the case for next Sunday’s showdown against the Chicago Bears.
It’s wild to consider the fate of the season for a team with high-priced starters at practically every position group will hinge on two veteran lineman who weren’t with a team for training camp.
Their talents will be a big plus. So will their experience – eventually – with Tomlinson alongside Morgan, who will be making his fifth career start at left tackle, and Zeitler alongside Belton, who will be making his third career start at right tackle.
“I think that’s just part of the job being a vet at this point,” Zeitler said. “I stayed after the first day talking through some…

title: Packers-Buccaneers Inactives: Only One of Two Veteran Linemen Will Play
full_text:
While Kevin Zeitler spoke optimistically that he’d be able to play after three just practices, the veteran starting right guard is inactive for the Green Bay Packers’ game at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday.
The other veteran guard signed this week, Laken Tomlinson, is active. He potentially will start at left guard and Donovan Jennings probably could be the starter at right guard in his Tampa homecoming.
Asked what he’d tell the coaches if they asked if he was ready, Zeitler on Friday said: “I’m just going to keep practicing the rest of this week. We’ve still got tomorrow. We’re just going to keep going and whatever happens, happens.”
With Warren Brinson placed on injured reserve on Saturday and nobody elevated from the practice squad, the Packers had to name only four inactives. The others:
Left guard Aaron Banks: The Packers’ $77 million starter is inactive for the third time in four games. He started against the Jets in Week 2 but dropped out at halftime. He was ruled out on Friday with knee and toe injuries.
“He’s just working through it. We’ll see where he’s at,” coach Matt LaFleur said on Friday when asked about Banks moving slowly while rehabbing with a trainer earlier in the week.
Right guard Jacob Monk: Monk was handed the starting job during training camp and got the nod for the first three games. He missed the end of the loss to Atlanta with an injured quad and was ruled out on Friday.
Over the long haul, Zeitler will be the starter at right guard. Just not on Sunday.
Defensive tackle Anthony Campbell: Campbell injured an ankle in his NFL debut against the Jets in Week 2. He will miss his second consecutive game. Coupled with Brinson’s injury, the Packers have only five defensive tackles – a potential factor for a sweltering day.
Inactives for #GBvsTB ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/9G1PbJELPn
Quarterback Baker Mayfield, of course, is out with a thumb injury sustained late in last week’s loss to the Vikings. Undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels will start and veteran Easton Stick was elevated from the practice squad.
Mayfield is one of the better quarterbacks in the game. Daniels is a complete unknown. When in doubt, he might prefer to run it; he excelled as a dual-threat quarterback at Kansas.
“Sometimes the defense wins,” Daniels told reporters this week. “When the defense is locking everything up, sometimes you have to be able to try to get out of the pocket and try to be able to go make plays. Because, at the end of the day, at the quarterback position your objective is to try to be able to move the chains every single play.
“If the defense is doing their job, my ability to be able to get out of the pocket, try to be able to get out and try to go find a receiver downfield, and if I can't receiver downfield the objective is to try to be able to move the sticks.”
Jalon Daniels is set to become the first rookie QB to start this season 🔜 pic.twitter.com/WnWEjXnHlE
Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon, without much tape to look at when studying Daniels, went back to the quarterback’s tape at Kansas. He’s going to want to sow the seeds of confusion.
"Defenses, whenever they see a rookie quarterback, they try to do everything that they can to try to be able to blitz the quarterback, try to be able to make him get confused, try to be able to disguise everything that they can, and I'm aware of that,” Daniels said. “Me being aware of that, I'm trying to do everything that I can to, like I said, lean on Easton, lean on Bake and try to be able to get every single answer I can to everything they've had on film.”
Their other inactives include this year’s first-round pick, outside linebacker Rueben Bain. Rookie fifth-round guard Billy Schrauth, who played at Fond du Lac (Wis.) High School before starring at Notre Dame, is active, as well.
Cornerback Benjamin Morrison, who played most of the Week 1 game at Cincinnati and started in Week 2 against Cleveland, also is inactive due to an injured quad.
The Packers haven't handled the blitz well this year and now will face "blitz monster" coach Todd Bowles. That's among 3⃣ reasons why they'll lose. https://t.co/QxzVB3QXAs Then again, the new linemen will be one of 3⃣ reasons why they'll win.⬇️ https://t.co/3KwFYpCPMF

title: Texans Open WR Tank Dell's Practice Window: What It Means & What's Next
full_text:
After stretching four weeks into the 2026 NFL season, we've finally got an update from the Houston Texans on what's next for wide receiver Tank Dell as he looks to make his return to the field for the first time in over 20 months.
And based on the newest intel heading into Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans, things seem to be trending in a really positive direction for Dell's pending recovery, despite what some previous buzz around the league may have hinted at .
According to Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans, the team will be activating Dell's 21-day practice window from injured reserve, along with offensive tackle Braden Smith and defensive tackle Kayden McDonald.
"This week, we expect to open the window for Tank Dell, Braden Smith, and for Kayden McDonald," Ryans said on Monday.
Knowing that Dell is going to be off the injured reserve list and on the practice field this week, it's the most noteworthy development that the Texans wideout has faced in his lengthy recovery process thus far.
Dell has been sidelined since December 2024 with a devastating knee injury he suffered against the Kansas City Chiefs, effectively damaging his ACL, MCL, LCL, meniscus, and kneecap, and has kept him out of the action for Houston's offense since.
However, knowing that Dell is going to be practicing this week, it means we're one step closer to seeing the Texans' pass-catcher and one of C.J. Stroud's favorite targets back on the field for a regular-season game.
As Dell's 21-day practice window is now opened, the Texans have three weeks from when their practice starts to make a decision on their wide receiver's roster status.
By the end of those three weeks, the team will have to elevate that player to the 53-man roster, trade or release that player to another team, or place them back on season-ending injured reserve.
For Dell, it's eye-catching for two reasons: he's finally able to get back on the field for an organized practice for the first time since training camp, but it also marks the next step in his long-awaited return to the field.
The Texans opening his window is a hint from the team that they know Dell is close to returning. The coaching staff will certainly want to get a look at their returning pass-catcher in multiple practices before they set him loose as a part of the 53-man roster, though this is a huge step towards getting to that point.
While the Texans are now on the clock with Dell's 21-day recovery, they have a bit of time on their hands before they're forced to make a decision on his roster status.
If the Texans open Dell's practice window this week, it gives them three full games before that 21-day stretch expires, which connects perfectly to Houston's Week 8 bye that begins at the end of October: they'll face the Titans in Week 5, the Jacksonville Jaguars in London for Week 6, and the New York Giants at home in Week 7.
After that Week 7 game finishes up–– and if all goes well in practice through the next three weeks–– the Texans will then likely be due to officially activate Dell to the 53-man roster, and give him another full week on their bye before he'd have a chance to make his season debut against the LA Chargers in Week 9.
So there's still patience to be had before we get to see Dell catching passes in-game from Stroud once again. Yet, knowing that his practice window is live certainly gives some extra optimism that his return will be coming sooner rather than later.

title: Texans' Snap Counts vs. Cowboys: What Stood Out in Week 4 Loss
full_text:
The Houston Texans have now lost the first four games on their 2026 schedule after the events of Week 4's loss to the Dallas Cowboys, 30-34 .
And in the fallout of the Texans' Week 4 loss, we've now gotten our hands on the snap count totals from both Houston and Dallas in this weekend's game, giving us a glimpse at who on the roster played a good chunk of the day, and who might've seen a bit more of the opposite:
And by looking at the Texans' side of things when it comes to their snap totals seen this weekend, there are a few noteworthy outcomes that deserve a bit of attention more than the rest for one reason or another.
Let's sort through four interesting aspects of the Texans' snap totals that stood out from their Week 4 loss to their in-state rivals :
After weeks of much clamor for Noel to get more snaps and targets his way compared to the first three games of the year, this game against Dallas really felt like the Texans were eager to involve Noel a bit more than they had before. And in the reps he got, he took advantage of them in a big way. Noel had the second most yards (85) and snaps (34/62% of the offense) within the receiver room behind only Nico Collins. And with the multiple explosives he generated, it gives the Texans more reason to get him involved moving forward.
After the Texans had known Azeez Al-Shaair was going to miss this week with a groin injury, the expectation remained that fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz would be the second starting linebacker to fill in next to Jake Hansen within Houston's front seven. But it wasn't Woodaz to get the call up. Practice squad elevation Kenneth Murray was the one claiming a lion's share of those linebacker snaps, outside of the eight that he was out of the mix due to injury. Only then was Woodaz thrown on the defensive side of the ball, which might be a sign of just how polished the Texans view their day three rookie at this point in his career .
This was the first weekend the Texans' defensive line has had to do without Mario Edwards Jr., who tore his ACL in Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts to sideline him for the rest of the season. As to how the Texans pushed forward without Edwards, Jaden Crumedy took the snaps as Houston DT3 behind Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai. He was mostly a non-factor, but the good news is that second-round rookie Kayden McDonald is gearing up to be elevated from injured reserve heading into Week 5.
This piece doesn't show up within the Texans' snap totals, which is because the player in reference didn't see a single look in any capacity in Week 4––that being second-round rookie tight end Marlin Klein . If anything, the Texans' first three weeks of offense seemed to hint that Klein was due for more snaps moving forward, not less. Instead, Houston sat their day two rookie out entirely, were limited in their tight end usage as a whole, and leaves you wondering as to what the front office's plan was when bringing the Michigan tight end into the building in the first place.

title: Texans' Defense Gets Much-Needed Lifeline as Rookie Returns From Injury
full_text:
The Houston Texans have been hit with several injuries on both sides of the ball across the first quarter of their 2026 season en route to their gloomy 0-3 start.
Among the names who have missed at least one game for the Texans since the beginning of the year include Nico Collins, Jadeveon Clowney, Ed Ingram, Azeez Al-Shaair, Henry To’oTo’o, and Jayden Higgins; all projected starters or key rotational pieces that have left Houston a little more shorthanded than expected.
However, it seems that the Texans could be getting some good news on the injury front for one of their top draft picks brought in from this summer, who has yet to make his NFL debut due to a four-game absence.
That's Houston's second-round defensive tackle Kayden McDonald , who, after Week 4's 30-34 loss to the Dallas Cowboys, is officially gearing up to play his first game in a Texans uniform come next weekend.
According to a recent live stream from KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , McDonald has said he will be activated from the Texans' injured reserve list for Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans.
"Kayden McDonald told me today that he will be activated next week [vs. the Tennessee Titans]. It's from Kayden... Kayden McDonald says he'll be back next week," Wilson said.
It's a pretty big break for a Texans defensive line that just suffered a big loss in the form of Mario Edwards Jr., who has been ruled out for the remainder of the 2026 season due to a torn ACL he sustained against the Indianapolis Colts in Week 3.
Being without Edwards, who was the Texans' third defensive tackle in their defensive line rotation netting a little over 30% of the snaps each week, meant that Houston was due to turn somewhere else for that interior depth for the foreseeable future.
And on the surface, McDonald makes sense for that role to seamlessly plug into that role Edwards once had; a young rookie with potential yet also high-level starting experience at Ohio State, where he was a pretty productive tackler and run defender.
But in the time that Edwards has been sidelined since the end of Week 3, McDonald has been as well. McDonald was placed on injured reserve before the season started with a lingering ankle issue that popped up in practice, and delayed the beginning of his rookie campaign by at least four weeks .
That meant, against the Cowboys without the presence of Edwards and McDonald, the Texans had to turn to Jaden Crumedy for those DT3 reps, who got a little over 20% of Houston's defensive snaps and didn't record a stat.
Perhaps Crumedy can be a serviceable backup for one game , but Houston could certainly use some more firepower within their defensive line depth.
Enter McDonald, who can do just that now that his four-week return timeline has ended.
McDonald was seemingly dealing with a minor injury, all things considered, and is primed to get on an NFL field for the first time in Week 5 against Tennessee–– likely with a pretty nice role within Houston's defensive line rotation from the jump.
However, the Texans will have to ensure that McDonald can go through a week of practice with the team upon his return from IR, likely as a full participant for at least one session, before they slot him into their defense for Week 5.
So over the course of Houston's next three practices before their road trip to face the Tennessee Titans, keep a close watch on how McDonald progresses to confirm his long-awaited NFL debut.

title: Texans Fall to Cowboys, 30-34: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Week 4
full_text:
The Houston Texans are now at a brutal 0-4 record on the 2026 season after dropping their Week 4 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys, 30-34 .
It's a record that the Texans haven't seen their name next to their name on the standings since the start of the 2020 season; the first of three years where Houston failed to win more than four games in a season, and was fully focused on retooling and rebuilding this roster to a playoff contender.
But fast forward six years later, the Texans are in a vastly different, and much better, situation than they were in that 2020 season–– yet still, they're found an exact same 0-4 record they started with then.
While they entered this season as what many viewed as one the top contenders to make it to the Super Bowl in the AFC, they now sit four games under .500; a massive hole to start the new year, and clearly, an assortment of problems to work out if they want to make a similar climb up the standings as they did last year.
With Week 4 in the books, let's sort through just how the Texans performed in their loss against the Cowboys by looking at the good, bad, and ugly seen across the day:
A large chunk of the Texans previous three losses could be credited to poor performances on the offensive side of the ball. But in this game against Dallas, scoring the ball wasn't much of an issue for Houston–– which came largely because of the standout outing C.J. Stroud and Nico Collins had in the passing game.
Collins (hamstring) made his return to the Texans lineup in Week 4 , where he certainly made his presence felt on the Dallas defense: seven catches on eight targets, 118 yards, and two touchdowns. It's only the second game of Collins' NFL career where he's hauled in over 100 receiving yards with a pair of scores.
Welcome back to the end zone, Nico Collins. @DALvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Vc3ml22f0x
So we know that all hope isn't lost for this Texans passing game when all key pieces within their lineup. Against the Cowboys, Collins was back at 100%, was a focal point of the passing attack, and delivered in order to help Houston lift up to their highest-scoring outing of the year thus far.
Even with those positives on the offensive end, though, the Texans proved to be far from perfect down the stretch. Stroud and Collins carried their weight extremely well, yet even a vintage performance on their behalf wasn't enough to lift this struggling Houston unit over the hump for that first win of the season.
The Texans' run game felt like it was going to be on a better trajectory after David Montgomery brought in three touchdowns during his Week 1 debut against the Buffalo Bills; the most rushing touchdowns the franchise has seen since Joe Mixon in 2024.
But since that eye-catching hat trick from Montgomery, there really hasn't been any real success generating in the run game in the three weeks to follow. Montgomery has been inefficient with a real lack of explosiveness. Woody Marks has been a bit more explosive, yet still not the lead back this Texans offense can confidently lean on week after week.
In this one against the Cowboys, the two Texans running backs combined for 46 yards on 16 carries, sitting right under 3.0 yards per carry. Such a result––on top of Houston's previous lackluster performances on the ground through the last few weeks––led to Stroud making their improvement a clear emphasis during his postgame presser.
"Yeah, we've got to find a way to get those guys a chance," Stroud said on Sunday. "Like, they're both special backs; both backs that can create. And I think they're trying their best, man. But I think we’ve got to find things that fit us; our run game execution needs to go up. And I have the utmost trust that it will."
It's hard to imagine the Texans and their elite secondary were the ones allowing Cowboys star wideout CeeDee Lamb to have one of his most memorable days as a pro. But boy, it was a pretty dismal day for Houston's pass defense.
Just looking at Lamb's stat line tends to tell a good bit of the story: 17 catches on a whopping 21 targets, 189 yards, and a touchdown.
There's some receivers in the NFL who are lucky to record those types of numbers in a single season, but Lamb managed to do it in just a few hours against a defense that many talked up as the best in the league before Week 1.
CeeDee Lamb today: 17 catches 189 receiving yards TD to take the late lead @DALvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/fkKX2N6kor
Being without Azeez Al-Shaair and Henry To'oTo'o in the linebacker room certainly took a major hit to the Texans' defensive success. Both of them are integral parts to Houston's defense each week they're healthy and on the field.
However, even being without both of them on Sunday, it's becoming much clearer that Houston might not have as dominant of a defense that many expected them to carry into 2026––especially when it comes to their talent in the secondary.

title: What C.J. Stroud Said After Texans Drop to 0-4 With Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
The Houston Texans have now dropped their first four games of the 2026 NFL season after their Week 4 loss to the Dallas Cowboys, falling in a 30-34 loss and now falling to a gloomy 0-4 on the year.
The offense showed a whole lot more life than they've had through their last three weeks of action. But even with that offensive improvement against this Cowboys defense, and a pretty strong performance from C.J. Stroud en route to over 340 passing yards and two touchdowns, Houston came up short once again.
Here's everything that Stroud said during his postgame presser from the Texans' Week 4 loss to the Cowboys and the team's fourth straight loss to open the new season:
"I'm just going to keep that between our team. But, I just wanted to get in front of them and let them know how much I believe in them and trust in them. I know we're not in a good spot and it's not where anybody wants to be."
"But, I've seen other teams do it before. I know we've done it. We''re minus one game of that. But, you know, I'm the utmost trust and hope in my guys. So, just trying to keep everybody together."
"Yeah, I thought we did a great job attacking them. I thought [Nick Caley] did a great job of calling it, and us executing it; had some big plays early on. And I think the more that we can play ahead of the sticks, the better we give ourselves a shot."
"So I thought they did a great job. I thought upfront, we blocked very well for the majority of the game, and I thought we ran great routes, created separation. But it was just unfortunate we can't win."
"We gotta finish. I think we've shown that we can create explosives, we can have high scoring games, we could, get ahead when we need to. But I think the best thing that we need to do–– really, the main thing we need to do is finish."
"And that's not just the end of the game. That's third down; I thought we were not great on third down today. I think we can finish better there. But also just as a team, just together, trying to finish every play, every down, playing it like it's your last. I think that's what we need to be able to fix.”
"I don't think anybody in our building has a mindset of not finishing. I think it's an execution thing. We've got to study more. We've got to be on our details better than another team is."
"Everybody––I know for a fact––in our building wants to win, was doing everything in their power, too. But I just take the execution; the finishing is the part where we can get better."
"Every year is different. Llast year's bread isn't going to feed us this year. I remember in college, Coach [Ryan] Day used to always say you have to be an iPhone; you have to upgrade every year. You've got to upgrade whatever that looks like–– from personnel, to plays, to execution, everything's got to rise up."
"And you can't look back and be like, 'Oh, well, we did it this time. We can do it again.' Like, you have to be able to flush successes and failures, and be able to do your job each and every play. It doesn't matter what happened the previous year. Doesn't matter accolades, the hate, whatever, on both sides. You have to be able to flush it, because that's our job."
"So... this is a new year, and we got to be able to, and we got to be able to get ourselves out of this hole. And we're only the ones who can do it, and we're all we got, Nobody's coming to save us. So we got to make sure we're looking ourselves in our eye, being accountable, being honest, and then going to work.
"Just finishing better, executing better. I think those are 2 main things. I think we're practicing good. I think. This game we were able to create explosives, but we got to be able to finish. And that's the main thing. So, um, yeah.
"It's not good enough. I've got to find a way to find bigger plays, I guess, on third down. Try to get first downs. I thought I took care of the ball; tried to do the best I can in that area. But, I think it doesn't matter at the end of the day; we ought to be able to win."
"So, if I have to do more, and put more on my plate, then I'm fine with that. We've got to go find ways to win. But that's the main thing. I think as a team, we all feel that way.
"Yeah, we got to find a way to get those guys a chance. Like, they're both special backs; both backs that can create. And I think they're trying their best, man. But I think we got to find things that fit us, that our run game execution needs to go up. And I have the utmost trust that it will."
"I think the backs are doing everything they can. I think our scheme is– we're tailoring everything to try and get that done. So, I've the most trust and respect in Cole [Popovich] and [Nick Caley] and Jerry [Schuplinski] and stuff to get that done. But yeah, that's something I think we definitely got to get better at, is running the ball."
"Yeah, it's hard to win football games. You have 13 penalties. A lot of them are critical as well. Some of them questionable, but they made the call, you gotta flush it in, and find a way to execute the next play."
"But, one thing I am proud of my team is just for fighting. We give ourselves a chance. We had the ball at the end, gave ourselves a chance on the Hail Mary, and, who knows, [we] could have come down with it, and nobody would have their head down. But, I like the way that we fight, man."
"I know it's not easy. I know it sucks we're 0-4. But I can look at my team and respect them. No one's tucking their tail. No one's feeling bad for themselves. Everybody's fighting to the end and trying to get a win. And I believe that we'll be able to flip the coin, and hopefully pull out some of these close games."

title: 7 Texans Takeaways From Crushing 30-34 Loss vs. Cowboys in Week 4
full_text:
The Houston Texans have now dropped to a lowly 0-4 after a deflating Week 4 loss to the Dallas Cowboys , 30-34.
It was a game that, overall, felt like the Texans have a lot more positives to bank on compared to their previous three outings–– largely because the offense was finally able to gain some more traction and score their highest point total of the year.
However, even with the offense coming to hold their own, it wasn't enough for the Texans to stamp their first win of the season on the books.
They're stuck at a winless 0-4, are even further behind in their hopes of rising up the AFC standings, and now face a situation that only one team in NFL history has been able to climb out of for a postseason appearance.
Let's break down seven of the biggest takeaways to gather from the Texans' disappointing Week 4 loss to the Cowboys:
It's hard to imagine that the Texans' elite secondary was the one that allowed for one of CeeDee Lamb's best games in the NFL. But it was his presence from start to finish that presented major issues for Houston–– which came to the point where Dallas targeted him a whopping 21 times in the game.
In all, Lamb turned those 21 targets from Dak Prescott into 17 receptions, 189 yards, and one touchdown, which just so happened to be the game-winner on this Texans' defense and took the life out of Reliant Stadium.
George Pickens was held in check pretty significantly; just two catches for 75 yards. Yet, it was Lamb who picked up the slack and took advantage of a Texans defense that clearly wasn't the same without Azeez Al-Shaair (groin) plugging up the middle of the field.
C.J. Stroud faced a largely similar outcome this week to what he's been used to three weeks into the 2026 season: despite a strong individual performance on his behalf, it was a poor supporting cast that led to the Texans' demise and another loss on the books.
Stroud didn't turn the ball over for yet another game. He completed over 67% of his 30-plus pass attempts for over 340 yards and two touchdowns. Really, he played exactly as you'd want a quarterback to perform with a lucrative contract extension on the line .
Yet, even while Stroud's holding up his end of the bargain, the Texans have now dropped their fourth straight. So while he was largely the center of conversation this offseason as Houston's biggest flaw on the roster, it's been quite the opposite a quarter of the way through the 2026 campaign.
While the Texans' offense had a lot of success to bank on against this Dallas defense, one area that they still couldn't get right was the run game.
Houston's running backs combined for 46 total rushing yards, led by David Montgomery's 10 carries for 24 yards. When factoring in Woody Marks, the two combined for under 3.0 yards per carry yet again as a unit.
Whether it be the lack of potency Montgomery offers, run-blocking woes for the offensive line, or another reason, the Texans have to figure out their lackluster run game moving forward . It's hard to imagine Houston's scoring attack having any higher ceiling than last year's without a better ground game.
Nico Collins showed exactly why the Texans and their offense are performing its best when Nico Collins is on the field and making plays–– which is what he was doing throughout the day against the Cowboys.
In his first game back from his two-week hamstring absence , Collins saw eight targets, caught seven of them for 118 total yards, and capped that off with a pair of touchdowns in the process that really gave the Texans' passing offense life from start to finish.
Welcome back to the end zone, Nico Collins. @DALvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Vc3ml22f0x
It's not hard to imagine this being a sign of things to come: Collins remains the No. 1 option in the Texans' passing offense, and will continue to see a hefty share of targets from Stroud for more scoring outings like this one.
After many had been clamoring for Jaylin Noel to get more snaps and looks to come his way on the offensive end, the second-year pass-catcher finally saw some of the most work he's seen throughout his entire career this Sunday, and he had a career day in the process .
Noel saw three total targets from Stroud that he hauled in for 85 total yards, good for a little over 28 yards per reception. Noel now has three weeks in a row where he's recorded over 25 yards per reception, despite hauling in just six receptions.
CJ Stroud hits Jaylin Noel in stride for a 52-yard gain. @DALvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/qbG0NIBb1d
It felt like every time that Noel had the ball in his hands––outside of an errant punt return he had in the second half––he was making big plays. That should be a pretty positive outcome for what his stock and overall involvement in this offense look like over the next few weeks.
An undisciplined day it was for the Texans. The team had a total of 13 penalties throughout the day, which would give up a total of 90 yards.
Throughout most of the Texans' season so far, they've remained pretty tight as it relates to the penalties they've occurred on a weekly basis. Houston had just 18 penalties recorded against them leading up to this game, which is the sixth-least in the NFL.
But Houston was just a few flags away from matching their season total in this one against Dallas. And in any game where you cause over a dozen penalties between offensive line woes and pivotal mistakes in the secondary, it's not exactly a winning recipe.
The Texans now sit in a pretty dark hole with an 0-4 record; an even worse spot from where they sat after their slow start in 2025 , and now face a start to the year that only the 1992 San Diego Chargers have been able to escape and make the postseason from.
Do the Texans have any chance at making history? You can never say never, especially after the way their offense played in this one. If Houston's secondary tightens up just a little bit, and Azeez Al-Shaair can get healthy quickly, it's not impossible to imagine Houston catching fire and rattling off a few wins in a row.
But expecting to make the postseason after being stuck four games under .500 is a tough task to ask for any team, no matter how many Pro Bowlers they have on the roster. Houston has a date with the Tennessee Titans in Week 5 for a chance at a get-right game, yet even then, there's a whole lot of work to do moving forward.

title: Texans Announce 5 Inactives for Week 4 vs. Cowboys — With One Big Surprise
full_text:
The Houston Texans and Dallas Cowboys have officially released their list of inactives for their Week 4 matchup.
When it comes to the Texans, they'll be without five select players on Sunday due to injury or simply as a healthy scratch –– and one of those names sitting on the sidelines comes as a bit of a surprise.
Let's look at the list of inactives for both the Texans and Colts heading into Week 4, and break down exactly what it means for Houston:
LB Azeez Al-Shaair OL Febechi Nwaiwu DE Chris Braswell OL Nate Thomas TE Marlin Klein

title: Texans' 3 Biggest Keys to Victory vs. Cowboys in Must-Win Week 4 Game
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a pivotal Week 4 game on tap this Sunday against the Dallas Cowboys––one in which they'll be trying to land their first victory of the 2026 NFL season after going winless through the first three weeks of the year.
And there's some reason to believe Houston can turn things around against their in-state rivals this weekend. The Texans are back at home after last week's road trip. Nico Collins is back healthy and in the lineup, and this team is certainly hungrier than ever to land their first win of the season.
For the Texans to get a win to go their way in Week 4, though, there are a few aspects throughout the day that certainly need to go their way to make that finally come to fruition.
Let's break down the three biggest keys to victory the Texans face against the Cowboys in Week 4, and finally put a long-awaited first win on their record.
The Texans will finally be getting their No. 1 wide receiver back in the lineup this week with the return of Nico Collins , and that's a huge lift for this passing offense that's been largely struggling without him for the last two weeks.
So there's no doubt that in Collins' return, the Texans need to get all they can out of Collins to try and lift this offense from the depths they've been at through their 0-3 start. Especially against a high-powered offense and wide receivers like the Cowboys have on their side, Houston needs to do the best they can to match that production themselves.
Using Collins' explosiveness, ability as a vertical downfield threat, and red zone target, can give Houston a lot of what they've been missing at wide receiver without him, and lead to a big day against this new-look Cowboys secondary led by Joey Porter Jr.
The Texans' run game hasn't shown many improvements from the way things ended up last year through their early sample size of this season. Houston is currently in the bottom three in the NFL for total rushing yards and the bottom eight for rushing yards per attempt; lacking a real sense of potency or efficiency.
So the Texans have to turn things around on the ground moving forward this year. And against a Cowboys run defense that's remained largely inconsistent through the first three weeks of the season (allowing over 530 rushing yards on the season), Houston has a perfect opportunity on their hands to get right.
Whether the Texans bank on Montgomery's ability as a power runner, Woody Marks' speed and explosiveness, or a combination of both, Houston can't afford for their run game to look as it has for the past two weeks if they want to have a successful offensive performance.
While the Texans are set to get reinforcements on the offensive side of the ball for key pieces like Nico Collins and Ed Ingram, their defense will be without one of their most important playmakers and leaders within their front seven, in Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair.
Being without Al-Shaair is a big loss for the Texans' defense on its own. He's their green-dot signal-caller and the team's leading tackler for the past two seasons. However, Houston will also be without another starting linebacker, knowing that Henry To'oTo'o still remains on injured reserve for the shoulder injury he sustained in Week 1.
So for Jake Hansen, who's expected to claim his role as the green dot, and rookie Wade Woodaz, they've got a tall task on their hands: move forward without Al-Shaair for at least one game, and hold their own in the middle of the field against a Dallas offense that's ranked seventh in scoring in three weeks.
If Hansen and Woodaz don't get picked on too heavily, we know the Texans have more than enough talent in other areas of their defense to compensate and step up. But the linebacker unit remains the biggest question mark of the day.

title: Latest Injury Update on Texans WR Tank Dell Isn't Too Promising
full_text:
As the Houston Texans neared closer to the start of their 2026 regular season, there was a lot of attention surrounding how wide receiver Tank Dell would begin the year, knowing that he was set to return from his devastating 2024 knee injury.
After Dell had avoided the PUP list to start camp and began practicing , there was some optimism generating on what his availability could look like once the season kicked off.
However, while an encouraging start to camp, Dell wasn't activated for preseason and was still getting his feet wet in practice. So the team decided to place him on IR for at least the first four weeks of the regular season and would decide to re-evaluate once the first month of the season was up.
Since Dell was placed on IR, the intel on what's next for his injury status has remained largely quiet. However, according to some recent intel that's surfaced with the end of that four-week window right around the corner, it seems like a return for the Texans wideout isn't exactly sitting around the corner any time soon.
During a recent livestream, KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson gave an update on where the Texans stood on the pending return of Dell.
And to this point, the Texans have issued "no timeline" on Dell's return. And at the very least, that return won't be “imminent."
“It is a serious injury, and he is not there yet. They also don’t have a home for him at this point with the other receivers they have up. They’ve given us no timeline,” Wilson said earlier this week . “I’ve checked on this. It’s not imminent. I can tell you that. If it happens, it’s later in the season.”
So at the very least, we probably won't have to expect Dell to be back in the mix once his return to practice window can officially open up at the end of Week 4. And chances are, he won't be ready to go for the next few weeks beyond that.
Dell still seems to be ramping up from the lengthy recovery that's been in place from the knee injury he suffered over 20 months ago––damaging his ACL, MCL, LCL, and meniscus––and appears to be struggling to hit that high-end, explosive speed to reach that 100% the team has been eager to get him back to.
And as to when that piece of Dell's recovery will come, remains to be seen . However, it has seemingly added a few more weeks onto the expected timeline of getting one of Stroud's favorite targets back in the fold.
At this point, there appear to be three clear routes that Dell and the Texans could go as it relates to his return to the field this season––if there is going to be a return at all:
Of course, the final option of those three would be the most drastic, and an outcome that nobody wants to see happen. Yet, the longer that Dell does remain on the sidelines each week, the smaller the window gets for him to get back on the field for the season as a whole.
So at the very least, keep an eye on Dell over the next few weeks, and whether or not more intel surfaces from the Texans' HQ to provide a bit more optimism on how his status could pan out.

title: Colts HC Shane Steichen Evaluates QB Play: Has Daniel Jones Been Good Enough?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts took the league by storm in 2025 after their first season with Daniel Jones leading the charge immediately paid dividends.
The Colts were on top of the NFL world after starting last season with an 8-2 record, and a big reason for their hot start was due to the offensive marriage between head coach Shane Steichen and quarterback Daniel Jones.
Jones had gotten the fresh start he needed, and Steichen got his ideal quarterback to run the offense as he envisioned, but it wasn't just their efforts that saw them start the experiment off with said success.
The 2025 Colts offense jumped out to a historically efficient start, and that's because Steichen and Jones were afforded the necessary supporting cast to reach the heights they knew they could.
However, even though the Colts largely ran it back on offense, something's changed through four weeks of the 2026 season.
Of course, Daniel Jones's infamous Achilles tear from Week 14 of the 2025 season has played a part in such regression: but is it a true regression, or is Jones trending back to his true self?
The Colts have managed to even up their overall 2026 record to 2-2 after four weeks, but it's largely been in spite of Jones's play.
Jones currently sports the second-most turnovers responsible for among any quarterback throughout the first month of the season with seven (four interceptions, three fumbles lost), trailing New England Patriots' Drake Maye (eight turnovers).
The Colts' starting quarterback has certainly looked like his peak 2025 self at times throughout the young 2026 regular season, but he's looked like his past self more often than not, and that's not a sustainable formula to bank on.
So, what did Colts' head coach Shane Steichen and Daniel Jones himself have to say about the team's quarterback play through four weeks?
Going into the Colts' Week 4 international matchup against the Washington Commanders, head coach Shane Steichen emphasized the need to take care of the ball moving forward.
Daniel Jones entered the week with five turnovers (three interceptions, two fumbles lost) through three games, but he didn't clean up his act after traveling overseas.
Jones threw an interception and lost a fumble against the Commanders, and Shane Steichen continued to put an emphasis on the non-negotiable that is not turning the ball over following the Colts' 30-13 victory.
"We just got to get those things cleaned up. That's part of the game. But you want to limit those turnovers as much as you possibly can," Colts' head coach Shane Steichen said about taking care of the football. "We'll go back and look at the tape and make sure we get that stuff cleaned up."
Daniel Jones hasn't been all bad through four weeks of the 2026 regular season, but he's certainly struggled more than he's thrived.
When asked to evaluate Jones's performance thus far, Colts' head coach Shane Steichen was brief but honest.
"I think he's done some really good things and some things we got to clean up," Shane Steichen said about Daniel Jones's performance thus far. "It's been four weeks into this thing and 2-2 right now, and so there's stuff to clean up, like always. But I think he's doing a good job."
I personally wouldn't say that Jones's performance thus far warrants praise, but at least the head coach and offensive playcaller still has confidence in his quarterback despite the rough start.
As alluded to, the Colts were able to thrive with Steichen and Jones leading the charge due to their complementary offense, but a lacking wide receiver core in 2026 has proven to be too much of a challenge thus far.
The Colts are without top wide receiver Alec Pierce for the foreseeable future as he rehabs his left heel injury that kept him out of the majority of the offseason, and this lack of a respectable deep threat has shrunk the offense, thus making it more difficult on the short passing game and run game.
Furthermore, veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen missed Week 4's game against Washington, but Ashton Dulin returned to the fray after missing multiple weeks with an ankle injury. Even though Indianapolis got a vertical threat in Dulin back, the offense still struggled to generate any explosive plays through the air.
The Colts brought in veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton to address this lack of an explosive downfield threat, reuniting him with Daniel Jones, but he's been a healthy scratch for both games since his addition.
Shane Steichen acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the wide receiver position, but ultimately decided that a revolving door of personnel should not dictate a quarterback's overall play, no matter how dire the situation presents itself.
"Darius [Slayton] is still learning the offense. He's getting into it. He's been here for two weeks. We'll see how next week goes. But I don't think so. I think that's part of the NFL. Guys are going to get hurt. Guys are going to get injured. It's next man up," Shane Steichen on the notion that Daniel Jones has started to showcase some poor tendencies because of his lack of a supporting cast through the air.
"I think [Laquon] Treadwell stepped up. Had some good catches. The ball got spread around a little bit, but overall it was not our best but it was good to win.
Throughout four weeks, Daniel Jones has been a below-average quarterback - and he knows it.
Entering Week 4, Jones sit among all NFL quarterbacks with the following statistics: 611 passing yards (23rd leaguewide), three passing touchdowns (T-23rd), three interceptions (T-24th), and is sporting the 25th-ranked QB Rating (38.9).
Against the Commanders, Jones did enough to get the job done, but he didn't start off hot. Jones had arguably his worst half in a Colts uniform to start the game, and he looked like the skittish, lost version of himself against pressure that forced him to part ways with the New York Giants.
In Week 4, Jones went 19-34 (55.9%) for 143 passing yards, one interception, was sacked twice, had one rushing TD, and lost a fumble.
It's fair to consider this a passable performance, especially considering the Colts ended up scoring 30 points overall, but in the grand scheme of things, this isn't cutting it come postseason pla -- the Colts' defense, who undeniably held up their end of the bargain against Washington, isn't going to face a depleted offense in the playoffs after all.
But as previously mentioned, Jones's lack of production is nothing compared to what's really holding the Colts' offense back; it's his second-most seven turnovers (four interecptions, three fumbles lost).
"Yeah, definitely got to play better. Got to clean that up. Can't afford to turn the ball over like that," Daniel Jones said about his performance through four weeks so far. "So, yeah, I think I just got to focus in on the details, understand can't do it and make better decisions."
So, if Jones knows that he's not playing up to standard, why does he continue to turn the ball over?
"I think they're all different," Daniel Jones said about his turnovers to start the season.
"Got to understand when to take a chance, when not to, when to protect the ball, when you have a chance to make a play. I think all that is something you're always studying and learning, and I definitely got to do a better job taking care of the ball."
On top of the concerning turnover rate to start the year, Jones has also started to panic in the pocket, and has been wildly inaccurate at times as a result. To be fair to him, the Colts' offensive line has taken a step back in pass protection, thus making life harder on Jones and the rest of the offensive passing game.
Entering Week 4, Jones had faced the 4th-highest amount of pressure among any NFL quarterback, according to Next Gen Stats.
Pass protection wasn't much better against the Washington Commanders, and Jones definitely deserves some grace, but he himself also needs to play better.
As alluded to, Jones and Steichen need a near-perfect situation outside of them offensively, and so…

title: Week 4 Stock Report: 3 Risers, 2 Fallers After Colts’ Strong Win in London
full_text:
After a worrying 0-2 start to the 2026 season, the Indianapolis Colts have worked their way right back into the thick of things in the AFC with back-to-back victories, most recently a 30-17 win over the Washington Commanders in London.
While four games is still a small sample size, each week brings us more information on which players are playing key roles for the Colts. Here’s a look at who’s trending up and who’s causing concern after an important victory overseas.
The Colts’ run game powered the offense on Sunday, accounting for just under half of the team’s total yardage and scoring all three touchdowns. And while Seth McGowan played a very small role, it’s becoming clearer that the Colts want him involved on the ground more as the season progresses.
On a season-high 19 snaps, McGowan logged his best statline so far: six carries for 31 yards and a seven-yard catch. He also added 102 kick return yards.
While the rushing numbers themselves are uninspiring, their proof that McGowan’s involvement in the offense is growing. For a team that leans so heavily on Jonathan Taylor to win games, having a developed and trusted backup to help keep Taylor fresh throughout the season will pay off in the long run.
Jaylon Carlies opened up the second half with a bang, coming away with the Colts’ first interception of the season. But it wasn’t just the splash plays that made for an impressive performance.
Carlies caught THAT. #INDvsWAS on NFLN pic.twitter.com/y0FdbDLmBM
Carlies paired five tackles with a 90.8 defensive grade from Pro Football Focus , despite playing a season-low of 30 snaps. While he was only on the field sparingly, the third-year man figured out a way to maximize his impact.
Given some of the questions surrounding the Colts linebacker group this offseason and into the season, having a guy like Carlies step up with an impactful showing in limited action helps the Colts get closer to figuring out the best possible rotation for their current linebacker group.
Sunday was perhaps the best game Charvarius Ward has played since joining the Colts.
Ward was dominant in coverage, allowing just two receptions for 13 yards on seven targets, adding three pass breakups as well. He consistently stayed stride for stride with Washington's receivers and made life difficult whenever they tried to throw his way.
After a rocky start to his Colts tenure, Ward is beginning to look more like the corner Indianapolis expected when it signed him. If Sunday was any indication, his play could be trending in the right direction at an important time for the Colts' secondary.
While Charvarius Ward was playing his best game as a Colt, Sauce Gardner was playing his worst.
Gardner allowed four catches on five targets for 117 yards and a touchdown, the most yards Gardner has allowed in a game in his career, according to Next Gen Stats. Even with third-string quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis in the game for Washington, their offense wasn’t afraid to attack the two-time All-Pro.
#Colts CB Sauce Gardner allowed 4 receptions for 117 yards and a TD on 5 targets in coverage against the Commanders in Week 4, the most yards allowed in a game by Gardner in his career, according to @NextGenStats .
The win helps to mask Gardner’s forgettable afternoon, which would’ve been under a microscope has the result fallen differently. Still, it was a noticeable step backwards from a player the Colts invested in to anchor their secondary.
Josh Downs simply wasn't involved nearly enough in a matchup that, when you look at it closely, seemed tailor-made for him.
With Indianapolis without their best deep threat in Alec Pierce, Ashton Dulin being banged up and Keenan Allen unavailable on Sunday, it seemed likely that the Colts pass game wouldn’t stray too far from around the line of scrimmage, and rely more on quick-hitting throws.
As a result, you’d think, would be a busy day for Downs, as he’s the Colts’ best separator and creator after the catch. And Indianapolis did try a heavy dose of the screen game.
But the 25-year-old Downs only logged four targets, three of which he caught for a meager 16 yards. To keep it blunt, that’s nowhere near the impact he should be having in these kinds of games.
