title: Colts Week 4 Grades: Defense Takes Another Step Forward
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are back to .500 after a 30-13 win over the Washington Commanders in London, and the biggest takeaway has to be the defense.
Granted, this two-week stretch came against a beat-up Houston offense and a Washington team forced to turn to a third-string quarterback, but the Colts defense finally looks like it is taking the right steps.
The frustrating part is that this game could have been even more lopsided if Daniel Jones could snap out of whatever funk he is in.
Here are my Week 4 grades.
Jones finished 19-of-34 for 143 yards, no passing touchdowns, one interception and a 53.9 passer rating.
He also lost a fumble on the second play and finished with the lowest offensive grade on the team, via PFF. Seven turnovers through four games simply is not good enough.
Jonathan Taylor handled business again.
Taylor finished with 97 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns, while Seth McGowan added 38 total yards on seven touches. Taylor is now the all-time leader in international rushing touchdowns with six.
This group had trouble consistently separating against a struggling Washington secondary.
Laquon Treadwell led the team with just 42 receiving yards, although injuries left the room thin. When guys did get open, Jones missed too many opportunities.
Tyler Warren caught all five of his targets for 41 yards.
With the receiver injuries, I would still like a little more production, but Warren and Mo Alie-Cox both held up better in pass protection. That was a much-needed step forward for Warren.
The run blocking was solid, but the pass protection left something to be desired.
Indianapolis rushed for 128 yards, but Jones was sacked twice and moved off his spot too often against a defensive line that entered the game ranked 31st by PFF.
The interior continues to be the strength of this defense.
Austin Ekeler's 29 rushing yards were the most by any Washington running back, and Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner were stout inside. I still need more consistent impact from the defensive ends.
Finally, some real progress.
Akeem Davis-Gaither earned a 91.7 defensive grade and Jaylon Carlies posted an 82.2, via PFF, the two highest defensive grades on the team. Carlies also recorded the Colts' first interception of the season.
This group was decent overall, but the deep shots are still concerning.
Sauce Gardner had arguably his roughest game as a Colt and was involved in two big completions downfield. Justin Walley helped in run defense and added a sack.
Cam Bynum was solid in coverage and against the run, but A.J. Haulcy had some issues on the back end.
Outside of the deep-ball breakdowns, this group did enough.
Spencer Shrader was money again, drilling field goals from 48 and 52 yards.
The punting operation also looked cleaner than it did early in the season, making this one of the better special teams performances we have seen from Indianapolis so far.
The Colts are back to .500, and for the first time this season, the defense is starting to look like a group that can actually be trusted.
Now the challenge is getting Jones back on track. If Indianapolis can pair this version of the defense with the offense we saw early in the season, this team could finally start putting together complete performances.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: 4 Things We Learned About the Colts in Week 4 Win Against Commanders
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have gone from 0-2 and searching for answers to 2-2 with a legitimate chance to take control of the AFC South.
That's quite the turnaround in the span of two weeks. Indianapolis still has plenty to clean up, and Sunday's 30-17 win over Washington was hardly flawless, but the Colts have started to show some signs of what this team can be.
Four weeks in, we're starting to get a clearer picture of who the 2026 Colts are. Here are four things we learned from Sunday's win in London.
The Colts learned just how valuable Alec Pierce is to their offense on Sunday. (Hint: that four-year, $114 million contract was well worth it.)
Between Pierce being sidelined, Ashton Dulin banged up and Darius Slayton inactive, the Colts lack a true field-stretching threat at wide receiver, limiting their pass attack to the short and intermediate areas. As a result, Washington was able to play tighter to the line of scrimmage, making life more difficult for Daniel Jones and an offense that took a while to find its rhythm.
Had Pierce been out there, his mere presence alters the offensive approach significantly. The defense would have to respect the deep pass, opening up space underneath for other pass catchers. Without the threat of the big play, the defense had one less thing to worry about.
Pierce's value goes beyond his own production. The Colts offense looked much more limited without him. His return can't come soon enough, even if he doesn't return until next season.
I don’t know what it is, but there’s something about playing in Europe that gives Jonathan Taylor super powers .
After rushing for 95 yards and two touchdowns, Taylor became the all-time leading rusher in international games, now holding the records for most career yards (408) and touchdowns (6). Sunday was also his third multi-touchdown game of the young season, underscoring his strong start to 2026.
Across the three international games Taylor has played in, the Colts have won all three. Maybe it’s time to schedule a trip to Europe every season.
The Colts’ defense looked downright ugly through the first two weeks of the season. Indianapolis surrendered 1,029 yards in losses to Baltimore and Kansas City, with big plays coming far too easily and the unit struggling to get off the field.
But something has clicked over the last two weeks.
The Colts held Houston to 223 total yards and 17 points in Week 3 before limiting Washington to 13 points on Sunday. The pass rush has been much more disruptive, the defense isn't missing tackles and the communication on the back end has improved dramatically.
There’s still plenty to clean up, but the difference between the first two weeks and the last two is hard to ignore. After looking like one of the NFL’s worst defenses to open the season, Indianapolis is finding its footing on defense.
The Colts haven't put together a complete game yet. But they've still won twice, against Houston despite scoring just 19 points and beating a beat up Commanders team playing with their third-string quarterback. While they've won both, neither were in entirely convincing fashion.
But that's also what makes these last two wins encouraging. When the offense has struggled, the defense has picked it up. When the passing game hasn't been there, Jonathan Taylor has carried the offense. When the offense has stalled in scoring range, Spencer Shrader has delivered.
There’s still a lot this team needs to clean up, but the Colts are learning how to win without everything going right. That's a valuable trait for a team trying to establish itself as the team to beat in the AFC South.

title: 5 Winners, 2 Losers From Colts' Week 4 Win Against Commanders: A Tale of Two Corners
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts evened up their 2026 season record to 2-2 after beating the Washington Commanders 30-13 in London.
Scoring 30 points and getting the job done against a depleted Commanders' offense deserves praise, but the Colts did this in spite of a couple of negative standout performances.
So, who were the Indianapolis Colts' biggest winners and losers from their international victory over the Washington Commanders ? We break it down below.
The Colts' star running back showed today why he not only deserves as many touches as possible, but why the offense needs to lean on him .
Jonathan Taylor rushed for two of the Colts' three touchdowns against Washington, with his 95 rushing yards on 20 carries (4.8 ypc) paving the way.
The Colts were scoring at such an efficient rate last season because they had a healthy offense that complemented itself well, but that has not been the case so far this season. Head coach Shane Steichen's offense has become rather one-dimensional through four weeks in 2026, and that lone threat comes from the legs of Jonathan Taylor.
The Colts' veteran linebacker infamously recorded zero stats in the season opener, but he's slowly but surely found his footing in the three games since.
Against the Washington Commanders, Carlies had just two tackles, but he also notched the Colts' first interception of the regular season.
Carlies still has work to do before he can be trusted to lead the Colts' defense from the middle of the field, particularly in run defense, but this development is still worth praising.
Laquon Treadwell is a former first-round pick who fell out of favor with the entirety of the NFL for the past several years, but his determination carved out a special teams role with the Colts and has evolved into earning serious playing time in head coach Shane Steichen's offense.
Shane Steichen and starting quarterback Daniel Jones have become comfortable throwing to the longtime veteran wideout, and it's slowly but surely making sense why.
Against the Commanders, Treadwell was the Colts' leading receiver, as he hauled in four of his five targets for 52 receiving yards.
The Colts' were without Alec Pierce (heel) and Keenan Allen (groin) against Washington, but that doesn't diminish what Treadwell was able to achieve in relief.
The starting cornerback had arguably his best game as a Colt against the Washington Commanders.
Charvarius Ward Sr., who aligned at left cornerback for 57 snaps, allowed two receptions for 13 yards on seven targets in coverage with three passes broken up, according to Next Gen Stats.
Ward Sr.'s availability and impact has been in question since he vowed to return to the gridiron after contemplating retirement due to his three concussions in 2025, but he's been a strong performer through four weeks so far.
Another week, more Spencer Shrader praise.
The Colts' kicker remains perfect on field goals in 2026 after going 3-for-3 on attempts against the Commanders. He three makes in question were from 44, 48, and 52 yards respectively.
There were questions surrounding his overall return to form from his torn ACL in 2025, especially after he struggled during the summer to prove he could fully rebound, but Shrader has since shed all concerns through four games in 2026.
The Colts' starting quarterback has become turnover-prone as of late, and that didn't stop against the Washington Commanders .
In Week 4, Jones went 19-34 (55.9%) for 143 passing yards, one interception, was sacked twice, had one rushing TD, and lost a fumble.
Jones definitely settled in down the stretch after the Colts began feeding running back Jonathan Taylor, but Indianapolis still won in spite of his performance. The Colts are lacking a respectable wide receiver unit and viable pass protection, but Jones still needs to play better.
The Colts aren't asking Jones to be a hero, and although they haven't given him the necessary supporting cast to thrive with, he has to lock in before it's too late.
Everyone knows that the Colts traded away two first-round draft selections for cornerback Sauce Gardner. But has he lived up to expectations?
For the most part, Gardner has been the lockdown CB1 that Indianapolis envisioned when they traded the farm for him, but today's showing against the Commanders saw a new low.
Sauce Gardner allowed 4 receptions for 117 yards and a TD on 5 targets in coverage against the Commanders in Week 4, the most yards allowed in a game by Gardner in his career, according to Next Gen Stats.
The Colts faced a Commanders offense that was down to their final active quarterback, a seventh-round rookie, and entered the game without their top wide receiver in Terry McLaurin available, which only adds to the disappointing showing in question.
It's fair to assume that Gardner will forget this performance and lock back in moving forward, but it's still worth pointing out - especially since his efforts required such a haul at the 2025 trade deadline.

title: The Good, the Bad & the Ugly from the Colts’ Victory in London
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts improved to 2-2 on Sunday with a 30-17 win over the Washington Commanders .
The Colts controlled much of the second half and pulled away late, but initially struggled to get going; the final score doesn't tell the whole story. There were plenty of positives to take from Indianapolis' performance, along with some glaring issues that could become bigger problems down the road.
So, what was the good, the bad, and the ugly from the Colts' victory in London?
It didn't matter who Washington had in the game at quarterback, the Colts' interior defensive line was relentless.
DeForest Buckner was back to his usual self, finishing with a tackle for loss, batted pass and three QB hits. Adetomiwa Adebawore logged a half-sack, and Grover Stewart added a pair of TFLs. Their dominance on the interior opened things up on the edge. Laiatu Latu shared the sack with Adebawore and Jaylahn Tuimoloau had a handful of impressive rushes himself.
A collective effort up front, and a performance Indianapolis will absolutely take from their defensive front.
Spencer Shrader was absolute nails for the second week in a row. The 27-year-old made all six of his kicks, including a trio of field goals, all from distance.
Shrader's first field goal try was good from 48 yards as time expired in the first half, giving the Colts a 10-6 lead at the break. The next two came from 52 and 44 yards, respectively, giving Indianapolis nine points from outside the red zone.
More importantly, Shrader continues to prove his worth over the long term. If he keeps this up, the Colts may have found their kicker for the next several seasons.
The Colts were flagged just once all afternoon, a five-yard penalty in the fourth quarter. For contrast, Washington was penalized 10 times for 84 yards, including a 87-yard touchdown that was called back.
In a game where the Colts' offense wasn't exactly humming, the fact they stayed out of their own way was a big reason for their later success. Indianapolis, outside of Daniel Jones' turnover issues, generally avoided the kind of mistakes that can decide a close game.
It’s also the second consecutive week for Indianapolis with one or fewer penalties, a significant improvement after committing five in each of their first two. Maintaining such a high level of discipline the remainder of the season will be a steep challenge, but as long as the Colts don’t become penalty-prone, they should find themselves being competitive week in and week out.
The usually trusty and reliable Sauce Gardner had one the worst individual performances of his career on Sunday. On five targets, Gardner allowed four catches for 117 yards and a touchdown, the most yards he’s allowed in a game, per Next Gen Stats.
Treylon Burks broke away from Gardner’s coverage with a nifty double move and beat safety AJ Haulcy to the football for the 47-yard touchdown. Gardner also had the lone Colts penalty of the game, a defensive holding which gifted Washington a first down.
Gardner has built a reputation as an x-factor in the secondary who can completely erase one side of the field on his own, but the Commanders got the better of him on Sunday. The silver lining for the Colts is that, if history is indicative of anything, Gardner is highly unlikely to get beat this badly again.
But until he does bounce back, the pressure to produce is on.
For an offensive line that’s been dominant in the early part of the season, Sunday’s performance in London is one Indianapolis would like to have back. The unit had their hands full against a talented defensive front, particularly in pass protection.
Daniel Jones rarely had enough time to stand in the pocket and progress through his reads and was sacked twice. Even if Washington couldn’t get home for the sack, they still created chaos.
On just the second play from scrimmage, Odafe Oweh bull-rushed left tackle Bernhard Raimann straight back into Jones, causing a fumble. They also recorded 6 QB hits as a defense.
Whether Indianapolis ran into a worthy opponent or simply weren’t on their game remains unknown, but it was an out of character performance for a typically strong group.
Offensive third downs were an area of significant difficulty for the Colts offense, converting just five of their 16 opportunities for first downs.
Jones was frustratingly content to take checkdowns and make throws in front of the line to gain. That’s partially due to having a banged up receiver room, but also a result of Jones’ own decision making.
Between Tyler Warren and Josh Downs, two of Indy’s best receiving options on third downs, the two moved the sticks just once. Jones did try to get both involved, particularly Downs, but couldn’t seem to push the right buttons throughout the game.
That restrained aggression from Jones made life difficult for the Colts offense. Indianapolis had opportunities to keep drives alive, but too often settled for short gains and put itself in difficult situations on the next play. Against a Washington defense that was hardly dominant, converting just five of 16 third downs simply wasn't good enough.
The Daniel Jones that showed up in London was not the same Daniel Jones the Colts saw in 2025. Instead, Indianapolis got a performance closer to the Giants version of Jones than the player they envisioned he’d become when agreeing to a two-year, $88 million contract this offseason.
Jones finished 19-of-34 for 143 yards, threw an interception and lost a fumble, repeatedly putting the Colts in difficult situations throughout the afternoon. The interception came as Jones threw off his back foot attempting to salvage a lost play, but wound up in the hands of Rasul Douglas, a play eerily similar to the interception Jones threw last week against Houston.
Jones clearly isn’t all the way back to the player that helped guide Indianapolis to an NFL-best 8-2 start a season ago, and with two consecutive underwhelming performances, he has a long way to go to get back to that level.
One of the pillars of Shane Steichen’s offensive approach the last two seasons has been getting off to a fast start, getting points on the board early to help dictate and control the remainder of the game.
Sunday’s opening drive was the polar opposite of a fast start.
The Colts turned the ball over on just the second play from scrimmage when Daniel Jones stumbled over his own left tackle. Their next five drive outcomes? Four punts and an interception.
It took until 3:23 to go in the first half for Indianapolis to get on the board through a Jonathan Taylor touchdown run. Clearly, not the efficient and urgent offensive approach that Steichen drew up. The Colts eventually found their footing, but they spent much of the first half playing catch up.
Everything about the Colts’ passing game was out of sorts. The offensive line was truly tested. Daniel Jones was uber-inefficient, but it wasn’t all his fault. He was without some key receivers who could’ve helped unlock the air attack.
The Colts were shorthanded at wide receiver, as both Keenan Allen and Darius Slayton were inactive on Sunday. That forced Jones to make more quick throws instead of pushing the ball down the field. Even with speedy options like Deion Burks and Ashton Dulin available, Indianapolis shied away from being aggressive.
As a result, the offense was consistently behind schedule and in lengthy goal-to-go situations. Indianapolis just couldn't generate enough through the air to keep the offense moving, putting even more pressure on the defense and Jonathan Taylor to carry the load.
Simply put, if this is what the pass game looks like without Alec Pierce, the Colts will be in for a long and frustrating remainder of the season.

title: 6 Instant Observations on Colts' Win Over Commanders: Has Indy's Outlook Changed?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts won a decisive matchup against the Washington Commanders in Week 4, a 30-13 victory in London that makes them undefeated (3-0) under head coach Shane Steichen in international matchups.
The Colts are now 2-2 on the season after getting out to a 0-2 start, and have the Pittsburgh Steelers and Tennessee Titans on the horizon.
So, what did we see during Indianapolis' Week 4 victory? We break it down below.
Daniel Jones has looked pretty good for someone who tore their Achilles late in the previous season, at least physically. There are some limitations that have lingered as a result, specifically as a rushing threat, but Jones has shown enough that suggests he's recovered enough to get the job done.
But through four weeks, Jones's performance implies the opposite. He's seemingly returned to form, not his early-season form from a year ago that had the Colts' offense humming at a historic rate, but his early-career form from when he was quarterbacking the New York Giants.
Below is Daniel Jones's statline from the Colts' 30-13 victory over the Washington Commanders:
19-34 (55.9%) for 143 passing yards, 1 interception, sacked twice, 1 rushing TD, 1 fumble lost
Daniel Jones had arguably his worst single-game showing as the Colts' starting quarterback. He was regularly seen floating in the pocket and panicking at the first flash of breakdown in pass protection.
Jones has produced just four touchdowns (three passing, one rushing) compared to his seven turnovers (four interceptions, three fumbles lost) through the first month of regular season play.
To be fair to Jones, he's been lacking a respectable wide receiver core and his vaunted offensive line has been in the bottom-five of pressure allowed to start the season, but he himself needs to drastically rebound if the Colts want to have any chance of contending come postseason play.
The Colts' top defensive player of the 2020s has no doubt returned to his All-Pro form.
DeForest Buckner entered the season with low expectations, given that he was 32-year-old defensive lineman returning from a scary neck injury, but he's looked like one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL through four weeks.
Buckner had four tackles, one tackle for loss, one pass broken up, and three QB hits against the Washington Commanders in Week 4. The Colts' longtime defensive tackle was a true game-wrecker despite not logging a sack, and has been the main reason Lou Anarumo's defense has found any success so far this season.
Jonathan Taylor is currently on a 10-game streak without 100 rushing yards, the longest of his career, but he's still proven to be the Colts' best offensive weapon.
Taylor had 95 rushing yards and two touchdowns on 20 carries (4.8 ypc) against the Commanders in Week 4.
The Colts offense looked incapable of putting together a scoring drive for the majority of the first half, but turning to Jonathan Taylor quickly reminded them that their best offensive weapon deserved more touches.
Taylor's aforementioned streak of 10 straight games without 100 yards rushing can largely be attributed to the Colts not having a quarterback who you can honor in the run game, with this season's version of Daniel Jones playing a part. Jones did rush for a touchdown in London, but a more consistent rushing threat from the quarterback position, coupled with an honorable deep passing attack, would open up the box for Taylor to benefit from.
While the Colts aim to address both of those limitations, leaning on Taylor to turn into Superman is honestly their best option moving forward - even if it's not as much of an advantage that a more balanced offensive attack would provide.
Daniel Jones needs to play better, but his offensive line needs to help him out.
The Colts' well-regarded offensive line has continued to be one of the best run-blocking units in the NFL, but their pass protection has dropped off from a season ago. They posted the 4th-worst pressure rate allowed by an offensive line entering Week 4's slate, and there was little-to-no improvement against the Commanders.
Left tackle Bernhard Raimann left the game with an apparent lower leg injury, but he did stay active on the sidelines with some pass-pro reps. Luke Tenuta filled the void while Raimann sat out.
Regardless if Raimann returns as early as next week, Colts' OL Coach Tony Sparano Jr. has a lot of work to do as far as pass protection goes.
The Colts famously traded away multiple first-round picks for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline. He's largely been the lockdown CB1 they envisioned when trading the farm for him, but today's matchup against the injury-riddled Washington Commanders gave us one of Gardner's worst single-game showings in his career thus far.
Sauce Gardner allowed four receptions for 117 yards and a touchdown on five targets in coverage against the Commanders in Week 4, the most yards allowed in a game by Gardner in his career, according to Next Gen Stats.
A one-off performance shouldn't be the end-all-be-all when determining whether a trade was worth it, but it does warrant questioning. The most concerning aspect of this showing in question was that Gardner was facing the Commanders' QB3, a seventh-round rookie taking his first professional snaps, and did not have to matchup against their WR1 Terry McLaurin.
It's fair to assume that Gardner won't play this poorly again, but it was a concerning showing nonetheless.
The Indianapolis Colts evened up their season record with a win, but was it enough to feel confident that they've found a groove? Not necessarily.
At this point, the Indianapolis Colts feel destined for their typical outcome under general manager Chris Ballard: an 8-9 or 9-8 finish.
Through four weeks, the 2026 Colts look very similar to any of their 2021-25 squads that produced mediocre results. There's simply no reason to believe that they'll start to put it together against true championship contenders with so many glaring holes. Perhaps the Colts have a trick up their sleeve and are waiting to reveal it when need be, but as of now, deja vu is strong with this team - and that's not a good thing.

title: Colts Receiver Corps Takes Big Blow Ahead of Clash With Commanders
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are nearing their international clash against the Washington Commanders .
Indianapolis's biggest strength is its offense, led by Daniel Jones and Jonathan Taylor. However, the receiver position is thin after Alec Pierce sustained a heel injury in Week 2 against the Kansas City Chiefs.
Now, ahead of this critical matchup in London, the wide receiver room is even more barren after it was announced that Keenan Allen will miss the game with a groin injury.
Colts downgraded WR Keenan Allen to out for Sunday’s game in London against the Commanders due to his groin injury.
Allen was coming off the heels of his best game this year against the Houston Texans. Allen secured six passes for 63 yards and the only touchdown in that contest for Indy.
Indianapolis didn't exactly have the most intimidating receiver corps, even with Allen on the field. Now, they'll have to figure out how to navigate the passing game with Josh Downs as the only consistent threat.
The wideouts who will suit up against the Commanders are Downs, Darius Slayton, Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, who was just elevated to the active roster from the practice squad today.
Dulin is still listed as questionable with an ankle designation, but appears on track to play Sunday.
We have elevated WR Nick Westbrook-Ikhine to the active roster from the practice squad for #INDvsWAS .
Expect Downs and tight end Tyler Warren to be peppered with targets from Jones, which might open up some opportunities for the rest of the receiver corps.
This is arguably the worst time to be this thin at the receiver position for Indianapolis. The Commanders are coming off a colossal win over the defending Super Bowl champs, the Seattle Seahawks.
Sam Darnold threw two interceptions and had a whopping 10 of his passes broken up by Washington's defense.
This was also with superstar Jaxon Smith-Njigba on the field, who accounted for 10 catches for 128 receiving yards and two touchdowns.
The problem is, Indianapolis doesn't have a receiver even close to what Smith-Njigba is capable of. Washington also smashed Seattle's ground game, allowing just 44 rushing yards on 18 attempts.
The keys to getting this offense going through the air will be to utilize Slayton and Dulin to press Washington's defense deep. This will allow easier throws to Downs, while opening up the ground attack for Taylor.
Washington will likely load the box to hault Taylor's effectiveness to force Jones to beat them with a lesser receiver corps.
On paper, this is a horrible matchup for the Colts' pass-catchers, so head coach Shane Steichen will have his work cut out for him.
Indianapolis rebounded last week against the Texans to get to 1-2. This isn't a 'must-win' game for the Colts, but if they can level themselves with a 2-2 record by getting a win over Washington, it puts them in a good spot.
The Colts' schedule gets easier after their Week 5 matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Heading into that game at Acrisure Stadium with a 2-2 record is exactly what this team needs after starting 0-2.
The first five games for the Colts are fiery, so if they can somehow escape with a 3-2 record, it will give them excellent momentum as they start the smoother avenue of their 2026 season.
But that 3-2 record can't be obtained without navigating this matchup with the Commanders. It will be interesting to see how the Colts operate their passing game without yet another key contributor on the field.

title: A Look Back at the Colts’ International History
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts haven't had many opportunities to play overseas, but when they do, they usually show up.
Indianapolis enters Sunday's London matchup against the Washington Commanders with a 2-1 record in international games, with both wins coming in Germany and its only loss coming by just three points in London.
And if there is one Colt who has really embraced the international stage, it is Jonathan Taylor.
The Colts made their international debut all the way back in 2016, when Andrew Luck and company fell 30-27 to the Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium.
Indianapolis trailed 23-6 entering the fourth quarter before scoring 21 points and nearly completing the comeback. Luck finished with 234 passing yards and two touchdowns, while Frank Gore added 68 rushing yards and a score.
That remains the Colts' only international loss.
Indianapolis returned overseas seven years later, and that is when Taylor entered the picture.
The Colts beat the New England Patriots 10-6 in Frankfurt in 2023, with Taylor accounting for the only touchdown of the entire game.
It wasn't exactly a dominant rushing performance — Taylor finished with 69 yards on 23 carries — but when Indianapolis needed points, he was still the guy. His one-yard touchdown on fourth down in the first quarter ultimately proved to be the difference.
Then came Berlin last season.
Taylor absolutely took over against the Atlanta Falcons, rushing 32 times for 244 yards and three touchdowns in a 31-25 overtime win.
That included an 83-yard touchdown run that tied the longest of his career and gave him his 65th career rushing touchdown, passing Edgerrin James for the franchise record.
Even more ridiculous, 228 of Taylor's 244 rushing yards came after contact, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.
And when the Colts needed somebody to finish the game in overtime, Taylor did exactly that, breaking loose for the game-winning eight-yard touchdown.
Simply put, Jonathan Taylor owns Germany.
Now Indianapolis heads back across the Atlantic looking to continue what has quietly become a pretty successful international track record.
Sunday's matchup with Washington will be just the fourth international regular-season game in franchise history and the Colts' first trip back to London since that 2016 loss.
The circumstances are different, but the formula doesn't need to be.
Get Jonathan Taylor involved early, lean on the run game and make Washington prove it can stop the player who has already delivered two of the biggest performances in the Colts' short international history.
If that trend continues Sunday, London could become the latest international stage for Taylor and the Colts to make some noise.

title: Jaguars Stock Report: Bhayshul Tuten Keeps Rising After Week 4 Win Over Bengals
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have plenty of things going their way.
After their impressive Week 4 win over the Cincinnati Bengals on the road, the Jaguars improved to 3-1 and continue to sit at the very top of the AFC South. But which Jaguars are seeing their stock rise after the 22-17 win, and whose stocks are slipping a bit? We break it down below.
It sure feels like the Jaguars are going to get a massive game from Bhayshul Tuten soon. Tuten has looked like he has improved with every week and every carry over the first month of the season, and the Jaguars are getting everything that they could have hoped from the second-year back who is in his first year as the Jaguars' top back. Tuten has reached at least 65 yards rushing in every single game, and this week he rushed for another 73 yards while having two touchdowns called back, including a 44-yard run.
Tuten ranks top-11 in rushing yards over expectation, EPA/Rush, success rate, and yards after contact per carry. He has been a legit weapon and workhorse for the Jaguars, and his time as the Jaguars' No. 1 running back should only be expanded in the weeks and months to come over the course of the rest of the season.
Arik Armstead was simply all over the place for the Jaguars on Sunday. He recorded six pressures to lead the team, giving him his fourth game as a Jaguars defender with at least six pressures. He was a force all game long, and he put together the kind of pass-rushing performance the Jaguars have needed to see from their defensive tackle room all season.
Only four defensive tackles have produced more pressures in a single game this season than Armstead did on Sunday: Gervon Dexter, Jonathan Allen, Jeffery Simmons, and Alim McNeil. That is good company to be in, and it is fair to say that he has turned a corner with six pressures over the last two weeks. The Jaguars needed him to step his game up, and he has.
The Jaguars started to point their offense in the direction of Brenton Strange , and he made them look smart for doing so. Strange set a career high in receiving yards with 95 and he could have had another 30+ yards and a touchdown added to those totals if Trevor Lawrence did not miss an open pass to the Jaguars' talented pass-catcher. Strange was truly a game-changer for the Jaguars on Sunday, and he bailed them out more than a few times on critical downs.
Strange was not a big part of the passing game for the first few weeks of the season, but Jacksonville knew they had a mismatch on their hands against the Bengals' linebackers and safeties. Strange dominated the Bengals' defense before and after the catch and had the highest yards per route (4.5) of any tight end in the NFL in Week 4 ahead of Monday Night Football. Not a bad day at the office.
It has been a stop-and-go start for the Jaguars and left tackle Anton Harrison at the start of the 2026 season. He had a stellar performance in Week 1, struggled in Week 2, rebounded with another stellar day in Week 3, and then took another step backward in Week 4 against the Bengals. Harrison was credited with five pressures to lead the Jaguars' offensive line, and it is a bit worrisome that he had his second tough day against a good defensive front this season.
Rookie defensive end Bryan Thomas Jr. played more snaps than veteran defensive end Danny Striggow Sunday, likely because the Jaguars wanted Thomas on the field more on passing downs. With that said, Thomas was the only Jaguars defensive lineman to rush the passer at least 10 times and not record a pressure. Thomas' value to the Jaguars is as a pass-rusher, but he got blanked on Sunday while the rest of the line got after Joe Burrow.
The injuries in the secondary are certainly concerning moving forward. That starts with starting cornerback Montaric Brown, who missed the game with a hamstring injury. It remains to be seen what Brown's status is moving forward, but he is now dealing with injuries while Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones continue to impress. Brown needs a big performance or two to get back his spot as a starting corner, but the timing does not appear to be on his side.

title: Jaguars Week 4 Snap Count Analysis: Explanation For Travis Hunter's Lack of Offensive Snaps
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars had plenty of big moments lead to Sunday's 22-17 win over the Cincinnati Bengals.
From red-zone takeaways to clutch moments from both sides of the ball, the Jaguars had several plays take significant steps in the win over the Bengals. When looking at the snap counts for Sunday's game, which of these players and their usages stand out the most? We break it down below.
Sunday marked the first time in Travis Hunter's career where he did not log a single offensive snap. He surely has had a small role at cornerback all season long, playing 15 offensive snaps and catching one pass for eight yards in the first three weeks of the season, but playing zero offensive snaps at all was a first. With that said, there is a very easy explanation for why the Jaguars did not let their unicorn take any snaps on offense.
The Jaguars entered the game with just four healthy cornerbacks after Montaric Brown and Christian Braswell were ruled out with injuries when inactives were announced. That meant the Jaguars had to elevate practice squad cornerback Jabbar Muhammad to the active roster. Once the Jaguars sustained two injuries at safety to Caleb Ransaw and Eric Murray, the Jaguars had just six active defensive backs for almost half the game.
"We knew with (Christian) Braswell being down, he was going to play every snap of the game," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game. "We had some 
things for him on offense that we didn’t feel like putting him out there because if he gets hurt on offense, we’re in a real bad spot. We 
didn’t want to put ourselves at risk there."
Hunter having a bigger role on defense than offense is not new at all, but it is not as if the Jaguars have pulled the plug on him getting fofensive snaps. It simply did not make sense to line him up at wide receiver in a week where so many defensive backs were injured.
The Jaguars will have some issues moving forward at the safety position if Eric Murray and Caleb Ransaw miss any time, and it certainly put them in a potentially bad spot on Sunday. The Jaguars only took four active safeties into the game after making third-round rookie Jalen Huskey a healthy scratch, which meant Rayuan Lane had to step in on the starting defense with 43 defensive snaps (57%).
Lane had gotten some reps on defense during regular-season games a year ago when the Jaguars would get into blowouts, but this was the first time he really had to step in during a tight game. Lane played almost 20 more defensive snaps than he has ever played, and he still played over 75% of the special teams snaps. Add in his fourth down tackle, and this was a nice day for Lane coming off the bench.
Josh Cameron played 22 snaps for the Jaguars (36%), which was a good bit lower than the 38 snaps the Jaguars had Brian Thomas Jr. play. But even with 22 snaps, most of which being blocking reps, Cameron still made his impact felt. Cameron only ran eight routes for the Jaguars, but he caught two passes for 42 yards to give him the most receiving yards of any Jaguars wideout on Sunday.
Cameron had a gaudy 5.3 yards per route as a result of his big game on limited snaps and he also had a 100% catch rate and led the Jaguars in EPA/Target. The fact he did that despite seeing just two targets says it all. Even in a limited role, he is a critical piece to what theJaguars will do each and every single Sunday.

title: Shipley's Dozen: 12 Takes on Jaguars' Gritty Win, Trevor Lawrence vs. Joe Burrow and More
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are getting on a roll.
The Jaguars were able to pull out a tough Week 4 road win against the Cincinnati Bengals on Sunday, leaving Paycor Stadium with a 22-17 win to improve to 3-1.
In this week's Shipley's Dozen column, we take a look at how the Jaguars found their way to a win, what it means moving forward, and everything in between.
There were a lot of moments where this game felt like the Jaguars' Week 2 loss to the Bengals last season. The Jaguars were far and away the better team in both instances, but penalties and other self-inflicted mistakes led to the Jaguars keeping the Bengals in both games. Then there was the long Bengals' offensive drive at the end of the game to get into the red-zone after the Jaguars failed to put the game away.
Had the Jaguars let a second winnable game against a team they are simply better than slip through their fingers, it would have been a tough pill to swallow. But this time, the Jaguars finished the game the right way and made enough plays on both sides of the ball to come away with a win. It was an important learning moment for a team that is still growing. The Jaguars are a much better team than they were the last time they were in Cincinnati, which is exactly what they needed to show.
For my money, the Jaguars had the better quarterback and offense on Sunday by a wide margin. Yes, the Bengals put up plenty of passing yards ... but, I mean, duh? They dropped back over 50 times. In those drop backs, they got the ball out at an incredibly quick rate and still took a ton of pressure. According to NextGenStats, Burrow was pressured 20 times (34.5% of dropbacks) against the Jaguars, the most in a game since Week 11 of the 2024 season (Chargers, 24).
 His average time to throw against the Jaguars was 2.64 seconds as 46.3% of his pass attempts were out in under 2.5 seconds.
In short, the Jaguars clearly were OK with the Bengals and Burrow dinking and dunking their way into 17 points and several failed red-zone trips. Burrow and the Bengals failed to make big plays when they needed to, and Burrow threw two costly interceptions. Trevor Lawrence, meanwhile, had what, one inaccurate throw on the day? He took care of the football, got first downs, and didn't put his team in bad spots like Burrow did. The better quarterback won on Sunday.
Travis Hunter's second act was certainly something. He had one of the better cornerback performances I can remember from a Jaguars defender in quite some time, making a few remarkably athletic plays. According to Next Gen Stats, Hunter recorded a career-high 58 coverage snaps against the Bengals and was targeted seven times and recorded two passes defensed. Across 11 matchups against Tee Higgins and Mike Gesicki, Hunter was targeted once and did not allow a reception.
I am simply fascinated at the idea of what Hunter will look like in a month, two months, and then by the end of the season. After just four games back from last season's knee injury, Hunter has taken to a full-time role at cornerback like a fish to water. He looks like the best player on the field more often than not only 11 games into his career. The next steps could put him insome remarkable conversations amongst the NFL's top cornerbacks.
The oddest sequence during the game felt like the Jaguars decision to punt at the start of the fourth quarter. The Jaguars had lined up for what would have been a 60-plus yard field goal on 4th-and-10, and the Bengals then got a penalty for 12 defenders on the field. Despite the field goal then being closer, the Jaguars trotted out the punt team instead and Logan Cooke hit a touchback from the Bengals' 41. It was a strange moment since the Jaguars had Little on the field and then took him off, but Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game the plan was never for him to kick.
"No, we weren’t going to go for that. We didn’t love the distance going into that, especially with that being the end that historically hasn’t been (reliable for kickers)," Coen said. "We were trying to draw them off, punt and pin, which we didn’t execute the pin even though we were really close and Antonio (Johnson) tried to throw it back, but we didn’t execute it to our standards. If we had gotten them on the one or the five (yard line), we would have been (thinking) ‘Oh, Okay,’ and we would have had more breathing room and felt better about it.”
Coen is right. Had the Jaguars planted the Bengals at the one or two-yard line there, nobody likely cares about how awkward this sequence looked. The logic makes sense, but it came down to execution.
Bhayshul Tuten ended up being the unluckiest player on the field on Sunday. He had two touchdowns wiped off the board, including a 44-yard touchdown that would have easily been the longest run of his NFL career. Tuten still finished the day with some very efficient production and he clearly had a big impact on the offense, but the fact that he had a potential career day taken away from him due to some overzealous officials is disappointing. Still, it goes to show that the big Tuten day is not far away at all.
Players who made impactful plays on Sunday: Travis Hunter, Bhayshul Tuten, Rayuan Lane, Emmanuel Pregnon, Josh Cameron, Nate Boerkircher. It was a good day for the Jaguars young crop of talent and recent draft picks, and the Jaguars' draft classes under James Gladstone are starting to show some real development early on in the season. This was the kind of game that Gladstone and the Jaguars' front office can hang their hat on moving forward. The 2026 class has still been mostly inactive over the first month, and Caleb Ransaw got injuredon Sunday, but there are some good draft returns thus far.
The Jaguars had some injury issues entering Sunday's game at the cornerback position with Montaric Brown and Christian Braswell, and then they had Eric Murray and Ransaw leave the game with injuries and not return. The secondary and its chemistry is amongst the most critical pieces of what the Jaguars do on defense, so the fact they will have to move some people around is not idea as they enter a key stretch. Look for rookie safety Jalen Huskey to become potentially key over the next few weeks depending on updates for Murray and Ransaw. The Jaguars mostly avoided injuries over the first month, but the bug has now hit the secondary.
We knew the Bengals liked to throw the ball, but holy smokes, man. They did not even pretend to have an interest in running the ball, and then they got stubborn about it after the game. The Jaguars play a much, much more serious brand of football than the Bengals do offensively, something I already thought coming into the game. But I didn't think the gap was this wide.
Joe Burrow on the Bengals run-pass balance, via @aydencrowley4 : "My response to that would be - let's throw it more." The Bengals had 54 throws and 15 rushes in Week 4. pic.twitter.com/IQQEOnwzE4
Brenton Strange having a massive day. The thing about this Jaguars' regime on offense that stands out from past offenses during the Trevor Lawrence era is that they actually take advantage of mismatches instead of attempting to win in the same way over and over again every single week. The Bengals' marks on defense this week was always set to be their linebackers and safeties, and the Jaguars quickly leaned into that mismatch by targeting Brenton Strange over and over in high-leverage moments.
Out of the six players involved in the Travis Hunter trade (Hunter, Bhayshul Tuten, Rayuan Lane, Mason Graham, Quinshon Judkins, KC Concepcion), it is pretty clear the Jaguars have the first- and third-best players. Travis Hunter looked every bit the part of a generational player against the Bengals and has officially hit his stride. Hunter's juke of Tee Higgins and his supernatural leap on his second PBU, in addition to his big hit, earn him the nod of Jaguar of the week.
Travis Hunter snatched Tee Higgins' ankles 😭 pic.twitter.com/AFCDe8csjZ
The AFC…

title: 8 Winners, 5 Losers From Jaguars' Win Over Bengals: Brian Thomas Jr. Responds
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars left Cincinnati with a much different feeling this time around.
After a 31-27 loss to the Bengals in Week 2 a year ago, the Jaguars righted some of their wrongs with a 22-17 win over the Bengals in Week 4 on Sunday. But who were the Jaguars who were the biggest winners from the game, and which Jaguars came out on the other end?
Brenton Strange entered Sunday's game with seven catches for 72 yards and a touchdown, but he greatly boosted his season's production with his performance against the Bengals. He caught seven passes for 95 yards to lead the Jaguars in receiving for the first time this season, giving the Jaguars their third different leading receiver in four games. Strange was clutch for the Jaguars on more than a few occasions on Sunday.
The Jaguars saw Brian Thomas Jr. have a much smaller role in the offense a week ago against the New England Patriots, but he was able to respond with a big week of practice ahead of Sunday. He then came up big for the Jaguars with a seven-yard touchdown for his first score of the season. He still did not get many targets, but it was a better day.
"Everyone is going to try and create a narrative. Maybe it isn’t a star day for everybody and everybody is going to try and create a narrative, but we’ve always been consistent in our messaging to BT (Brian Thomas Jr.), to everybody else, to this locker room, and all he can do is stay the course. He showed up in a major way for us today," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said after the game.
The Jaguars saw Travis Hunter have perhaps the best performance of his career ... for the second week in a row. Hunter was all over the field for the Jaguars, recording two pass brekaups for the first time in his career and having an interception and long return negated by a penalty in the first-half. He looked like the type of talent that is very much worth a big trade up to No. 2 overall.
"He played his ass off today. He had a ton of PBUs, he had the huge tackle where he ended up knocking that guy out pretty good. 
I thought he balled today," Coen said. "We knew with (Christian) Braswell being down, he was going to play every snap of the game. We had some 
things for him on offense that we didn’t feel like putting him out there because if he gets hurt on offense, we’re in a real bad spot. We 
didn’t want to put ourselves at risk there. I was very proud of how Travis played defensively today.”
The Jaguars needed their pass-rush to come up big for them on Sunday, and that is exactly what the unit did against an improved Bengals' offensive line. Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker, and Arik Armstead all had big moments, from Armstead's pressures and third-quarter sack, to Hines-Allen forcing a Burrow interception to Jourdan Lewis in the first-half.
Imagine the kind of day Bhayshul Tuten would have had if the Jaguars did not play with an officiating crew whose atittude toward the game was similar to overeage hall monitors? Tuten rushed for a team-high 73 yards and his eight runs of 10-plus yards are tied for the sixth most in the NFL this season. He consistently was able to make something out of othing against an improved Bengals' front, and he made plays in the passing game, too. Tuten is the real deal through the first month of the season.
Josh Cameron had two catches for 42 yards, including the Jaguars' biggest gain of the day on a 29-yard catch-and-run. Add in what he did in the running game and the DPI penalty he drew downfield, and Cameron proved himself to be an important part of the offense even without getting another look in the red-zone. Cameron's arrow is pointing up, and it feels like he is playing better every week.
I thought Parker Washington would have nearly 100 yards and torch the Bengals' defense. Instead, he had just one catch for seven yards and had a few odd plays where he simply did not make the plays he has made so often over the course of his career. Washington will need to improve over the course of the next few weeks to wash away what felt like a bit of a wasted game for Washington.
The Jaguars secondary has taken some tough hits over the last few days. Montaric Brown and Christian Braswell were both missing from Sunday's action due to injuries, then the Jaguars saw safeties Caleb Ransaw and Eric Murray leave with injuries. Ransaw left the game in the first quarter with a knee injury and dd not return, which felt like a particularly tough break for a player who missed his entire game with a foot injury.
The Jaguars allowed four sacks on Sunday, and it felt like a lot of the pressure the Bengals were able to generate came off the edge. Kris Jenkins and Dexter Lawrence recorded sacks as well, but each seemed to benefit from Trevor Lawrence being forced to move up in the pocket and into harm's way due to the pressure coming off the edge. Anton Harrison and Cole Van Lanen will have better games than the ones they had on Sunday.
Tuten was a winner on the day because he was able to put togehter a really efficient and productive outing against a good Bengals defensive line. With that said, he also has to qualify in a way as one of the losers of the night considering he had two different touchdowns wiped off the board due to holding calls. One of these was a 44-yard run that finally showed Tuten's home run ability, but we will have to just wait for that to show back up in the weeks ahead.

title: Game Balls From Jaguars' Road Win Over Bengals: Brenton Strange Comes Up Clutch
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars needed to simply find a way to win in Week 4, and that is exactly what they did.
The Jaguars are leaving Week 4 with a 22-17 win over the Cincinnati Bengals that improves the Jaguars to 3-1 on the season, marking the first time in franchise history the Jaguars have ever started 3-1 in back-to-back seasons.
So, which players deserve game balls for helping the Jaguars when it came to getting past the Bengals hurdle that has hung over them for years? We break it down below.
Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange had his biggest game of the season on Sunday, catching seven-of-eight targets for 95 yards. Had the Jaguars not missed him on a wide open route deep down the middle of the field in the second half, the Jaguars would have seen Strange have one of the best games of any tight end in football so far this season. He has the ability to make that impact each week, and he displayed it in a favorable matchup against the Bengals.
“Yeah, that guy just does a lot for our team. He can block in the run game, in the pass game, all that stuff," Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence said after the game. "Then, obviously you see what he can do with the ball in his hands. He’s a matchup. I think obviously today was the most he’s been involved this season, but that’s our offense. It’s not everyone’s day every Sunday. That’s the hard part. There’s only one football and our guys show that they’re ready."
Strange's biggest impact came on several critical third-downs, including a 3rd-and-18 early in the game on the Jaguars' first scoring drive of the day. He was the Jaguars' engine on offense, though Trevor Lawrence and Bhayshul Tuten deserve consideration as well.
With the Jaguars facing several injuries at the cornerback position on Sunday, there was a lot of pressure on the defensive line to step up and make things easier for the secondary. The Jaguars managed to do exactly that, with the defense recording a staggering 11 quarterback hits as the Bengals dropped back over 50 times. In a week where the onus was on the pass-rush to make its impact felt, Arik Armstead may have been the most impressive.
Josh Hines-Allen (three quarterback hits), Travon Walker (two quarterback hits), and Travis Hunter (two PBUs, negated interception) all deserve consideration too, but I felt like Armstead was in Burrow's face all day and directly led to several big plays for the Jaguars' defense. Armstead had, to me, the best performance he has had with the franchise since signing with the team during the 2024 offseason.
Cam Little didn't get to attempt a massive kick, but it didn't matter. He went 3-of-3 on field goals to show off some consistency, and two of those kicks were from 55 and 54 yards. Every point matters in games like this one, and Little was able to put the Jaguars in good spots time and time again over the course of the game. Little now has 15 career made field goals from 50-plus yards and this was his fourth career game with multiple makes from 50-plus yards. Since entering the NFL in 2024, Little is one of eight kickers with at least 15 made field goals from 50-plus yards.

title: Good, Not So Good From Jaguars' Last-Minute Win Over Bengals: Trevor Lawrence Gets It Done
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars ended the first month of the season with a 3-1 record thanks to a much-needed Week 4 win.
The Cincinnati Bengals were always set to be a tough test for the Jaguars, but the Jaguars avenged last year's loss to the Bengals with a last-minute 22-17 win on Sunday. In a 60-minute game that goes down to minute No. 60, there were of course plenty of highs along with plenty of lows.
So, what was the good and the not so good of the Jaguars' big Week 4 win? We break it down below.
Trevor Lawrence was quietly excellent against the Bengals . He finished the game with 18-of-23 for 227 yards and a touchdown, and even his misses looked good (the two incompletions to Parker Washington). Really the only bad throw Lawrence had on the day felt like the second-half throw he missed to a wide-open Brenton Strange in the middle of the field. Otherwise, Lawrence played well considering some of the down-and-distances the Jaguars were in.
Lawrence finished the game with a passer rating of 122.3 and now has eight passing touchdowns to two interceptions through the first four weeks. He did what the Jaguars needed him to do considering how the game unfolded. Lawrence has been effecient and stepped up seemingly every single time the Jaguars have needed him all season, and that carried over to Sunday.
The Jaguars' pass-rush came alive at just the right time. The Bengals gave the Jaguars plenty of chances to pin their ears back to rush the passer by dropping back an eye-popping 56 times. It felt like the Jaguars' trio of Josh Hines-Allen, Arik Armstead, and Travon Walker were able to keep Joe Burrow just a bit off balance all game long, leading to him throwing an interception to Jourdan Lewis in the first half and a few other misses.
After recording 13 quarterback hits over the first three weeks, the Jaguars had 11 quarterback hits on Sunday. Hines-Allen and Walker led the way with five combined, and this felt like one of the best games the Jaguars' pass-rush has had under Anthony Campanile. They had a big task on hand, but it sure felt like they met the test.
Travis Hunter was simply all over the field for the Jaguars on Sunday. He had a pick-six and a 30-yard return that was negated by a questionable roughing the passer call in the first-half, but he didn't stop there. Hunter had his first-ever multiple-pass breakup game of his career with two different PBUs, and he also had a vicious tackle near the sidelines that showed he is more than just an athletic cover man.
Hunter answered the bell each time he needed to on Sunday, and he has now put together the best two games of his NFL career in back-to-back weeks. He is a legit play-maker and the ball just keeps finding its way to him. He is getting into a groove right now, and he is quickly climbing the ranks when it comes to the NFL's best cornerbacks.
It felt like the Bengals did not even want to think about running the ball on Sunday. Joe Burrow attempted 54 passes, but the Bengals' running backs combined for just 12 carries for 17 yards (1.41 yards per carry) and the longest rush the Jaguars allowed was just a six-yard carry to Chase Brown. Brown actually caught more passes (11) than he had carries out of the backfield (nine), a sign that the Bengals knew any attempts to run the ball would be futile.
How about the Jaguars' tight ends? The Jaguars were able to effectively run the ball out of 12 personnel when they needed to at key points, and Nate Boerkircher had a big 15-yard catch to set up a Jaguars score. Add in Brenton Strange having one of the best games of his career with seven catches for 95 yards and the Jaguars' tight ends stepped up in a big, big way on Sunday. The unit had not seen a ton of looks in the passing game over the first few weeks of the season, but that was certainly amended on Sunday.
The Jaguars are just one game in front of the 2-2 Indianapolis Colts, but the Colts hardly looked stellar against the Washington Commanders. There should be plenty of faith in the Jaguars to pull away from them at some point in the near-future. The bigger worry than the Colts has always been the Houston Texans, but the Jaguars have some breathing room on them now. The Texans are now three games behind the Jaguars after their 0-4 start, which makes this win all the better for Jacksonville.
Joe Burrow threw 54 passes, for some reason, so it is not exactly a horrible thing that the Jaguars allowed the Bengals to throw for 428 yards. That came out to just 7.9 yards per attempt, which was two whole yards below the 9.9 yards per attempt day that Trevor Lawrence had. But there still felt like too many times where the Bengals' backup receivers were making explosive catches with Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins off the field, which should never happen.
Liam Coen said after the game that he had never been a part of anything like the Jaguars' first half, where the Jaguars had 10 penalties for 100 yards. The Jaguars had two touchdowns and an interception wiped off the board on Sunday, and penalties did not let up in some key moments at the end of the game, either. The Jaguars were a very, very good penalty team entering Week 4, but that went completely out of the window on Sunday.
The Jaguars saw Lawrence get sacked four times on Sunday despite just 27 dropbacks, a figure that they will need to go down in the future. They played a reinforced Bengals' defensive front that was always bound to make it a tough day for them, but the offensive line needs to be better in pass-protection in big games moving forward. If not, it could prove to be the Jaguars' fatal flaw down the stretch.

title: 7 Observations on the Jaguars' Statement Win Over Bengals: Travis Hunter Dominates
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are 3-1.
The Jaguars took down the Cincinnati Bengals with a close 22-17 win on Sunday that went down to the wire, ending with a Rayuan Lane tackle of Chase Brown on fourth-down at the Jaguars' 12-yard line with just 0:56 left in the game.
So, what did we see during the big week 4 win? We break it down below.
Confidence is a big thing at the cornerback position, and the Jaguars have seen Travis Hunter's confidence grow in bunches in recent weeks. Hunter's snaps at cornerback have ramped up with each week, and the injuries the Jaguars faced at the cornerback position entering the game meant they needed Hunter to step up even more. He certainly did that with a strong start to the game that showed just how much more comfortable he is getting on the field, a sign of big things to come over the rest of the season.
Hunter had what looked like a stellar interception and then a dazzling return in the first quarter, intercepting Joe Burrow and then shaking Tee Higgins out of his cleats on his way to a 30-yard return to the Bengals' 36, but a roughing the passer call negated the big play. Hunter then responded with an impressive pass breakup in the red-zone shortly afterward to help limit the Bengals to just a field goal. Then on the final defensive drive before halftime, he laid down a physical hit on Bengals wide receiver Dohnte Meyers to show off his speed and physical tackling ability.
Bengals pick up the first down but Travis Hunter flies in for the big hit 😳 JAXvsCIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/K29JxAC8EH
The Jaguars had penalties wipe out big plays several times in the first quarter alone, a sign of the Jaguars still needing to grow when it comes to high-stakes games and tough road environments. In the first quarter, the Jaguars: Had a holding penalty on the opening kickoff to negate a Ameer Abdullah return near midfield; an offensive pass interference to negate 3rd-and-5 from the Bengals' 36-yard line; had a roughing the passer call negate a Travis Hunter interception that he returned 30 yards to the Bengals' 36. The Jaguars were flagged six times for 44 yards in the first quarter, and it stopped them from getting off to a better start.
Travis Hunter snatched Tee Higgins' ankles 😭 pic.twitter.com/AFCDe8csjZ
It continued into the next quarter, too. The Jaguars had an 11-yard sack of Joe Burrow to force a 2nd-and-21 after the Hunter interception was called back, but a facemask on Jarrian Jones gave the Bengals 1st-and-10 from the Jaguars' 14. Then a holding on Ezra Cleveland negated a 44-yard Bhayshul Tuten touchdown run. It didn't even stop there, with Robert Hainsey getting called for a holding at the Bengals' three-yard line that took it back to their 13. Tuten then had a *second* touchdown negated by a penalty. Really! The Jaguars felt like they grew out of their penalty issues, but they had seven against New England and had some big ones on Sunday. This is an area they still need to grow from after 10 penalties for 100 yards in the first-half.
We said earlier in the week that we felt like people were overreacting a bit to Josh Hines-Allen's lack of pass-rush production over the last two weeks. Hines-Allen showed why during a game that saw the Jaguars seem to generate plenty of pressure on Joe Burrow throughout the game. Hines-Allen had one of the most impactful rushes of the game, with the Jaguars' defensive captain bull-rushing Orlando Brown Jr. into Burrow's lap on a key first-half dropback to force an interception by Jourdan Lewis.
Jourdan Lewis intercepts Joe Burrow and takes it inside the red zone JAXvsCIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/pA8oW82xnm
Lewis was able to return the interception all the way to the Bengals' 18-yard line, and the Jaguars eventually punched it in with a seven-yard touchdown pass to Brian Thomas Jr. to make it a 13-3 game at halftime. The interception does not happen without the pressure, a great example of the Jaguars' rush and coverage working in unison to create big plays.
I thought the man coverage-heavy plan from the Bengals' defense w ould mean a big day for Parker Washington , but that just didn't happen. None of the Jaguars' receivers really had a big day in what was mostly a tight-end focused day and a low-pass volume plan from the Jaguars, but it also felt like Washington did not take advantage of the few looks that went his way.
Washington's first target came in the red-zone, but Bengals linebacker Barrett Carter was able to break it up. Washington's second target was a higher degree of difficulty on a 3rd-and-10 deep ball inside the Bengals' five-yard line. Washington had to slide for the grab, but it did hit him in the chest on a play we have seen Washington make over and over throughout his career and as recently as Week 2 against the Denver Broncos. This felt like a weird one, even after his screen got called back.
The Jaguars were already facing some serious issues at the cornerback position when it came to injuries entering the game, with both Montaric Brown and Christian Braswell ruled out before the game due to injuries . Things did not get much better for the Jaguars over the course of Sunday's game, with the Jaguars losing two more defensive backs due to injuries before the game ended.
Jaguars safety Caleb Ransaw, who has functioned as the team's third safety through the first month of the season, injured his knee during the first-half and did not return. The Jaguars also saw veteran safety Eric Murray leave the game with a concussion in the third-quarter and he was ruled out as well, leaving the Jaguars with just two healthy safeties in Antonio Johnson and Rayuan Lane. There are some real-deal injury issues the Jaguars are facing, which means the depth is about to be tested.
The Jaguars' Passing game completely flowed through Brenton Strange for the first time this season, and he made sure the Jaguars looked smart for it. Strange was the Jaguars' featured pass-catcher on Sunday, catching 7-of-8 targets for 95  yards and setting the Jaguars up on several of their scoring drives, including a first-down conversion on 3rd-and-18 on the Jaguars' first scoring drive of the game. Strange then had the 15-yard catch on 3rd-and-8 on the Jaguars' final offensive drive.
It is clear that the Jaguars' passing attack will be matchup-dependent and will not go through any one player very single week. But this week was always set up well to be a Strange week due to the Bengals' issues at safety and linebacker. The Jaguars were able to take advantage of the Bengals' weakness, something past Jaguars' offenses have not been able to do in the past.
The Jaguars had more negative plays in the running game than they normally do, but it still felt like the running game had another huge day. The Jaguars saw Bhayshul Tuten pick up yards after contact and still put up another solid day of production even after having two touchdowns wiped off the board, including a stellar 44-yard touchdown that would have been the biggest run of his entire career/
Then there was the Chris Rodriguez Jr. touchdown with 6:35 left in the game. Rodriguez looked like the explosive and reliable option the Jaguars signed him to be on a 25-yard run for the longest run of the Jaguars' season, giving them a 22-10 lead. The Jaguars' running game has been critical to their success all season long, and it paid off again Sunday.

title: Jaguars Hit With Worst-Case Scenario at CB Before Week 4's Bout With Bengals
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have announced their inactives for Sunday's Week 4 game against the Cincinnati Bengals, and there is some bad news at cornerback.
The Jaguars have been facing injuries at the cornerback position throughout the week, and now they will officially be without a key piece at the position in Montaric Brown, in addition to backup cornerback Christian Braswell.
In addition to Brown and Braswell, the Jaguars will be without the following players during Sunday's battle against the Bengals: wide receiver CJ Williams, safety Jalen Huskey, linebacker Jack Kiser, offensive lineman Daniel Faalele, and defensive end Wesley Williams. Wesley Williams, Huskey, and Faalele have been healthy scratches in each game this season, while Kiser and CJ Williams have been healthy scratches over the last two weeks.
But considering the challenge the Jaguars have on hand with Ja'Marr Chase, Joe Burrow, and Tee Higgins, missing two of the top-five cornerbacks on the roster is not ideal. The Jaguars were always going to have a tough task with slowing down the Bengals' passing attack on the road, but the injuries only erase the already slim margin for error at the position.
The Jaguars will be set to lean on the trio of Travis Hunter, Jarrian Jones, and Jourdan Lewis, and it would be tough to imagine either Hunter or Jones will be leaving the field very often. The Jaguars did elevate practice squad cornerback Jabbar Muhammad to the active roster Saturday and he could see time on both defense and special teams as a result, but the pressure will be on this room considering the test the Bengals' offense presents.
“Yeah, goldfish mentality, right? That's what it has to be, though. You know he's a potential Hall of Famer," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said earlier this week about facing Chase.
"And so is he going to make some plays, absolutely. It's just, again, so much of this week, similar to last, is it's about our response. It's about the way that we bounce back and the way that we continue to respond, both collectively as a team and then individually throughout the game. It's like, man, all right, he makes a play. Who cares - all right, let's go. It's about the next one."
The Jaguars will kick off against the Bengals at 1 p.m. in Cincinnati, with both squads 2-1 entering the matchup. A win would make the Jaguars 3-1 for the second year in a row for the first time in franchise history.

title: 3 Jaguars Who Must Step Up in Week 4 Against the Bengals: Defense Takes Focus
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars will need to be at their best to take down the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 4, and their best will require some signature performances from key veterans.
So, which Jaguars veterans are potential X-Factors who will need to step up vs. the Bengals in Week 4? We break it down below, taking an important focus on the defense and their big challenge against Ja'Marr Chase, Joe Burrow, Tee Higgins and the rest of the Bengals' passing game.
The Bengals' passing game is of course highlighted by Chase, Burrow and Higgins, but there are other weapons the Jaguars have to be cognizant of. Chase Brown is effective on the ground on shotgun runs and is a passing-game weapon out of the backfield, while the Bengals also like to use tight end Mike Gesicki as a slot receiver for all intents and purposes. This means a lot of passes to the flats and middle of the field, which makes Foyesade Oluokun an important part of the defense's plan.
Oluokun and linebacker Ventrell Miller have had strong starts to the season, but Oluokun is the veteran leader and communicator of the Jaguars. He is tied for No. 2 on the defense in snaps with 138, and he will be on the field more often than not as the Jaguars look to slow down the quick-hitting Bengals offense. He has generated turnovers in games like this one before, and one more would be big.
The Jaguars are facing some injuries at the cornerback position , which means they will need safeties Antonio Johnson and Eric Murray to step up in a big way. Johnson will likely get plenty of reps in the slot against the Bengals' pass-catchers, which means Murray could be the last line of defense against the Bengals' downfield passing attack as the high safety. With big, fast and explosive downfield options in Chase and Higgins, Murray could be key to ensuring the Jaguars limit big plays in the passing game.
Communication will be key for the Jaguars' secondary more this week than any other week this year thus far. Murray will have to take point in that regard and ensure the Jaguars are making the right calls and in the right spots when the Bengals look to attack them downfield and after the catch. With the amount of three-safety sets the Jaguars may play, Murray could be to Caleb Ransaw having a productive outing as well.
The Bengals have a lot of new faces along their defensive line , and this includes on the edge. The Bengals have a talented edge group with Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, and Cashius Howell, and the Jaguars will need a strong performance from offensive tackles Anton Harrison and Cole Van Lanen to ensure the offense slows them down enough for the passing game to keep up with the Bengals' own passing attack.
Harrison had one of the best games of his NFL career in Week 3 against the New England Patriots, though the Bengals offer a different challenge. Mafe is the Bengals' best edge rusher and will be lined up with Harrison more often than not, which means Harrison has a big task entering Sunday's likely offensive shootout.
