title: Titans' Inactives List vs. Ravens is a Massive Relief in Light of Injury News
full_text:
For the first time in the 2026 season, the Tennessee Titans spent all of this past week dealing with injury news. Backs Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears both missed a practice, while guards Fernando Carmona and Jackson Slater each hit the injured reserve list.
Titans fans were bracing for the worst with inactives as a result. Yet, with the list officially being released, Tennessee appears to have caught a massive break ahead of today's road duel with the Baltimore Ravens.
Not only is Spears (who was questionable) active, but so is third-string G Garrett Dellinger. The latter appeared to be the Titans' emergency plan at RG, but entered today questionable with an illness. As of now, he's at least in contention at the position.
Today’s Inactives #TENvsBAL pic.twitter.com/wla4PbcgHb
The Titans' didn't come out completely unscathed, as expected. Tennessee will be without RB Michael Carter, CB Jaylon Jones, G Drew Moss, T Brandon Crenshaw-Dickinson, TE Kylen Granson, and DT Jackie Marshall in Week 4.
Things could still be a whole lot worse for Tennessee, particularly on the offensive line. Dellinger being in play at least guarantees a preferred option will be available at RG. Both Atonio Mafi and Pat Coogan are reportedly warming up as well.
In the backfield, Spears will once again be prepared to head up secondary duties for Tony Pollard. His questionable status last week led him to just three carries, but the backup back was still able to relieve Pollard on passing downs for Tennessee.
If Spears had been out toda y, rookie Nick Singleton was likely in line for a serious game-day upgrade. However, Titans fans will likely have to wait a little longer to get an extended look at the former Penn State Nittany Lion, even if he does check in for complimentary minutes against Baltimore.
Depth on the ground will be especially important if the rain plays a part in Baltimore. The heavier the downpour, the more likely it is that both the Titans and Ravens lean on their rushers. In New York's nasty weather last week, Pollard and Giants RB Cam Skattebo combined for 37 carries.
The line may have taken a hit, but Tennessee will at least enter Week 4 with a fully healthy backfield and an array of options to replace Carmona and Slater. We'll stay tuned today (with fingers crossed) to see who exactly takes over and how it impacts the Titans.

title: Where to Watch and 2 Things to Expect: Titans vs. Ravens in Bittersweet Road Duel
full_text:
Week 4 is upon the NFL season, and the Tennessee Titans are still looking for a victory. Robert Saleh's group has come painfully close two weeks in a row now, consistently battling odds to stay in contests to the bitter end.
As expected, the Baltimore Ravens are widely favored against Tennessee in today's game. For the third week in a row, a Titans win would be deemed an upset by most.
With rainy weather set to take hold for the second straight game and the stakes at a season-high for the winless Titans, here's all the info fans need ahead of showtime. We'll start with where you can tune in.
The Titans duel the Ravels today, Oct. 4, at 12 p.m. CT. You can catch the game on CBS (NewsChannel 5 in Nashville). The game will also be streaming live on NFL+ and Paramount+.
Tennessee is one loss away from the four-defeat streak that kicked off their 2025 season, before the Titans finally eeked out a win on the road in Week 5. Here are two things to expect post-kickoff today.
This was always going to be the Derrick Henry game. It's the star RB's first duel against his former franchise, for which he played eight seasons and rose to the position he's currently in. Bittersweet would be an understatement, but the Titans have to treat this as they would any other battle.
The rain could certainly exasperate this point, but regardless of the weather, Baltimore will call his number. Saleh's defense should be expected to put a heavy focus on bottling Henry up. The New Orleans Saints did just that two weeks ago, and they're the only team to beat the Ravens so far.
Look out for a run-heavy first half and, if things go to plan for Tennessee, a second in which Lamar Jackson is forced to get a little more creative under center. The two-time MVP is difficult to stop in his own right, but the Titans would much rather that their chances through the air than be slowly dealt a loss by way of triple-digit numbers from Henry.
On the opposite side of the ball, we should be able to comfortably anticipate a bit more wheeling and dealing from the Titans' offense. In other words, Tennessee is almost sure to take a few more risks.
This is not to speak for OC Brian Daboll, but how else do you follow a seven-point performance in a loss? Criticism is loud surrounding Cam Ward. Daboll's play-calling clearly hasn't cut it up to now. If the Titans change, things can really only go in one direction: Downfield.
In trying to get out to a faster start and shake the frost from Ward, some of these riskier looks could even come early. The onus here falls on both Ward and Daboll, but neither of them have had as much to prove (in Tennessee) before now as they do in Week 4.
Ward became known in his rookie season for taking, and often connecting on, contested deep shots. He's not a sedentary QB. That has to break through again at some point, and today's matchup with Baltimore is certainly the right circumstance.

title: Predicting Titans’ Starters vs. Ravens in Week 4: Injuries at RG Demand an Answer
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are set to take on the Baltimore Ravens in what will surely be an emotional game. What's worse, at 0-3, the Titans can't let those emotions get in the way of a true must-win game on the road.
The history of the Titans-Ravens rivalry is long and complicated, and this next chapter will be no different as arguably the greatest Tennessee Titan ever, RB Derrick Henry will be facing off against his old team for the first time.
Tennessee will undoubtedly need all 22 to be able to pull off what would be a shocking upset, so let’s go ahead and take a look at who those 22 starters are expected to be. Starting with players unexpected to change:
QB: Cam Ward                                                                                                                                                                                  TE: Gunnar Helm                                                                                                                                                                                         DL: Jeffery Simmons, John Franklin-Myers, Jacob Martin, Jermaine Johnson                                               CBs: Alontae Taylor, Cor’Dale Flott, Marcus Harris (Nickel)                                                                                            Specialists: Joey Slye (kicker), Tommy Townsend (punter), Morgan Cox (long snapper)
Now, the position groups that could see some movement in Week 4.
RB Tyjae Spears is dealing with a shoulder injury and is officially listed as questionable. Head coach Robert Saleh said Spears will have to clear a few hurdles to play, so this one bears watching as we get closer to kickoff. If he can’t go, expect rookie Nick Singleton to see an increased workload in this one.
Ayomanor has sneakily established himself as the third best receiver on this team through three weeks. He hasn’t lit the league on fire by any means, and he’s certainly had some plays he wants back, but he’s starting to flash at a promising rate.
So much so that the second-year wideout was on the field for 48 snaps to Calvin Ridley’s 20 last Sunday. I don’t see any reason why this trend won’t continue for the foreseeable future.
The Titans have been hit with a brutal injury bug at the right guard spot. With Fernando Carmona and Jackson Slater both on injured reserve, the team was forced to promote guard Garrett Dellinger to the active roster in hopes of him providing some relief.
Unfortunately, Dellinger has now popped up on the injury report with an illness and is listed as questionable. Saleh has kept his cards close to the vest all week, but this may be the perfect excuse for them to give the rookie a chance.
Coogan’s natural position is center, so there will likely be some growing pains throughout the game. However, there’s also a higher ceiling with someone like Coogan, so in the end, I think he’s the one who ultimately gets the nod, but it wouldn’t surprise me if they go with Dellinger as long as his health permits.
Last week, Barton out-snapped Gray 44 to 30, but with Saleh emphasizing how they’re going to continue to try and find ways to get the third-year linebacker on the field, I think this is the week we finally get an extended look at the Hill-Gray tandem
Winston didn’t practice on Friday (shoulder) and is listed as questionable, but Saleh didn’t seem overly concerned with it earlier in the week, so I’ll give Winston the benefit of the doubt. If he can’t go, safety Tony Adams will be the next man up.

title: Will Titans' Nick Singleton Finally Get His Time to Shine in Week 4?
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans' backfield is one of the team's most consistent, yet delicate, fixtures. Veteran Tony Pollard leads the way in the final year of his contract; a reliable piece seemingly primed to exit this rebuild right at its peak.
Tyjae Spears would be naturally next in line, as Pollard's multi-year backup. However, Tennessee drafting Nick Singleton ( who Pollard loves ) out of Penn State earlier this year suggested a potential competition for that eventual RB1 takeover. With Spears questionable for Week 4 with an ongoing ankle issue, could tomorrow's matchup against the Ravens be Singleton's time to shine?
You'd certainly think so, but we thought that last week too. Pollard ended up with an uncharacteristic 17 carries vs. the Giants (compared to Spears' three) and Singleton didn't see a single touch. A lot went into that reality, and little to none of it made sense.
Singleton's zero-snap showing came on the heels of his season debut facing off with the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. The rookie back saw four carries in the third quarter, for 10 yards, before being pulled back to the sideline.
Not an outlandish outing, but Robert Saleh still praised Singleton after the game, and foreshadowed his potential to get extended minutes in New York. Nothing has been said since Singleton didn't see the field, and we're back in the same scenario heading into Week 4.
With the rain set to pour once again, you have to think that Singleton will get the nod if Spears can't go. In that case, extra carries may be all the rookie needs to find his footing on the professional level.
Regarding Spears' specific state, Saleh said that the second-hand-man would have to "clear some hurdles" to play in Baltimore. The difference between this week and last is obvious: Spears may not actually take the field this time.
Veteran back Michael Carter was promoted to the Titans' active roster earlier this week. That's a move of depth that would make more sense if Spears can't go. However, Carter certainly isn't projected to contend with Singleton for complimentary minutes.
Saleh has proven that he isn't afraid to play his rookies. Week 4 appears to be the most promising window for Singleton to get significant minutes yet.
With the aforementioned rainy weather expected to play a part in Baltimore, Singleton could go from no touches last week to a serious share this time around. A heavy load for what would be his second regular season game, but exactly the sort of opportunity that could prove his worth.

title: Commanders QB Marcus Mariota Suffers Second MCL Sprain, Expected to Miss Time
full_text:
The Washington Commanders' quarterback room took another hit Sunday in London , and this one could make Jayden Daniels' upcoming practice week even more important. According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , Marcus Mariota suffered an MCL sprain during Washington's loss to the Indianapolis Colts . It's the second MCL sprain Mariota has dealt with this season after suffering the first during the preseason.
Better view here on Marcus Mariota’s right leg. Ouch. Ankle pinned by defender and knee bent inwards. Might get X-Rays to rule out fibula injury. Probably mostly concerned on an MCL injury and/or high ankle. Good thing Jayden Daniels might play Week 5.. https://t.co/FOMDsXsTdL pic.twitter.com/FM9rhFvLol
Mariota left Sunday's game in the first quarter and did not return, forcing rookie Athan Kaliakmanis into action much earlier than anyone expected. The seventh-round pick had some promising moments, including his first NFL touchdown pass, but Washington obviously didn't enter the season expecting him to be one snap away from becoming its starting quarterback. That leaves Washington with a quarterback situation that could get thin quickly. The good news is Daniels was already moving toward the next step in his return before the Commanders left London. Quinn said last week that the plan was to get him through a full week of practice once the team returned, and Mariota’s injury only makes that checkpoint more important. That doesn’t mean Washington should suddenly rush Daniels back because Mariota is hurt. If he’s ready, he’s ready. If he isn’t, Kaliakmanis may be the guy they have to lean on until Mariota can return. Either way, the Commanders entered this week hoping to get a better answer on Daniels. After losing Mariota too, they may need that answer a little more than they expected. title: Washington’s 17-Point London Loss Looks Stranger the Deeper You Go — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders outgained the Indianapolis Colts 317-257, averaging 5.2 yards per play, gaining 88 more passing yards and finishing the game plus-one in turnover differential (two takeaways). Now, if you stopped right there and didn't read a single thing further, you'd think Washington won, not lost by 17 points , as those numbers are not something normally associated with losing a game. To understand the loss, you have to go back over the painful ordeal, starting with Odafe Oweh forcing and recovering Daniel Jones' fumble on the Colts' opening possession. Washington took over on the Colts' 21-yard line and gained just eight yards before sending Drew Stevens out for a 31-yard field goal. On the very next Commanders possession, they drove 70 yards to the Indianapolis 5-yard line before Mariota was sacked, and the drive ended on another Stevens FG. Literally, the first quarter closed with Indy having only 20 yards in total offense. Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said , "I loved the way the defense started, creating some takeaways, but to only get field goals out of those, I thought those were ones that we needed to nail." Three categories tell the tale of the tape in this game: third downs, fourth downs, and red zone efficiency. Washington was 2-of-15 on third downs (13.3%), while the Colts were 5-of-16 (31.3%). On fourth downs, the Commanders were 1-of-4, and the Colts were 1-of-1; in the red zone, Washington was 0-for-2, and Indianapolis was 3-of-3. One of the day's oddest numbers: Washington had only 12 first downs despite gaining 317 yards; in short, they generated chunks of offense without sustaining enough drives to finish them. The penalty situation told an odd story in this game: Washington had 10 accepted penalties for 84 yards, while Indianapolis had only one for five yards. Amik Robertson's penalty was ticky-tacky at best, and allowed a drive that produced a Jonathan Taylor touchdown to continue. Quinn after the game: "I thought between the penalties and not converting on some touchdowns on the takeaways, those were two big parts of the game." If one play wrapped the whole afternoon into a nice little package, it came late in the third quarter. Trailing 20-13 and facing third-and-11 from their own 13-yard line, Athan Kaliakmanis connected with Antonio Williams for what appeared to be an 87-yard touchdown that would have put Washington an extra point away from tying the game. Instead, an illegal shift wiped the play off the board. An offensive holding penalty was declined; Washington backed up to third-and-16, Kaliakmanis scrambled for eight yards, and Tress Way came out to punt. Now, no one is saying here that, by rule, this may be an infraction; the timing of both flags coming out was odd if you follow the refs, and this doesn't get called every time it's done in the league (the holding was a complete phantom call, it never happened).
Here’s the play where #Commanders WR Antonio Williams’ 87 yard TD was nullified by two penalties: Illegal shift & Offensive Holding on Dyami Brown pic.twitter.com/LRYOfqokcP
That's how you end up looking at a box score Monday morning, wondering how any of this adds up . The Commanders created explosive plays, moved the ball better than Indianapolis in stretches, and did enough defensively to give the offense extra opportunities. What they couldn't do was stay out of their own way long enough for any of it to matter. The staff didn't help much, as the team seemed unprepared at times and also decimated by injuries at other times . Indianapolis didn't need to dominate Washington between the 20s. They simply won when the field got shorter, and the downs became more important. The Colts scored touchdowns on all three red-zone possessions, while the Commanders failed to score a touchdown on either of theirs, failed on three of four fourth-down attempts, and spent too much of the afternoon trying to overcome their own mistakes. Washington gained 317 yards Sunday, but yards were never really the problem. Turning them into points was, and that’s how a game the Commanders statistically had every reason to win ended with a 17-point difference on the scoreboard. title: Commanders Report Card: Who Deserves the Blame for London Collapse?
full_text:
For a few days, an optimistic future for the Washington Commanders was finally easy to envision.
All that stood in the way of their return to .500 was the Indianapolis Colts in a London-hosted Week 4 matchup. After a wave of season-opening injuries crested with Jayden Daniels' prior elbow dislocation , longtime backup quarterback Marcus Mariota and his reawakened defense had inspired hope that Washington's supporting cast could hold the line until his impending return.
No such luck followed the Commanders' trip overseas. Anyone who checks a game score online can guess as much, with a 30-13 defeat doing little to convince anyone that the remaining group fought to the bitter end in their fall to 1-3. The Colts, the injury bug, and yet another week of questionable coordination stymied the team's potential resurgence, leaving few position groups limping out of the breakdown unscathed.
The combination of what Mariota provided before exiting early in the first half and third-string understudy Athan Kaliakmanis' debut left very few meaningful takeaways for fans to analyze. Mariota fit in as smoothly as ever in the Commanders' offense before his knee injury, while Kaliakmanis looked like a seventh-round rookie who'd yet to be tested from behind his spotty offensive line.
That is to say, he still warranted that recent draft selection with some obvious throwing talent. He isn't the most accurate deep-ball slinger, but he's certainly less afraid to give his sprinting receivers a chance than your average deep-cut rookie. The few connections he made on 30+ yard tosses were the kind to make anyone stand up, with one particular beauty to Treylon Burks earning him his first professional touchdown credit.
Athan Kaliakmanis goes DEEP for a beauty of a touchdown! @INDvsWAS on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/JXB6CmxI9w
If nothing else, he'll be a fascinating developmental watch as the season trudges on, though his lack of play-extending legs makes him a tougher fit in a pocket known to give up pressure. In the meantime, the Commanders may find it tough not to reconsider Daniels' return timetable following his predictably raw entrance.
Rachaad White getting ruled out earlier in the week certainly hurt the remaining backs' odds of flourishing, but the Commanders' rushing leaders on the afternoon should clarify just how much Bill Croskey-Merritt has disappointed as the lead option on the ground. He was outgained by Mariota, who played for less than one quarter; Kaliakmanis, who'll only use his legs if he has the chance to deploy the earliest open-field spin move imaginable; and, most strangely of all Austin Ekeler , the familiar Commanders player who was still on the couch this time last week.
As fun as Croskey-Merritt's dashes off of short catches were, 15 rushing yards on nine carries just doesn't scream efficiency, especially with Ekeler looking as smooth as he did. This wasn't the ideal setting to fully judge the Commanders' run game, with the coaching staff trying to figure out how to set Kaliakmanis up for success in real time, though it's clear that White will be welcomed back with open arms as a versatile Daniels battery mate.
This position group may as well get an "Incomplete" grade. They were even more hampered without Mariota in the game, and while the backs had to trek on without their RB2, Terry McLaurin had to watch this one from the sidelines, too.
That effectively removed much of the threat the receivers had of stunning the Colts, given their sudden dependency on a rookie decision-maker, though Stefon Diggs and company did their best to meet Kaliakmanis on his long-range prayers (even if Diggs himself ended up getting outmatched by a pair of reserves in Burks and Dyami Brown). There was some solid role-playing, though little game-changing playmaking when most of the platoon wideouts were called upon.
This was an especially disappointing outing for the tight end room, especially now that starting option Chig Okonkwo has returned to Washington's starting lineup. He only recorded five yards on two receptions, not nearly enough to make up for his positional peers.
John Bates wasn't up to his usual excellent blocking standards within a scheme that's especially needy for playmakers, and that's not to mention the still-silent Ben Sinnott. Kaliakmanis could really benefit from a big target to get open in the flat with a simple move or two, and he's clearly still without that jumbo pass-catcher as things currently stand.
The Commanders' blocking rotation is a disaster. Even if they were fully stocked with their best blockers, Laremy Tunsil and Sam Cosmi, they'd still be lugging several subpar starters on their roster.
For one, they couldn't do much to keep Mariota safe from Indianapolis' sack threats; in a sick reflection of the poor blocking that once plagued Daniels' pocket, more shoddy guard depth haunted the quarterback room yet again. Nick Allegretti was nowhere to be found- the previously starting center seemed to have been demoted once again after a brief foray at right guard, completely superseded by the likes of Matt Gulbin and Lucas Patrick.
For those asking Nick Allegretti wasn't on the injury report all week. He's healthy, just not playing.
Injuries are one thing, but the Commanders' front office absolutely has to locate some alternatives if their previously envisioned lead center can't make it a month before hitting the pine.
The defense gave it all they had, playing with enough tenacity to disrupt Daniel Jones' passing attack during the game's early going. Odafe Oweh recorded a sack and a fumble recovery early on; the Colts' attempts at screen catches were repeatedly halted, and Frankie Luvu's presence was felt.
Odafe Oweh pushes the tackle into Jones and causes a sack and fumble. Washington's ball. #RaiseHal pic.twitter.com/tLAPSwQMN1
They didn't let go of the rope so much as they ran out of the necessary stamina to hold their grip on the game, soon succumbing to their quick 6-0 lead once the Mariota-less offense stalled. Even when Kaliakmanis was able to occasionally troop down the field for a moment of relief, these guys never seemed to get a break before eventually collapsing as Indianapolis outscored Washington 30-7 the rest of the way.
The league leader in aerial touchdowns allowed heading into Week 4 didn't relent a single strike to Jones and any of his pass-catchers, a big step in the right direction as the Commanders look to figure it out without the currently injured Trey Amos and the relegated Mike Sainristil .
Amik Robertson and Rasul Douglas were everywhere, sprinting down from deeper coverage into the action without Nick Cross to help. Together they recorded 15 tackles, and Douglas got his first interception of the season on an errant Jones idea .
They're doing as good a job of persisting past occasional injury scares as anyone, and it's shown with a cohesiveness that's only improved as the young season has progressed. Even if such a defeat shouldn't leave anyone feeling great, the defensive backs can walk away from this one with their heads up.
Another week of ho-hum play from the special teams. Tress Way continues to punt about as well as anyone could ask, while Drew Stevens enjoyed a perfect 3/3 outing on field goals and extra points, though the return team still raises an occasional eyebrow at the play.
Jaylin Lane had to be carted off the field after an ankle injury during the game's second half. Another area in which the coaching staff will have to improvise.
Dan Quinn and his merry band of signal-callers deserve a little grace for the situation they fell into, with Kaliakmanis lacking the mobility they're used to with Daniels and Mariota, making for a tougher on-the-fly fit, though he could have been utilized better considering his lack of experience. Going for it on a fourth-and-one with fringe running back Craig Reynolds, surrendering the ball on downs and allowing the Colts to commence their scoring wave,…

title: Everything Dan Quinn Said After Commanders’ Loss to Colts in London
full_text: The Washington Commanders’ trip to London didn’t go the way they hoped, and the loss came with even more injury concerns. Dan Quinn spoke afterward about Marcus Mariota, Jayden Daniels , the costly penalties and where Washington goes from here. Opening statement “I’ll get rolling with some updates on some injuries. Talk about Marcus. I was just gutted for him. I thought he really started off strong. Long run, playing well, and I thought he had an excellent week of practice leading up. The team thinks it’s an MCL injury, and when we get the scan tomorrow, we’ll have further knowledge of what we’re dealing with and length and all those. Charles Omenihu hurt his groin again. Same thing. We’ll find out more tomorrow as we’re going. Jaylin Lane had a serious ankle injury. The hope is that he’s flying back tonight, but I’ll get a better update with you as well when we get back home into that. Then past that, I thought AK came in after 12 plays. It’s not the ideal space to begin it, but I thought he also showed a lot of confidence, some fearlessness with that, and made some of the throws to highlight why he is where he is. As far as a full team, I didn’t think we did enough around him into that spot. I loved the way the defense started, creating some takeaways, but to only get field goals out of those, I thought those were ones that we needed to nail. Our team is really tough, and I told them tonight, man, we are the ones that are built for this type of adversity. We’re back to a division game, and we’re going to do all we can to get ourselves ready. We’ve got a 70-man roster, and we’ll lean into that as we find out more about some of the guys on injuries and also some returning from injuries.” How much does it change things with Marcus going out, and how much did the Colts change things after that? “Yeah, it’s a significant change because you don’t do quite the same. I thought he was off to an excellent start. But it’s a factor for sure, when there’s less things that you have to deal with offensively. So, it was a factor.” And then Terry, what happened? How did he get hurt on Friday, and how does that impact everything? “Yeah, he was injured Friday, and we wanted to give him every chance to see if he’d have a shot, and it was best to hold him out. He desperately wanted to go. I should have a good update of where we’re at as we get into some work with him into Wednesday, but it was just the best play to hold him out, John. It was during Friday, and we just said, okay, let’s see what the next day looks like and then into the next day, and it just made the most sense to hold him.” What went into the decision to start Matt? “I think we want to just keep competing where we’re at at the O-line spot, finding the five with Sam being out. We liked some of the things that we saw with Lucas, and we’ve liked some of the things we’ve seen in practice with Matt. We thought, okay, let’s put him into the space as well. Nick got a little bit banged up at the end of last week, and he was going to be limited at the start. So we thought this was the best chance for this week of where we’d go. That’s all it was.” Not necessarily a longer-term move? “No, I don’t see it that way. And we’re hopeful Sam’s turning quickly, too. So if that’s the case, we see Matt center first, but inside when you’re not starting, you’re playing two spots. And we thought that gave us the best space heading into the game.” What did you make of the penalties, and how do you guys continue to clean those up? “Yeah, and you probably saw me upset with that. There’s as much of that just the entire day, 10 to one to go. Whether it’s points off the board or once the hit on — we certainly got plenty of work to do. I’d like to look at them and see. But I thought between the penalties and not converting on some touchdowns on the takeaways, those were two big parts of the game.” Despite all that, Antonio gets the 87-yard play. It looks like it’s going to be the tying score and then there’s the penalty. How disheartening was that? “It was hard. At the time, I didn’t see what or who for the illegal shift. But I think it’s indicative of the two of them. Antonio’s got it, and so to be outside and rip the ball to him, that was a big play. I like the way he’s developing, Ben, at receiver and making some plays. But definitely it was deflating for sure, and those are difficult to overcome because points were difficult to come by. So when you get a big, long one, that’s what we needed to get done, and so it definitely was tough.” Do you anticipate looking at a veteran quarterback, or is there optimism Jayden could possibly come back? “That’s the hope for sure for us, for Jayden coming back. He’ll have a full week of practice beginning Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. That’s the goal, Ben, that he could get into that space. And once we see where Marcus is, that part too, we’ll have a better understanding. But that’s the goal for Jayden, to throw a full-on week. He was able to do some limited this week, and this week would be the plan for him to do all the reps.” Can you take us through the fourth-down decision? “Sure. In that spot, different parts of the field, JP, it’s okay, we’d be a go from two or a go from one. So we had one that we thought had good design for that time where we shifted people in to go. In that instance, man, we’ve got to get the space to create it. It was less than one. When you go for it, there’s risk involved. We thought this one was the best plan to go after it at that distance. So with different ones, you punt or go, but that one we thought, hey man, this gave us the best spot to go for it.” And Reynolds was the back on that play. Was that by design or did that just happen? “It was by happenstance. We did an on-the-ball shift, so it was more by happenstance. We didn’t full sub. It was a specific package that we had worked on.” How does the risk on that play factor in when it’s not Jayden or Marcus at quarterback, but it’s AK, and the field position might be better? “Yeah, I get what you’re saying, Ben. For sure, I thought we were off to a good start defensively, but I also have a lot of confidence that inside a yard like that we’ll get the down. So that part, I don’t want to overthink it just based on the result.” Did the referees explain why they rescinded the pass interference? “They said that another official had a view that it wasn’t. I’m looking forward to watching it, but that was their reasoning: that a deep judge had a different view that said, ‘Hey, it wasn’t a foul.’ In that spot, it’s not something to challenge. You kind of have to just take it and move it on.” With Jayden potentially getting back out there, that would be a huge lift for the offense as a whole. But around him, how do you think the offense is supporting him as he comes back?" “I thought Jayden, at the start of the Dallas game, was exceptional because he’s on the move. So the second play with him is critical, where he can get outside the pocket, and he ripped a bunch of throws in that space. For us, having the run game is going to be a big deal. Hopefully Sam’s on his way back, too. So when you’re putting those two together, to me that’s the sweet spot, where you can balance both of them together. We don’t want to make it where he’s a drop-back player, and they do all your magic on every time. So the run, the run action, certainly owning the ball is a big piece of it. Jayden’s exceptional at that in terms of the location, where to go. That’s always been his case. So that’ll be a big piece to it, too.” If you have a call you don’t agree with, what is the process for documenting that and talking to officials about it? Do you do it right after the game? “No. We collect them, and then we send them in Tuesday by a certain time, and then we get responses back. So it’s the same process for everyone. It’s probably good you’re not on Monday, so it’s the next day. You’re limited to a certain number. More often than not, I want the…

title: 5 Winners, 7 Losers From the Commanders’ 30-13 Loss to the Colts
full_text:
The Washington Commanders had plenty go wrong in London on Sunday, which is usually pretty obvious when you lose a football game by 17 points. What makes this one a little harder to explain is that Washington actually outgained the Indianapolis Colts 317-257 and won the turnover battle 2-1. The Commanders had chances to make this a completely different game, especially early, but penalties, missed opportunities, and an offense that couldn't finish drives eventually caught up with them in a 30-13 loss . There were still a few individual performances worth taking away from it.
Odafe Oweh It didn't take long for Oweh to make his presence felt. On Indianapolis' second offensive play, Oweh got to Daniel Jones for an eight-yard sack , knocked the ball loose, and recovered it himself at the Colts' 21-yard line. That's about as much as you can ask one defensive player to do on a single snap. Oweh finished with a sack, a tackle for loss, a quarterback hit, a forced fumble and a recovery. Washington only came away with three points after he handed the offense a short field, but that's certainly not on him. Javon Kinlaw Kinlaw's final stat line isn't going to jump off the page, but this was another one of those games where watching him told you more than the three tackles did. The big number here is two passes defended, which isn't something you normally see from an interior defensive lineman. Kinlaw got his hand on Jones' first pass of the afternoon and later broke up another throw intended for Josh Downs in the third quarter. He was disruptive, and for a defensive front that spent a good portion of the afternoon making Jones uncomfortable, Kinlaw was a big part of it. Amik Robertson Robertson wasn't perfect , and his unnecessary roughness penalty in the second quarter was costly, even if it was ticky-tacky and shouldn't have been called. Instead of Indianapolis facing a fourth down, the Colts got a fresh set of downs and eventually scored their first touchdown of the game. Outside of that, though, Robertson was everywhere. He led Washington with nine tackles and added a pass breakup while once again playing with the type of fight we've seen from him since the season started. He even left briefly after getting banged up and returned to the game. One thing is becoming pretty clear with Robertson: he's going to keep competing no matter what is happening around him. Rasul Douglas Douglas gave Washington its second takeaway of the afternoon when he intercepted Jones in the second quarter with the Commanders still leading 6-0. He finished with six tackles and a pass breakup to go along with the interception, and once again put the offense in position to do something with an extra possession. Washington went four-and-out instead. Douglas did his part. Treylon Burks This one doesn't need much explaining. Burks caught one pass all afternoon, but it went for 47 yards and Washington's only touchdown. The score came immediately after Indianapolis had stretched its lead to 17-6 and gave the Commanders some life again at 17-13. One catch. One big one.
Former Rutgers Football QB Athan Kaliakmanis first NFL touchdown  is a 47-yard bomb to Treylon Burks 🥹 👉 https://t.co/D8itI4EQhX pic.twitter.com/dl75pWLzmb
Penalties PENALTIES!!! Washington finished with 10 of them for 84 yards. Indianapolis had one for five. That alone is ugly enough, but it was when some of Washington's penalties happened that really hurt. Robertson's unnecessary roughness helped keep a Colts touchdown drive alive. An illegal shift penalty erased what would have been an 87-yard touchdown to Antonio Williams in the third quarter, and Stefon Diggs later had a 21-yard reception wiped away by offensive pass interference. You won't beat many teams doing that to yourself. Of course, trying to explain to me that the Colts committed only one penalty in a sixty-minute game makes me curious how we got there . Turning the film back on for a re-watch, I see several non-calls, and it's odd that the referees seem to have swallowed their whistles in certain situations.
Commanders LT Brandon Coleman on the penalties: "I mean, we say the same thing every week, like, we gotta fix it. But it's just bullshit. There’s stuff that we know we gotta do and there’s stuff that we gotta fix. I hate to say it, but, like, you always say that shit. Like, we…
Situational Offense Washington moved the ball enough to make this game interesting. What it couldn't do was finish anything. The Commanders went 2-of-15 on third down, 1-of-4 on fourth down and didn't score a touchdown on either of their two trips into the red zone. Indianapolis, meanwhile, went 3-for-3 once it got inside Washington's 20. That's a pretty simple explanation for how one team can finish with more yards and still lose by 17. Turning Takeaways Into Points Washington's defense gave the offense two chances to put Indianapolis in a hole early. Oweh's forced fumble and recovery gave the Commanders the ball at the Colts' 21. They got three points. Douglas' interception gave them another possession while leading 6-0, and it ended with Washington stuffed on fourth-and-one. Two takeaways. Three points. Last week against Seattle, Washington showed exactly how much turnovers can change a game when you actually make the other team pay for them. This week was the opposite. Running Game Washington officially finished with 100 rushing yards, but that number needs some context. Marcus Mariota had 35 of them on one run before leaving the game, and Kaliakmanis added another 16. Washington's running backs combined for just 49 yards on 18 carries, with Jacory Croskey-Merritt held to 15 yards on nine attempts. Austin Ekeler had 29 yards on four carries, but outside of him there just wasn't much happening on the ground. Pass Protection The Colts only finished with two sacks, which makes this look better on paper than it actually was. Indianapolis was credited with 11 quarterback hits, and Kaliakmanis took his share of punishment after suddenly being thrown into his first NFL action. Mariota's knee injury also came on a sack in the first quarter. That's far too much heat on any quarterback, much less a rookie who wasn't expecting to play. Injuries As if Washington didn't already have enough of these. Mariota left with a knee injury and didn't return. Charles Omenihu was ruled out with a groin injury, and Jaylin Lane had to be carted off after suffering a lower-leg injury on a kickoff return. The Commanders entered the game already without Daniels, McLaurin, Rachaad White, Sam Cosmi, and Nick Cross. Losing 30-13 was bad enough. What Washington's injury report looks like after returning from London could hurt even more. Matt Gulbin Gulbin got the start at right guard with Sam Cosmi out, and this wasn't the kind of opportunity he wanted to put on tape. It's not fair to pin all of Washington's problems up front on one guy, but the Colts finished with 11 quarterback hits, while the Commanders' running backs managed just 49 yards on 18 carries. Gulbin was part of an offensive line that never let Washington get comfortable, especially after Athan Kaliakmanis was forced into the game. By the end of the afternoon, Washington still had plenty of questions about how well the offensive line can hold up without Cosmi. title: Commanders Game Pulse: Washington Falls Apart in 30-13 Loss to Colts
full_text:
The Washington Commanders are in London , looking to build on last week's win over the Seattle Seahawks and get back to .500 against the Indianapolis Colts . Marcus Mariota will make his second straight start with Jayden Daniels sidelined , but Washington will also be without Terry McLaurin , Rachaad White, Sam Cosmi, and Nick Cross. The good news is that Frankie Luvu and Chig Okonkwo are back after missing the last two games. Commanders Game Pulse will track the action throughout the morning, with a full check-in after each quarter. You can also catch the full game feed at the bottom of this page, including play-by-play updates and social posts during the game. Commanders Game Pulse tracked the biggest developments throughout Washington's loss, with a check-in after every quarter.
- The most interesting and telling stat in this entire game is the penalties. Washington had 10 penalties for 84 yards, and the Colts had one for five yards. Now, even if you live in a world where you believe the Colts committed one penalty, then I advise you to rewatch this game closely because you are wrong. - Athan Kaliakmanis had some good and some bad in his NFL debut. It's still wild to me that his first NFL touchdown pass came against Sauce Gardner; that might be a trivia question one day. - Washington falls to 1-3; more importantly, they'll leave London with way more injury questions than when they arrived. A big takeaway for me was the Commanders' inability to do what they did well in Week 3: get takeaways and turn them into points, as the team essentially left 11 points on the field after only a field goal.
- Washington was able to creep back into this one with a big throw from Athan Kaliakmanis to Treylon Burks for a touchdown over Sauce Gardner. Kaliakmanis also connected with Dyami Brown for 48 yards on Gardner. - Jaylin Lane showed guts most of the morning, taking some serious hits on returns until he was injured on one. The cart had to come out after he had what appeared to be an ankle/lower leg injury. - The Colts' offense is finally starting to click, and they're finding Tyler Warren more. Washington must find a way to get between him and the football. - Amik Robertson had a great series of plays in the third quarter. One thing is for sure with this guy: he will keep fighting no matter what...what more can you ask for. - PENALTIES!!!
- The big story here is Kaliakmanis having to come into the game. He's taken a lot of hits on his way to going 6-of-12 for 33 yards. He had one nice deep ball to Antonio Williams that nearly went for a big play, but it sailed just a little long. - Washington has put tons of pressure on Daniel Jones, and he's looked rattled since the start, turning it over twice. Washington needs to work on consistently getting points off those takeaways. - The Colts have all but killed Washington's run game except for a 35-yard run by Mariota and a ten-yard run by Austin Ekeler; otherwise, they've rushed it 11 times for 17 yards.
- Marcus Mariota looked good in the first quarter, going 3-of-4 with 46 yards passing and one carry for 35 yards, until leaving with a knee injury. Rookie Athan Kaliakmanis was forced into his first NFL action. - Washington's defense has done its job holding the Colts to 20 yards of total offense in the first quarter and keeping Colts QB Daniel Jones uncomfortable. Jones has already fumbled once. - Washington has had two good shots at the end zone but settled for field goals both times.
Here’s the play that Marcus Mariota got hurt on. He’s now headed to the locker room. pic.twitter.com/DszMaJu5mq
- The Commanders will once again be playing without Jayden Daniels as Marcus Mariota gets his second straight start since Daniels injured his non-throwing elbow. This week, the team will also be without star receiver Terry McLaurin (hamstring) and running back Rachaad White (shoulder). - Getting linebacker Frankie Luvu and tight end Chig Okonkwo back is huge for Washington after both missed the last two games. - The Colts will be without receivers Darius Slayton and Keenan Allen, but still have running back Jonathan Taylor, who only needs 78 rushing yards to become the NFL's all-time leading rusher in international games. - Washington has allowed only 82 rushing yards per game through three weeks. If that part of the defense shows up in London, they'll have a chance to make Taylor wait for the record and give Mariota's offense a much easier afternoon.

title: Commanders Inactives: Terry McLaurin Joins Jayden Daniels on Sideline vs. Colts
full_text:
The Washington Commanders will face the Indianapolis Colts Sunday morning in London, looking to build on last week's win over the Seattle Seahawks and get back to .500. Washington already knew they would be shorthanded against the Colts in London, but Sunday's inactive list made things even tougher. Wide receiver Terry McLaurin is officially inactive after being listed as questionable with a hamstring injury that popped up late in the week . He joins quarterback Jayden Daniels, running back Rachaad White , guard Sam Cosmi, and safety Nick Cross , who had already been ruled out before game day. Here is the full list of Commanders inactives:

title: Jonathan Taylor Is 78 Yards From NFL History — Commanders Can Stop Him
full_text:
If the Washington Commanders didn't already have enough to worry about with Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor on Sunday in London, here's more. Taylor needs just 78 rushing yards to pass Travis Etienne Jr. and become the all-time leading NFL rusher in international games. He'll enter the Washington game with 258 rushing yards on 66 carries through three games, averaging 3.9 yards per carry, with four rushing touchdowns. Taylor put himself in a position to break the record by rushing for 244 yards against the Atlanta Falcons in Berlin, Germany, last season. He finished that game with 286 yards from scrimmage, according to NFL Research; both were single-game international records.
JONATHAN TAYLOR 83-YARD TD RUN 😱🔥 O.M.G. 🤯 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/JS2Tfg28bN
This is where the rubber meets the road as the Commanders enter this game having allowed only 246 rushing yards through three games , which is the third-fewest in the NFL. The team allows only 82 rushing yards a game with a 25% run-stuff rate that leads the league. For everything Washington's defense has struggled with, stopping the run hasn't been one of those things, although Taylor needs four fewer yards than the team gives up per game, so this might be hard to prevent. On another note, Taylor hasn't exactly been lighting things on fire this year . He has yet to rush for 100 yards in a game, and he's coming off a season-low 68-yard performance against Houston. But 78 yards is very attainable, meaning Washington definitely has its work cut out for it to keep him away from the record. Which, to be clear, the Commanders probably don't know or care much about, as they're focused on getting the win and containing Taylor. They'd just rather not be the team that gives him his first 100-yard rushing day of the season in the process. The Colts could lean on Taylor even more, especially with their receiver room dealing with injuries. He only needs 78 yards to leave London with another NFL record. If Washington's run defense looks anything like it has through three weeks, the Commanders have a legitimate chance to make him wait. If they can keep him below that number, there's a good chance they also did their job against one of the biggest parts of the Colts' offense. title: Commanders-Colts London Weather Forecast Has One Twist Before Kickoff
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have already had to deal with plenty of things outside the norm this week as they prepare to face the Indianapolis Colts in London on Sunday. There was the long flight across the pond, a five-hour time difference from the East Coast, and now a 9:30 a.m. ET kickoff for everyone watching back home. As if that wasn't enough, anyone waking up early in London Sunday morning could also be greeted by fog around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Fortunately, that part of the forecast doesn't look like it will hang around long. According to the Met Office forecast for the area around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, mist and fog are expected through the early morning hours before conditions begin clearing around 8 a.m. Sunny intervals are expected by 9 a.m., with sunshine taking over beginning around 10 and continuing through the afternoon. That timing is obviously important, considering Washington and Indianapolis aren't scheduled to kick off until 2:30 p.m. local time.
By the time the Commanders actually take the field, what started as a foggy London morning should look completely different. The Met Office currently has the temperature at around 20 degrees Celsius at 2 p.m., or roughly 68 degrees Fahrenheit, before climbing to about 70 degrees by 3. Sunday's high is expected to reach around 72 degrees. There is also less than a five percent chance of precipitation throughout the day. The wind shouldn't be much of an issue either. Around kickoff, sustained winds are expected to sit at roughly three miles per hour, with gusts around 13. That's enough to remind you the game is still being played outside, but nowhere near the type of conditions that should force either offense to change what it wants to do. Even with the early fog and mist, field conditions shouldn't become much of an issue either, as Tottenham Hotspur Stadium uses a dedicated artificial surface for NFL games rather than the retractable grass pitch used by Tottenham. For Marcus Mariota , that means he shouldn't have to worry about throwing a wet football or dealing with heavy winds in his second straight start in place of the injured Jayden Daniels . It also shouldn't create much of a problem for Drew Stevens if Dan Quinn has to send his kicker onto the field in an important spot. Of course, Indianapolis gets the same advantage.
Weather forecasts can always change, especially overnight, but right now there isn't much in the forecast that should become a major factor in Sunday's game. The early fog is certainly something worth watching, especially for anyone heading toward Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in the morning, but it is expected to clear several hours before kickoff. After that, Washington is looking at mild temperatures, sunshine, almost no chance of rain, and very little wind. Considering everything else the Commanders have had to adjust to this week, they'll take it. The trip to London has already given Washington enough things outside the norm to deal with. As of Saturday night, the weather doesn't look like it's going to add another one. title: 10 Commanders Quotes That Define Washington Entering Week 4 vs. Colts
full_text:
The Washington Commanders finally got a win last week , but now the challenge shifts overseas . With Marcus Mariota getting another start, Jayden Daniels getting closer to a return , and the Colts waiting in London , here are 10 quotes that help define where Washington stands entering Week 4.
Question: “Daronte, how encouraged have you been with the rush through three games, and what kind of challenge does Jonathan Taylor specifically present ?” "Well, Jonathan is unique in his own way . He also has game-breaking speed. He’s physical, he comes downhill in a hurry, and so we’ll love the challenge this week. To answer your first question in terms of how we’ve been so far, been pleased with our ability to be dialed in as much as we can, and having some awareness of the run-gap integrity and setting edges. And so we want to continue to try to improve on that as best as we can and not give any creases or any daylight opportunities best we can."
Question: “You mentioned a couple of times overall with the secondary that you want to see that improvement. What do you think are some of the specific areas that you need to get better at?” “Keeping the chunks off the tape.”
Question: On his tight-window throws to Terry McLaurin and giving a receiver an opportunity. "Well, with Terry, those 50/50 contested are more, 80/90 for us. And he's done it constantly through his career. I think he's arguably one of the best contested receivers in the NFL. And I know if I just give him a chance, he's gonna come down with it more times than not. But a lot of credit is due to him. To create separation, he has to find different edges, create advantages, and he constantly finds that little bit of separation. And so, there's a lot of trust that goes into it. Terry's the ultimate pro. He's always asking questions about how I'm seeing things, where he can be better in his routes. And for a quarterback, that just makes you feel very, very comfortable when you throw him ball. And the more that we can continue to build that, he's always gonna be there for us."
Question: “Beyond the results on Sunday, what identity do you want to establish in London?” "Our identity is important for us in terms of our play style and how we want to play. In last week’s game for us, we thought it was the best complementary football, meaning all three phases set one another up. A defensive interception and takeaway resulted in offensive points. A punt that could pin somebody back created field position. And so for us, that is who we are, feeding off one another. And that way all three phases are a part of the success, and that shared success is what we’re looking for."
Question: “DQ shared with us yesterday that he believes being clutch is something that can be conditioned and trained and learned. What’s something that you can do from your experiences to help, whether it’s a quarterback or just another player on the offense, turn on that clutch ability when the game is on the line?” "From my lens at least, we talk a lot about calm is contagious, right? So if I can be calm in those moments for those guys and just walk out and give Marcus an opportunity to talk through an old play or something, he’ll just go and take it and run with it, man. It’s just like we talked about — those guys bring it to life. And we’ve repped all these situations out on the practice field, and that’s where the confidence comes from, where, hey, when you get it, whether it’s a two-minute at the end of the half or a four-minute, go execute. They’re ready to roll."
Question: “Coach, one more on Sonny. I know you talked about not wanting to have to speed up his growth if you don’t have to. Where is his growth now compared to where you hoped it would be before you got to see him in a regular-season game?” He’s probably a little ahead of schedule, if I’m being honest with you. He’s ahead of schedule, which is not really surprising based off of if you got to know him in the offseason in terms of just the draft process, and you kind of see how cerebral he is and how serious he is, how mature he is in terms of how he takes the craft. A lot of young guys, they don’t honor the craft until three years in, which he came in-again, his professionalism or working to be a professional is why you see the learning curve shortening a little bit. And so you just have to stay the course. Don’t read the news clippings and just keep pressing forward.
Question: “Is anything in the back of your head in terms of falling awkwardly, getting hit on the elbow, concerns about getting reinjured?” "No, that’s what the brace is for. So if I had those concerns, then I would have got surgery."
Question: On conversations he’s had with Jayden Daniels about the return-to-play process. "Well, I think we have a great team. Whether it's the medical staff, whether it's his own staff as well. Like they're gonna make a collective decision that is best for Jayden and we are gonna support that. And at the end of the day, I think if he's out there and he can play, he should play. This is his team. And the more that we can help support that and give him all the tools that he needs to be successful, that's what our roles are. So, for what it's worth, I think at the end of the day, he's gonna make a decision that best fit for the entire organization and we're gonna support that."
Question: On proving to the world he can still play at a high level. "I think at the end of the day, like I've always had a belief in myself. So that prove it has never really crossed my mind. I just wanna be able to help these guys out and find ways to win. And if that means me playing well, great. If that means me managing the game and making sure that we're eating up clock, I'm taking care of the football, like I'll do whatever it takes to win. And I'm at that point in my career where that really is all that matters. So, I'm not here to prove anything . I really have just believed in myself all this time and the more that I can just help these guys out and win games, that's what's most important."
Opening statement: "As far as Jayden, he had a great week. It was awesome to have him back on the field in a limited fashion. He’ll be out Sunday. Marcus will start. That’s a huge positive step for us and for him. We’ll assess where we are next week when he gets a full week of practice all the way through. But it’s typical of him working incredibly hard to get back, doing everything that he can behind the scenes to go do that as fast as he can. So he is a true competitor on and off the field." Question: “How close was Jayden to possibly being an option for this week?” "Certainly anytime you can practice, that’s a big deal. And so for him to get back, that was a big step for us, John, to see what it looked like and where it would go. Typical for him, he’s more ready than you expect. So that’s just kind of how he is. But we’ll get the whole week for him and get back at it. Get his elbow, his body, everything back right. But it was really impressive to see it."
Washington showed against Seattle what can happen when all three phases work together. Now the Commanders get another chance to build on it, this time in London against a Colts team that presents a different set of problems.
